In the event that an irrational number $\alpha$ is sufficiently densely packed (i.e., its continued fraction expansion meets a specific requirement), it has been demonstrated that, as the sequence of integers $q$ progresses infinitely, the associated horizontal line segments in the upper half-plane of the mod $2$ modular surface undergo an even more equitable distribution, at a rate proportional to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{q}}$. This new distribution outcome coincides with the most accelerated speed at which lines can become evenly spaced throughout the real line. Furthermore, researchers have discovered that a related scenario involving sequences of irrational translations in the upper half-plane of the mod $3$, $4$, $5$, or $7$ modular surface each exhibit the most accelerated speed of equidistribution, at a rate proportional to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{q}}$. This new distribution outcome is also found to be associated with a logarithmic estimate of the depth to which certain Diophantine inequalities based on the Legendre symbol can be quantified.

A sign * in this text denotes an element of a set specific to ordinary local rings. The term 'k-rational' refers to a type of local complete intersection (LCI) surface that has a certain characteristic in its dual intersection ring. When a LCI surface has a k-rational property, it can be further categorized into two: k-Du Bois and purely k-rational. The k-Du Bois class includes subcategories such as k-rational, k-Euler characteristic rational, and k-essential. Our research explores properties of k-Du Bois local complete intersections, particularly surfaces, by examining their characteristics and relationships to other classes. It also investigates the behavior of k-Du Bois local complete intersections when they undergo certain operations.

Research into the intermediate magnetism phase in cesium lithium halides has been ongoing for 40 years. We have discovered that applying a moderate external electric field can transform the spin waves within the magnetically ordered phase in cesium gold iodide. Near room temperature, this transition changes from a long-range ordered state to a phase characterized by antiferromagnetic vortices. Furthermore, simulations reveal that the temperature at which this phase transition holds constant when the external electric field changes. This suggests that increasing the electric field ultimately leads to a phase characterized by short-range spin correlations at even higher temperatures.

In this research, we combine Sterile Neutrino, Axion-Like Particle, and Dark Matter theories to create a unified framework known as Axion-Sterile Neutrino Shadow Matter. To accomplish this, we establish a model based on an SO(10) gauge group and include various gauge and Higgs boson fields along with three left-handed Weyl doublets, six right-handed Weyl triplets, and two right-handed Weyl triplets that are not part of any fundamental representations. By applying an extension of the Shadow Matter concept to Sterile Neutrino spaces, we generate reasons for Large Right-Handed Neutrino Directions (LRHNDs) and establish the prerequisites for obtaining Sterile Neutralinos with masses in the MeV range as Dark Matter candidates. Furthermore, we integrate Axion-Like Particles into an SO(10) Shadow Matter framework by making use of an auto-transforming gauge boson with B-L symmetry, resulting in possible Axion-Like Particle masses in the GeV range. To implement this unified framework, we determine the various symmetry-breaking vacuum expectations values and calculate the mass spectra of various exotic particles, including Sterile Neutralinos, Axion-Like Particles, and Majorons, within the context of Axion-Sterile Neutrino Shadow Matter.

This study optimizes previously established upper limits on the stabilizer rank of any two-qubit magic state and any three-qubit magic state. Specifically, the upper limit on the stabilizer rank of any two-qubit magic state is now capped at 322, while the upper limit on the stabilizer rank of any three-qubit magic state is now capped at 262.

This research employs the Essence model, originally proposed by Ma et al. in 2012, but modifies it by replacing the perfect fluid with the FRW universe's FRW perfect cosmological fluid and utilizing the Tsallis distribution to describe the Friedmann equation. The model's parameter, $\alpha$, plays a crucial role in linking the Friedmann equation to the Tsallis energy density. By setting $\alpha$ as a real value, the investigation mirrors the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker universe's dynamics, and when $\alpha$ is complex, the Equation of State parameter, $P_w$, becomes dependent on the universe's time flow. The model is then analyzed using the current value of Hubble parameter and an optimization technique known as the Markov Chain Monte Carlo method to determine the model's free parameters. The analysis indicates that the Tsallis energy density meets the universe's energy condition, and the Equation of State parameter exhibits a minimally complex nature.

The LAMOST time-domain survey began conducting annual observations from 2014 to 2017, maintaining four $K$2 plates that tracked changes in stars with amplified light. These areas contained 1,737,672 unique stars across the entire sky, with the highest concentration containing 664,416 stars. To identify stars exhibiting significant brightness fluctuations, analysis used time series of narrowband photometry and a validation procedure. This led to the selection of 1,613,668 active stars, with the majority (79.9%) exhibiting single peak variations. After applying a distance-based classification, it became clear that most variable stars with limited sky coverage required further investigation. Initial findings included 508,655 stars that varied at one frequency, with the remaining active stars exhibiting more complex patterns. These results are comprised of 224,655 stars whose patterns could not be fully established and 190,677 stars whose light fluctuated in multiple bands. Additionally, a sub-sample consisting of 49,635 stars that fit the $DR17$ classification was compared to the Gaia data, revealing discrepancies in period and amplitude for certain types of stars that require further correction.

Recent research has identified SRAM cells as a suitable source of true random numbers due to their sensitivity to process variations, which causes their write access times to fluctuate. These timing discrepancies, however, are diminished when SRAM cells operate at lower voltage levels. To capitalize on the SRAM cells' randomization properties while minimizing energy consumption, we propose TuRaN, an true random number creation module that can be integrated into existing microcontrollers. TuRaN utilizes SRAM cells to generate random numbers, which are then utilized to prevent SRAM data corruption resulting from system malfunction or attack. By regulating the SRAM cells' operating voltage and introducing a minimal latency delay, TuRaN can still support modern encryption standards. For example, when integrated into a 32-bit microcontroller, TuRaN's latency exceeded the required time for AES-128 encryption, operating at a 0.42 voltage voltage, which resulted in a 26% increase in area efficiency compared to traditional hardware generators.

A basic model of a single-electron resistor (SER) is outlined and utilized to design two novel molecular structures that operate as nonvolatile single-electron transistors. The design involves attaching additional ligands to a nonvolatile SER to prevent charge tunneling between distinct charge states. The assumption that the SER operates at thermal equilibrium allows for the evaluation of design effectiveness. Two sets of molecular designs satisfying the criteria are proposed and simulated, one set based on a platinum octamer and the other on a platinum dimer. The results indicate that these molecules can function as nonvolatile memory elements with stable charge states and exhibit minimal leakage during reset. Additionally, the time required to switch between charge states is found to be comparable to existing single-electron transistors. However, significant consideration of spin contamination and charge self-interaction is needed for realistic calculations.

A novel approach has been introduced, allowing the evaluation of complex Feynman integrals through simple causal representations, leveraging advanced techniques in loop calculus and numerical computation. By utilizing cutting-edge techniques such as polynomial resolution and rational parameterization, even the most intricate Feynman integrals can be analyzed, even those beyond standard trigonometric and logarithmic classifications. Once expressed in a causal form, these integrals can be efficiently evaluated using numerical methods, achieving unprecedented precision. A key challenge underlying this methodology involves identifying the integral's fundamental degree, a concept further elaborated upon in the provided explanation.

Quantum walks exhibit similar patterns as Colored Random Walks, which have been studied extensively by immersing a particle in a colored environment that rotates according to a fixed law. This work focuses on a basic one-dimensional two-state quantum walk model and derives an equation that expresses the probability amplitude distribution as an infinite series of the walk's initial states. We then analyze this equation to understand its convergence, revealing that it simplifies under two specific conditions, resulting in a direct relationship with the heat equation. Our findings demonstrate that the probability distribution's convergence rate is influenced by the walk's initial state. While the probability amplitude series converges, the associated probability distribution does not converge in most cases, instead exhibiting periodic or oscillating patterns. We utilize numerical methods to illustrate the complexity of the probability amplitude series and its relationship to the known probability distribution, which poses significant computational challenges, particularly for longer simulation times.

In this study, we investigate the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The mathematical frameworks governing this study involve three interactions: $\sigma-\omega-Rho$ and specifically the $\sigma$ and $\omega$ interactions as described by vector meson dominance theory, coupled with the MIT bag model for hadrons and the NJL model for quarks. By analyzing numerous Rho coupling values, we observe that the $\sigma-\omega$ interaction's stability limits are largely influenced by the $\sigma$ vector meson radius, which in turn strongly correlates with the hadronic bag radius. Consequently, hybrid stars' mass ranges and maximum masses are primarily determined by the $\sigma$ vector meson radius and subsequently the hadronic bag radius.

The $q$-deformed optomechanical system, which incorporates fast and slow light, is explored through the use of two $q$-deformed bosonic oscillators. By leveraging the $\ affine$ $q$-deformation, the Fock state number resolution and transmission clarity are shown to be improved, with the enhanced optical sensing capability and improved transmission quality both reaching the fundamental limits, as evidenced by $\langle \delta N_{th}^q\rangle_{\min}=1/2$ and $\langle (\delta N)^2\rangle_{\min}=0$.

In a model where an $I = 1$ particle couples to an $I = 0$ particle and a particle with undefined parity (S), it's observed that the adverse characteristics of R-parity scissors modes can be explained by the Two-Rotors model. Specifically, the dense schedules of adverse R-parity scissors modes can be accounted for, and reflections of R-parity scissors modes with respect to the equilibrium axis can be described by utilizing the collective model's parameters. Additionally, the relationships between R-parity scissors modes and the mirror and reverse mirror operations are clarified.

The reduction in thickness of a ferromagnetic spin structure in ferromagnetic metal/insulator ultra-thin films can now be studied using advanced experimental tools.  This thin-film format also enables the incorporation of antiferromagnetic spins, enabling the exploration of extensive magnetic property sets.  By adjusting the number of atomic layers and the type of interface, researchers can access various complex magnetic property states.  This research area has experienced recent resurgence due to advancements in sample preparation and measurement techniques.  Notably, studies have revealed novel properties resulting from the co-existence of ferromagnetic spin and antiferromagnetic spin components, as well as the presence of complex orbital fluctuations.  This research area holds tremendous promise, as it may harbor novel computational tools and techniques to adjust spin components, offering potentially groundbreaking applications.  This article summarizes recent research findings focusing on spin and orbital fluctuations in thin-film structures, highlighting recent breakthroughs and their underlying physical drivers.

The equilibrium properties of a cold atomic gas, cooled down using the Doppler cooling method, can be described through unusual statistics that account for the disappearance of particles and downshifted fluctuations in energy. Building upon this, this paper explores the statistics of a gas trapped in an optical lattice, heated by interaction with two lasers, resulting in particle disappearance and energy excitation. By employing the Bogoliubov transformation, we calculated the energy spectrum of the trapped gas and derived equations that describe the behavior of density and energy distribution functions. From these results, we found that at a specific wavelength, density function exhibits downshifted fluctuations, while energy distribution function exhibits unusual, gapped behavior. Conversely, at another wavelength, density function exhibits conventional Gaussian fluctuations, and energy distribution function exhibits Divergent behavior.

Cryptocurrencies have gained popularity as a flexible investment option. Unlike traditional investments, which are often tied to national laws, cryptocurrencies offer a decentralized alternative. With over 5,000 active cryptocurrencies in circulation, investors can quickly access new financial opportunities. This diversity also attracts investors, as exchanging traditional money for cryptocurrencies can be challenging but offers a chance to quickly gain exposure to various assets. The main draw for investors has shifted from cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange to their potential for earning profits through price fluctuations. In response, an active cryptocurrency trading market exists, where investors buy and sell to maximize gains. Our study analyzed daily price data for 1,448 cryptocurrencies between January 2017 and December 2020 and examined the relationships among these prices. The analysis revealed that the number of active traders and trading volume can influence price correlations. We found that higher-order relationships among the top-hitting prices of cryptocurrencies exist and are significant. Furthermore, the structure of the cryptocurrency trading network, formed by connecting pairs of cryptocurrencies with similar price relationships, varies over time. Notably, the network's density and fragmentation were found to be high due to unstable and decentralized investor behavior. Notably, the COVID-19 pandemic had a significant impact, decreasing the network's connectivity and strengthening short-range relationships. Our research provides insights into the complex and evolving relationship among cryptocurrency prices, which can inform investment strategies.

The formation of clouds and precipitation in the atmosphere can be influenced by clusters of sulphuric acid and water. The role of vibrational motion in these clusters needs to be understood. Using a computationally intensive method called path-integral molecular dynamics at temperature and energy variational approach, the properties of ammonia and hydrochloric acid clusters have been calculated. The results of these simulations show that correcting for the movement of atoms due to temperature, by including the concept of distributive marginal distributions to describe quantum behavior, improves the calculation of properties such as heat of formation, particularly for smaller clusters where the contribution of vibrational energy becomes significant.

We create a continuous representation of group equivariant linear operators that act on data sets and maintain distances, similar to how Perelman compactified the space of Ricci flow solutions. This representation is used to establish compactness for a specific class of infinite data sets, and it also enables us to remove infinity from the space of distances between these data sets.

The reaction to the Thermal Hall effect, a phenomenon where an applied thermal gradient induces a transverse heat current, is examined in relation to its analogues within both electromagnetism and general relativity. Upon analyzing these reactions, it is found that while electromagnetism maintains symmetry under time reversal, general relativity does not. This discrepancy arises from Einstein's theory disregarding thermodynamic time reversal. Consequently, the reaction to the Thermal Hall effect differs significantly between electromagnetism and general relativity, leading to a complete dissipation of thermal Hall anomaly within a gravitational environment. This research aims to shed light on the thermal Hall anomaly's violation of Einstein's relations, offering insights into the non-gravitational components of quantum field theory.

In various machine learning scenarios, it has been observed that certain neural networks tend to prefer solutions with fewer parameters over those with more parameters. While concepts such as regularization and bias-variance tradeoffs can provide some insight, they do not fully explain the parameter counting behavior exhibited by some neural networks. We have identified and analyzed additional factors that contribute to this bias, stemming from the regularization effects of representation complexity, which interact with learning algorithms in conjunction with performance, ultimately shaping parameter counting. These factors are influenced by the interplay between model architecture and optimization techniques. By elucidating these circumstances, we can gain a deeper understanding of how model simplicity emerges spontaneously in neural networks.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite significant advancements, it remains difficult to achieve accuracy comparable to human judges, especially when grading complex, open-ended essays.  Recent successes with Transformer-based models have improved AEG performance, yet scores often fall short of human standards.  Past research has explored augmenting input data with synthetic essays to enhance model performance, leading to notable improvements in AEG accuracy.  Focusing on BERT and RoBERTa models, this study delves into applying data augmentation to improve AEG performance.  Experiments revealed that distilling pre-trained models using unsupervised distillation methods yields superior results, with enhancements outperforming existing benchmarks.  Furthermore, this study examines multiple synthetic data generation techniques, revealing that generating data with minimal relevance to the target task prevents model degradation and, in cases, causes the model to struggle with its original task performance.  Specifically, the findings indicate that the use of sentence-level data augmentation results in notable improvements in AEG accuracy, reaching 2.8% better performance when compared to the non-augmented model, with results even more pronounced on longer essays, resulting in a 3.3% improvement.

The area of marginal dependence models is primarily concerned with the analysis of univariate time series. Despite this, the literature often incorporates models that rely on an implicit common underlying process, thereby restricting their practical applications. This study aims to provide a comprehensive framework for marginal dependence models, critiquing existing methods and offering a new metric to assess temporal relationships within a single series, which adapts to various cases where multiple factors are involved. The proposed framework then transitions to common factor models, focusing on the estimation of common parameters, while allowing the unobserved factors to remain latent. The main contribution here is the development of a test statistics to assess the relevance of individual series to common factors, thereby facilitating series selection. The methodology is then demonstrated through applications to both artificial and real data.

A two-sector model of social mobility treats society as divided between a skilled sector offering opportunities and a unskilled sector with limited prospects. Skilled jobs are awarded through a competitive process governed by skills, while unskilled positions are allocated by a paternalistic figure who also fills skilled roles. We examine how this system affects skill dynamics and social mobility patterns. Unskilled individuals may remain unskilled and uneducated or strive for skilled jobs, which are rare and difficult to achieve. The current system results in suboptimal social mobility; to improve this process, the allocator opens up an additional, temporary pathway for unskilled individuals to gain skills, thereby increasing the number of skilled jobs available. We also investigate an alternative where the allocator lowers the unskilled barrier by boosting unskilled productivity without altering the skill requirement for skilled positions. Modifying either of these systems raises social mobility and, in doing so, also increases inequality in society. To understand these findings, we develop a Markov process representing the passage of time and the skills of unskilled individuals. This process has a particular structure that leads to repeating patterns, or cycles, in skill acquisitions among unskilled individuals. We interpret the duration and unskilled cycles of this process as key metrics governing the effectiveness of different system modifications.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the particle's statistics. For non-relativistic particles, the symmetry of wavefunctions under parity is the primary basis for determining the particle's statistics, as described by a spherical tensor operator. This results in bosonic statistics for particles with integer spin and fermionic statistics for particles with half-integer spin. This approach can be taken as the foundation for deriving the spin-statistics connection.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations or even centralised cryptocurrencies such as Monero, it can provide a suitable balance of anonymity and transaction efficiency for use in sidechains or private versions of toll roads, or as a middle ground in scenarios where full decentralisation is not required.

The practical feasibility of various direct solver methods for linear systems depends on the system's grid size and shape. While the space dimensionality $d$ might seem like the primary factor, our investigation reveals that system structure can be more significant. By analyzing structured solvers for consistent systems resulting from elliptic partial differential equations on $d$-dimensional grids with $n$ points, we discuss direct solvers that exploit symmetry, block structures, and block-diagonal forms. We derive explicit runtime estimates for each type, emphasizing the impact of solvers' overhead and showing that for sufficiently large $n$, solvers' speeds are largely determined by the system's space dimensionality $d$, rather than vice versa. Notably, despite involving seemingly intractable computations, our worst-case runtime estimates are surprisingly close to practical expectations, largely exceeding actual costs only marginally.

The production of three highly energetic bosons, specifically $W^{\pm}W^{\pm}\gamma$, is extensively examined using next-to-leading order perturbative methods within the context of the Standard Model. Moreover, the study considers potential beyond Standard Model scenarios involving a top sector involving an additional vector boson $\tilde{W}$ and scans the parameter space of $\tilde{W}$ coupling to top and right-handed bottom quarks and gauge boson. By utilizing Alpheus, a numerical tool for evaluating matrix elements, the production yields and associated distributions of these processes are calculated for the LHC at 13 TeV. This study also assigns robust sensitivity limits to the $\tilde{W}$ resonance width and masses above 2 TeV, resulting from varying couplings between $\tilde{W}$ and bottom quarks, ranging from 20 pb to 200 pb, which are consistent with current experimental findings.

In 2019, Hebrew joined the Universal Dependencies project, with a treebank developed from the Israeli constituent lattice bank, primarily consisting of written texts. This paper reports on the update to UD 2.7, incorporating new annotations and removing early errors. Additionally, the study revisits Hebrew parsing performance, finding it inferior to other languages and identifying domain-specific challenges. To improve parsing, a new task and dataset, COMPAS-HE, have been created, with tasks and data developed in collaboration with Israel's National Library. COMPAS-HE combines instruction and knowledge formation with the help of expert librarians.

We establish that for any fixed $1 < p < \infty$ and $M > 0$, there exists an $M$-independent dimension $n(M)$ and a probability measure $\mu$ on the standard $\ell_p$ space such that $\mu$ does not compress to a finite-dimensional subspace of $\ell_p$ and the $\varepsilon$-isometry distance between $\mu$ and its image under a given $\varepsilon$-isometry on $\ell_p$ exceeds $n(M)/2$. This distance is defined as the minimum number of $\varepsilon$-isometry operations required to achieve the transformation. Our work builds upon a previous result by Krasnyuk, who showed that the distance between two distinct invariant measures on the Heisenberg group has a linear lower bound under an $\varepsilon$-isometry. In our case, the lower bound on the transformation distance exhibits a linear increase with $\varepsilon$. Our method of proof involves constructing a directed graph of finite-dimensional $\ell_p$ spaces and showing that for a specified Dirac measure and an associated iterative algorithm, which adds newly $\varepsilon$-isometric images to a growing set of spaces, there exists a point of discontinuity in the graph where the algorithm's behavior changes under an increasing sequence of $\varepsilon$. This point determines our probability measure $\mu$ such that it cannot be compressed to a finite-dimensional subspace of

One major limitation of traditional modeling techniques is that they often generate detailed predictions but offer few insights into the underlying system behavior. This issue is particularly evident in fields where data is scarce, varied, and frequently contaminated with errors. To address this concern, we introduce a novel approach, collaborative data-driven modeling. This novel approach, rooted in dimensionality reduction and machine learning, focuses on extracting meaningful process insights from noisy operational data. Several case studies successfully demonstrate the efficacy of this method in uncovering hidden patterns and relationships within complex processes, including an analysis of NASA's Cassini Mars landing and simulations of coupled climate-chaos and financial-lunar cycle systems. The outcomes clearly illustrate the ability of collaborative data-driven modeling to uncover subtle, skillful influences, thereby facilitating the detection of skillful agents operating in these environments.

Current assessments assume that channel errors exhibited in received words are independent and evenly distributed, however, this assumption does not accurately reflect the circumstances when channel errors exhibit correlations. Research has been conducted to analyze and evaluate the performance of density parity-check codes under scenarios of varying levels of error correlation. This paper builds upon previous knowledge by providing a comprehensive framework to construct degree-degree correlated LPDCs capable of withstanding correlated noise. Furthermore, through numerical analysis, an example of such a code and its associated error rate performance is demonstrated. Lastly, an algorithm and a proposed strategy for designing correlated LPDCs are proposed.

A novel digital security filter, designed for adaptive signal processing systems, uses system-level synthesis to create a secure analogue output from an insecure digital input. This secure filter, based on an ALMA-based algorithm, can effectively counteract control mechanisms' vulnerabilities to manipulation. By employing a cryptographic code and an irregular electrical connection, the circuit's resistive feedback resistors are randomly set, generating unpredictable analogue dynamics in the output signal. The analytical framework developed, yielding tight bounds on the Hermite interpolating series, enables the data rate and processing delay of the secure filter to be quantitatively assessed. Experimental results confirm that the new security filter prevents control mechanisms from being manipulated while maintaining functional connectivity to the input signal.

A critical component in quantum key distribution (QKD) safety lies in distinguishing photon statistics, however certain attacks can deceive this system by manipulating the light source. Our enhanced system combines measurement-based QKD with decoy states, using a normalized phase reference for quantum states shared between QKD channels and decoy channels. Since randomizing the phase can weaken QKD security, we modify a commercial QKD system by allowing partial phase randomization, limiting the phase reference range. As a result, the probability of malicious activities is decreased, while maintaining a high level of legitimate signal security. Our system successfully defends against hacking attacks, particularly fast-correlated photon attacks, and offers improved security features.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning models are impacted by the source of the training data. To explore this, we conduct our analysis using a 1.3 billion parameter language model, evaluating the difference in performance when it is trained with varying sources of data, including web pages, Wikipedia, online forums, and product reviews. Our results show that models trained on web pages and online forums outperform those trained on Wikipedia and product reviews, and that these differences in performance are accompanied by greater lexical diversity and more effective use of contextual information in online forums and web pages. Additionally, we observe that models trained on web pages and online forums are more resistant to out-of-vocabulary words and punctuation-based wordpieces, and are able to achieve comparable results even when subjected to formatting and spelling errors. Our findings suggest that training data from platforms such as online forums and web pages can provide more robust performance in in-context learning tasks, and may be more effective in addressing challenging natural language processing tasks, particularly those found in real-world applications and datasets.

Galaxy cluster observations have revealed numerous large-scale cosmological objects, and their study has shed light on the early universe. To better comprehend the evolution of these clusters, researchers have developed computational models, which we examine by tracking the dynamic development of a galaxy cluster over 10 billion years. Our models show that initial cold gas clouds in galaxy clusters can either grow or disappear, depending on the strength of radiative cooling, magnetic fields and thermal conduction. We discovered that an equilibrium exists between the growth of cold clouds and their destruction through various processes, and this balance significantly affects the cluster's overall development. We present a diagram that illustrates the dynamic interplay between these processes and the amount of cold gas in galaxy clusters, and use it to understand the long-term evolution of galaxy clusters. Our models also show that the distribution of gas in galaxy clusters can change over time, and that electronic magnetic fields play a crucial role in this process. Finally, we present simulations of a galaxy cluster formation, including the development of a cold accretion stream, and observe the dynamic interplay between gas clouds and background plasma.

The discovery of the $CP$ violation in charged kaons during the 1990s, 
alongside the observation of $CP$ nonconservation in beauty quarks in 
experimentation, marked a significant turning point in the field of 
particle physics. The standard model effectively explains these findings, 
but they also prompt questions about the underlying nature of $CP$ 
violation. This review presents an overview of recent $CP$ violation 
discoveries, focusing particularly on beauty and charm hadrons, before 
delving into discussions on possible connections to new physics and the 
usefulness of these measurements in determining the mass of the Higgs boson.

New calculations have been conducted for bosonic hard scattering events in superstring theory, resulting in corrected cross section formulas. These corrections stem from loop corrections related to tachyon, dilaton, and gravity, as well as an unexpected contribution involving the NS-NS sector. The cross sections' logarithmic behavior aligns with the Gross conjecture, while non-logarithmic components follow a different pattern. The underlying mechanism for the Gross conjecture's compliance is the duality between the Poisson and Witten matrices. Additionally, the string scattering amplitudes were found to comply with the Soft-Wirtinger relation and related constraints. The compliance with the Gross conjecture and the Witten-Anichini relation indicates that the string scattering amplitudes are free from divergent non-logarithmic terms.

To effectively manage the surge in mobile data traffic, 5G networks are designed to be highly efficient and environmentally friendly. In 5G, the "Smart RAN" approach has been implemented through Self-Organizing Networks (SON) technologies to optimize cell performance and reduce energy consumption. However, optimizing 5G base stations and RANs while considering service quality and energy efficiency remains an open challenge. To address this issue, this paper focuses on developing sustainable strategies for 5G networks by introducing a new framework for managing radio resources across different generations of mobile networks. The proposed R&A5GN model, based on cloud-based mobile network architecture, allows for efficient management of downlink radio resources and is compatible with both legacy and 5G RANs. To achieve this, a multi-objective optimization model is developed, addressing power allocation, bandwidth allocation, and base station selection to maximize QoS and reduce energy consumption, while also ensuring fair resource allocation. The R&A5GN model is formulated as a mixed-integer non-convex optimization problem, along with three alternative models that provide a convex approximation of the original issue. The proposed strategies are simulated using MATLAB and simulated results are presented for different scenarios, demonstrating that the strategies can significantly reduce energy consumption in 5G networks while maintaining high QoS levels.

The goal of zero-speech voice synthesis is to create a voice model that can be learned without any labeled data, by leveraging instead transcripts derived from acoustic units and linguistic patterns. We approach this challenge by employing AudioSet, a large dataset that provides short, annotated sounds with corresponding transcription labels. We develop a unified representation to model both speech and transcription data, and apply a conditional generation method to synthesize speech from a given transcript. Experiments yield improved results on the given dataset, outperforming previous methods and generating high-fidelity speech with reduced artifacts.

The control of rigid-body motion in a specified environment involves solving a collision avoidance problem, which has been approached through the lens of optimization in recent years. Employing a multi-stage optimization framework seems a suitable method to tackle this challenge, considering the intricate pathways and collision sites that need to be negotiated. This method requires an efficient optimization algorithm to handle the technical difficulties presented by multi-stage optimizations, such as varying numbers of variables and constraints across stages, along with potential complications arising from the non-convexity of the problem. Our proposed solution involves using data-driven McCormick envelope relaxations to tackle the complex non-convex collision equation, thereby converting it into a convex form that can be efficiently optimized. The proposed approach is then simulated using a Collide! environment simulation of a pelvis-sphere model and showed notable results in terms of reduced duality gaps, confirming its effectiveness. Our proposed method is now available as a publicly accessible Python tool.

A fundamental principle in quantum theory, the no-broadcasting rule, dictates that a particular quantum state cannot be effectively copied multiple times when operating within a specific imprecision threshold. We investigated the boundaries of data extraction from an arbitrary quantum state, not including its initial formation, by a single measurement in a predetermined basis. Our analysis reveals that, in the absence of additional constraints, there are no quantitative limitations on data extraction than can be applied universally to all quantum states. However, when subjected to stricter requirements - namely that the extracted information must originate from a singular subsystem and that the measurement in question is unique and cannot be duplicated - a lower bound on extractable information is imposed, one that relies heavily on previous research conducted by Devabathra et al. and is quantifiable through the use of a specific dimensionless quantity called the skewness. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that any restriction on data extraction that can be applied universally to all quantum states must be tied to properties of the state's density matrix, specifically its marginal density matrices representing various subsystems. Lastly, our research suggests that, under certain conditions, lower bounds on data extraction may be imposed by the concept of pinning, even in the absence of additional constraints such as those associated with a quantum computer's functionality or memory capacity.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by combining the movements of a forced pivot. The angular displacement and rotation velocity of the cup influenced the movement of the coffee, which responded by shifting relative to the cup. The resulting flow was then released as surface waves that determined the sound and appearance of splashing. The nature of the liquid movement classified the outcomes into three distinct regimes: (i) gentle rocking with minimal wave formation, (ii) increased wave growth leading to regular sound patterns, and (iii) further acceleration resulting in larger waves, more intense sounds, and a greater difference in density between the coffee and water. The patterns observed from this study align with previous research on capillary waves and the chaos theory of Lewis and Ryhning.

In many decentralized optimization tasks, graph topology plays a crucial role in determining communication patterns and system performance. Researchers have recently explored the potential of arbitrary topologies by focusing on convex optimization problems. However, in various real-world applications, it is often necessary to handle optimization problems with non-convex constraints, which necessitates a further challenge in optimization theory - graph partitioning. This study addresses the partitioning issue by developing an innovative Distributed Robust Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DR-DSGD) method from a robust optimization perspective. We derive key performance guarantees for DR-DSGD and evaluate its effectiveness using numerical experiments on real-world datasets.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated in the initial stages of collisions correlates strongly with the total entropy produced, albeit only after thermalization occurs. Consequently, we determine that a significant portion of entropy originates from non-equilibrium mechanisms and attribute this to the expansion process.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The results show that highly energetic jets originating from the core can travel long distances and play a significant role in shaping the surrounding environment, while weaker jets may be completely embedded in a magnetized plasma. It's found that the force exerted by highly energetic jets on the surrounding material is significantly greater than that of weaker jets, and can play a crucial role in disk evolution and the development of the protostar. The collision of highly energetic jets with cooler material can lead to magnetic reconnection and further energize the jets, and it's also possible that weaker jets can be amplified and strengthened in this way.

This research focuses on optimizing the operation of industrial processes within specific speed limits. A control strategy is developed to balance performance and saturation constraints for a specific type of system, which can be complex and have unpredictable behavior. A direct approach is utilized to formulate an optimization problem, which is then solved to obtain control settings within established limits. A feedback control mechanism is also proposed to prevent over-saturation of system actuators. The methodology is applied to two practical case studies: (1) controlling a heated tank to maintain desired temperature and overflow level, and (2) managing a semiconverter switching circuit to reduce harmonic vibrations. The study demonstrates that the method can produce superior performance outcomes compared to existing saturation-based control techniques.

This research project seeks to deepen understanding of how Solar Pressure effects manifest in nearby celestial bodies, specifically among those that exhibit circular orbits similar to that of Earth. To achieve this, it presents a previously developed model which identifies areas where Solar Pressure resonances occur, followed by the creation of a demographical map that categorizes celestial bodies into three groups based on their orbital characteristics. Numerical simulations are conducted to refine the model's accuracy and reveal variations in commuting times, leading to the creation of several open source software tools for calculating commuting times and evaluating resonant zones.

A new approach is developed to study the symmetry properties of finite tight-binding models used to simulate light-matter interactions. This methodology, which leverages the existing framework of second-quantization, enhances the model's symmetry by incorporating a comprehensive Augmenting Algebraic Model. This model's symmetry properties are analogous to their continuum counterparts, allowing for a precise comparison. It is demonstrated that the model's symmetry properties remain intact even in the presence of non-zero velocities and diamagnetic terms. However, a subtle issue arises from the velocity operator's quadratic nature, which breaks certain symmetry expectations. Despite this limitation, the model's symmetry properties can still be utilized to develop simplified diagonal dispersion-based models that effectively describe a wide range of semiconductor materials, including their transition from direct to indirect bandgap behavior.

In various applications like robotics and game design, identifying the shape and position of objects within predefined categories is crucial but often challenging due to diverse objects within each category. Existing object recognition algorithms are typically designed to recognize objects across different instances but often fail to account for variations within a single category. To address this issue, this study proposes PACE, a system that determines the shape and position of objects within predefined categories by utilizing learned models for object recognition and combining them with semantic keypoint data. PACE's performance is evaluated on a new dataset containing 3D boxes from real-world scans of 40 categories and reaches expert-level accuracy. Additionally, PACE's robustness is demonstrated in optimizing object placement and is shown to be superior to previous object recognition algorithms in these tasks. Furthermore, PACE's potential for real-world applications is shown through its successful use in completing object shapes from partial 3D scans and generating new object instances through pose variation.

This study develops methods to estimate the parameters of Cauchy distributions, both individually and simultaneously, providing associated confidence intervals that account for bias. A sample of n data points is used to create these estimates and the associated intervals, utilizing the sample's median as a pivotal quantity. The methods proposed share similarities with those already established for normal distributions, offering ease of implementation that does not rely on specific software or programming. The study's findings are supported through simulations, examining the bias and variability of the estimators and confidence intervals, particularly how they perform for small data sets.

A new statistical method called basket trials assesses the efficiency of evaluating multiple patient subgroups using a single trial design. In this approach, sample sizes are calculated based on desired power and comparing treatment effects between groups. Since treatment arms in basket trials are often tested against the same control group, this method leverages information across patient subsets by sharing controls. Consequently, the required sample size for each subgroup is smaller than traditional trials testing each subgroup in isolation. Notably, this method focuses on comparing treatment arms rather than subgroup analyses. Consequently, sample sizes are calculated for the overall treatment vs. control comparison, rather than individual subgroup analyses. The method uses Bayesian statistics to estimate these sizes, which aligns with the typical analytical framework for basket trials. In this study, the method is developed to accommodate two-sided alternatives, which includes working out recruitment deadlines, as well as incorporating prior knowledge in the form of standard normal beliefs. Numerical examples illustrate the efficiency of this method, which often results in lower required sample sizes compared to trials testing subgroups in isolation.

To improve the performance of high-precision motion systems that experience changes in dynamics due to varying operating conditions, such as temperature or load, this research presents a novel nonlinear control approach. The suggested method employs a family of linear parameter-varying controllers designed using an advanced system identification technique. The storage of these controllers in an online database allows for swift retrieval and activation when a shift in operating conditions occurs, ensuring optimal performance at all times. The approach was successfully applied to a real-world motion control system and validated through experimental tests.

We introduce a general framework, called Partial Network (PRNet), designed to perform partial-to-partial alignment tasks such as shape registration and prediction. Unlike traditional methods which rely on full objects, PRNet is capable of aligning partial object views by utilizing multiple viewpoints and robustly handling varying incomplete data. Through self-supervised learning, where alignment constraints are applied to all view combinations, PRNet leverages local features to derive accurate partial object correspondences. As a result, our method excels in aligning partially occluded images and can seamlessly apply predictions from one partial view to another. Furthermore, by utilizing pairwise rather than instance-based learning, our approach is highly efficient and scalable. We evaluate PRNet on diverse partial-to-partial alignment tasks and demonstrate its superior performance across multiple datasets, ultimately leading to consistent and predictable predictions.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we demonstrate that the nilpotent quotient of $Stab_\varphi$ also possesses the $R_\infty$ property. Additionally, we characterize the automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}$. Given an automorphism $\varphi$ in $\mathbb{Z}$, we determine the conditions under which the nilpotent quotient of $Stab_\varphi$ exhibits the $R_\infty$ property, and the conditions under which it fails. Similarly, for the generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_m^n(\pm d)$ and $\Gamma^n(\pm d)$, we identify the criteria for an automorphism $\varphi$ for which the nilpotent quotient of $Stab_\varphi$ exhibits the $R_\infty$ property, and the criteria under which it fails.

To determine which future collider is most suited for detecting SM instability, 
we compare the discovery potential of three options: a 26 TeV future pp collider, 
a 28 TeV future pp collider and Higgs boson precision measurements, at the 
LHC's successor with its current sensitivity and with improved luminosity.
We calculate the required luminosity needed to reach the current sensitivity at 
three different luminosity thresholds: 100 fb^-1, 3 fb^-2 and 300 fb^-2.
We find that the first option can achieve the current sensitivity with high 
energy runs equivalent to 3-4 fb^-2 luminosity at the LHC with its current 
energy, while the second option requires either much higher luminosity or 
substantial energy losses. Additionally, we find that precision measurements 
yield similar results and suggest that the current sensitivity can be reached 
with lower luminosity or higher energy with the third option, if the 
fraction of luminosity recorded at high energy is optimized.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultrafast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from simulations accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this technique is capable of incorporating and accounting for uncertainties in the experimental data.

To investigate the internal structures of $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons, the calculation of their electromagnetic form factors is carried out using Bethe-Salpeter wave functions. The results obtained are then compared with those from lattice simulations and phenomenological analyses. Although our approach matches the latter on average, it reveals notable discrepancies, particularly in the $D^*_s$ electric form factor. This suggests that the contribution of higher Fock space components, if any, is negligible. Therefore, the calculated form factors primarily reflect the two-body (quark-antiquark) nature of these mesons.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Segmentation of unseen images during training is a significant challenge in medical image analysis. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs)-based methods have shown potential in solving this problem, but they are generally resource-intensive and difficult to implement. We propose an innovative approach using a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) called Cyclic Division GAN (CDGAN) to tackle this issue. CDGAN employs a novel loss function that simplifies the training process and allows for deeper network architectures, thereby enhancing image segmentation quality. Compared to existing methods, CDGAN demonstrates improved performance and computational efficiency.

Research in natural language processing has focused on determining word order
in sentences and then employing recurrent neural networks to generate human-readable
output. Conversely, this paper's goal is to forecast a user's action in a
communication system. We propose an innovative, feature-extraction RNN architecture
capable of transforming variable-length action histories into fixed-length feature
vectors. In doing so, an action selection module can easily utilize these features
via a simple comparison with existing classes. To facilitate efficient feature
extraction, this paper presents an innovative RNN-based model, incorporating a
radial basis function (RBF) kernel. Evaluations of our proposed model on a
communication dataset demonstrate superior performance over multiple benchmark
baselines.

To better understand the behavior of red dwarf active region jets, researchers simulated a major flare of a red dwarf star using complex computer simulations, assuming that the chromosphere and corona of the star have similar structures. Although the simulation primarily focused on observing a specific event, the researchers also generated artificial data and observed the effects of a major flare on radio waves, including temperature and density, and compared these observations to actual data and images taken during a similar event in 1985. The simulation revealed that the radiation from particles heated by the flare could have a significant impact on radio waves and other observations, and the researchers therefore reconsidered their previous interpretations of the 1985 data, including images taken using the IUE satellite. The simulation also showed that the radiation from particles heated by the flare can have a broad spectrum of ultraviolet and X-ray radiation, and this might be the source of certain features in the 1985 data, and the simulation of this feature matches actual data including images taken using the IUE satellite. The simulation revealed that the radiation from particles heated by the flare can take a long time to reach the observer, and this might be the source of certain time periods in the 1985 data, and the simulation of this feature matches actual data including images taken using the IUE satellite. The simulation concluded that the radiation from particles heated by the flare can have a long duration and a broad spectrum of ultraviolet and X-ray radiation, and this might be the source of actual data including

We carry out a study of deformations of G2 instantons on nearly G2 manifolds. By translating the nearly G2 structure along a vector field and exploiting the deformation equation's linearization, we find that the deformation space of a G2 instanton is isomorphic to the first cohomology group of the complex of real vector forms with a twisted differential. Furthermore, we establish that the first real Chern form of a G2 instantons' deformation complex corresponds to the Nijenhuis tensor associated with the almost product structure derived from the nearly G2 structure. Additionally, we examine how the deformation of a G2 instanton influences the associated characteristic form and describe the relationship between the real and complex forms' cohomologies.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

Consider the set of natural numbers starting with $m$, and let $S_n$ be a subset of these numbers that increases incrementally. Given a prime number $p$ and an integer $q$ greater than $p$, the subset $S_n$ is said to be a $p$-core $q$-sequence if, when divided by $p$, the difference between consecutive terms never results in a zero remainder. This paper explores the dimension of the smallest possible $2$-core $p$-sequences for any prime number $p$, and it proves that the dimension of the sequence $S_n = \{m, m+1, m+2, \ldots, m+n-1\}$ modulo $p$ is approximately $\sqrt{\frac{\pi^2}{4}n^2}$, which solves a long-standing problem first proposed by Andrews and Verrall. To achieve this, the authors employ the fractal dimension of the sequence, and a graph on $0$ and $1$-dimension by considering the results of modulating these numbers by $p$. This investigation involves analyzing the walks on the additive residue graph, and it also provides an exact calculation for the dimension of a $2$-core $p$-sequence, and it proposes a conjecture for its dimension that could potentially be generalized to other $p$-core $q$-sequences.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like self-driving technology but have been hindered by vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks. Research has discovered that these models are susceptible to attacks that can be performed using 3D convolutional operators. To address this issue, a new method called TPC has been proposed, which uses unique transformations to protect point cloud models against adversarial attacks. The TPC framework applies specific transformations to point cloud data during training, ensuring that the expanded data set remains consistent across different transformations. The projection depth of 3D convolutional operators is limited (typically five) and can be covered by these transformations, which include: translation along a, b, c axis; rotation within the ab, bc, ca planes; scaling by factors of 0.5, 1, 2; and shearing in the a, b directions. Empirical tests on a self-driving dataset have shown that models trained using TPC are highly resistant to attacks from three different types of 3D convolutional operators, and also perform better than models trained using PGD (Progressive Gradient Descent) both on clean and adversarial data.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing model-based ALOHA and CSMA protocols to share the spectrum among radar units. In slotted ALOHA, each unit divides time into equal-sized slots, conducting a single measurement per slot, with unoccupied slots remaining available for other devices. We analyze its performance under a single radar scenario, achieving a data collection rate of 50% per slot. This rate can be optimized through dynamic adjustment of slot size. In contrast, CSMA involves binary transmissions, with units taking measurements and then adjusting their timing parameters based on previous results. We examine two approaches - non-adaptive and adaptive CSMA - and find the adaptive version yields higher data collection rates. In dense scenarios, CSMA offers better performance, while ALOHA is more suitable for less congested environments. Additionally, using model-based transmission control reduces data loss and increases efficiency. We present simulation results for various network densities.

Recent advancements in photonic technology enabled the creation of devices capable of inducing correlated responses to uncorrelated inputs, resulting from the entwined interaction of photons. The Hong-Ou-Mandel effect serves as a renowned experiment demonstrating entwined photon behavior; recent studies have showcased the integration of two-photon absorption (TPA) processes within this setup, allowing for the utilization of common, available equipment to study TPA effects. The current understanding of these experiments emphasizes changes in interference patterns due to various optical phenomena, misaligned beams, or residual phases. Conversely, we propose that under specific conditions, the Hong-Ou-Mandel interference pattern remains preserved, yet accompanied by an overall decrease in transmission; this can be explained through spectral considerations of TPA processes. The coexistence of intact interference patterns and non-zero, TPA-induced transmission decreases may facilitate higher sensitivity detections of TPA effects, potentially leading to enhanced precision in TPA-related measurements.

We derive a differential equation that governs the logical circle-equivariant
elliptic cohomology theory, specifically for projective spaces based on finite
fields. By solving this equation, we formulate the logical circle equivariant
elliptic cohomology functors of these projective spaces. Notably, the functors
apply to spaces over any ground field, regardless of its characteristics.

Temporal knowledge graph inference involves identifying relationships between entities within a knowledge base and inferring new relationships. Building on previous research, we developed representations of temporal entities that are model-agnostic, meaning they can be used across different models without modification. These representations enhance the performance of model-based approaches and outperform other methods in inference quality. Moreover, since our representations are model-agnostic, they can be applied in scenarios where models cannot be provided. We explored the effectiveness of using these representations in conjunction with low-rank methods, and found that combining them yields superior results compared to using just low-rank methods or our representations alone in temporal knowledge graph inference. Our research achieved state-of-the-art performance on FB15K-237, a benchmark dataset.

In the field of rigid-frame models for ground sound, the Green's function represents the ground pressure caused by a moving point source on the ground surface. Researchers have developed methods to approximate the Green's function using various expansions, but evaluating its derivative at the ground surface is a complex task that requires careful analysis. The complexity arises from the ground's finite impedance and boundary conditions, which can lead to singularities in the Green's function derivative. The impedance and its relation to the ground pressure and pressure gradient form the basis of the rigid-frame model's equations of interest. Therefore, deriving closed-form expressions or numerically computing the impedance and the pressure gradient is a critical goal of the theory. Building on previous work in this area, we have developed a stochastic framework to approximate the impedance and the pressure gradient caused by a plane wave in a homogeneous ground. The approach involves modeling the ground as a stochastic surface and leveraging probabilistic techniques to derive stochastic equations for the pressure gradient. The effect of sound frequency, ground properties, and surface roughness on the pressure gradient is investigated through probabilistic analysis, which provides a comprehensive understanding without relying on specific scenario numbers.

A common understanding of quantum nonlocality is that it arises from contraints set by the Bell inequalities. However, this perception needs to be adjusted as research demonstrates that quantum nonlocality can also be expressed through inequalities-free correlations. These correlations not only serve as a full set of nonlocality indicators but also enable new nonlocality demonstrations that surpass previous versions in terms of resource efficiency. Notably, these demonstrations remain valid in the presence of collective measurements, a significant consideration given that individual measurements are often subject to errors. Furthermore, these inequalities-free nonlocality demonstrations based on correlations offer an invaluable tool for exploring the nonlocality inherent in specific quantum states, thereby enhancing our comprehension of nonlocality and its fundamental properties.

Gukov and Kitaev introduced flat lines as a means to examine parity invariant topological lines incorporating both 't Hooft and fundamental lines in eight-dimensional exceptional field theory. This concept is revisited, and the utilization of flat lines as an efficient tool for describing parity invariant lines in various topological theories is discussed. Furthermore, the incorporation of Poisson-Lie duals of hyperbolic cosets as a means to extend the scope of flat lines beyond exceptional theories is explored. This enlargement encompasses types of line defects previously unaccounted for in the original flat line framework, such as D-type lines, which arise in $\mathcal{N}=4$ Chern-Simons theories, and are found to localize consistently across diverse topological theories.

A few layers of MbC (where M equals Eu, Y, or La) exhibit unusual electrical properties, known as phonoelectric effects. Researchers have discovered that these doped hydrogen borides might be potential superconductors at very low temperatures. To investigate this further, we used a computational model to create a theoretical framework of the materials. Our results suggest that EuCB$_2$ could display some superconducting properties, however we found that YCB$_2$ and LaCB$_2$ are unlikely to be superconductors. We identified that the strength of the chemical bonds between the elements and the presence of defects within the material affect its potential for superconductivity.

This paper presents an iterative convex optimization method for allocating compute resources to parallel jobs under specific constraints. It assumes a pool of homogeneous machines is available to run jobs, each machine having a fixed number of processing units. The optimization occurs at two levels: cluster and node, due to the division of a large workload into smaller clusters and the allocation of those clusters to available machines. This binary partitioning approach is referred to as Run Allocation Over Flattened Partitions (RAFP) and is contrasted with other optimization techniques. The results of using RAFP to optimize job allocation are positively evaluated.

This article investigates the charmability and stiffness of arithmetic groups, a concept initially introduced by Serre. By leveraging Mordeis' stability theorem, we establish that numerous arithmetic groups are stiff. We also demonstrate that certain groups with exceptional simplicity are stiff. Furthermore, we prove that the group $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ is not stiff. Additionally, we introduce the idea of charifiable subgroups within a larger group, and we categorize arithmetic groups that fulfill specific criteria as charifiable. Utilizing a combination of finite group theory and number theory, we determine the charifiable groups among polynomial groups, a category that includes $SL_2(\mathbb{Z}[t])$.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and fault tolerance capabilities. Traditional safety assessment methods utilizing hazard and risk analysis are ineffective in guaranteeing this resilience. We develop and apply a novel approach that formalizes and validates a reliable system design, able to function in case of component failures. Our method is specifically tailored to meet the requirements of fail-operational systems and is employed to validate a practical example.

In the realm of security, the terms 'cluster' and 'grouping' are often used, 
yet, there's a crucial difference: cluster analysis. Specifically, we apply 
cluster analysis to identify diverse patterns of behavior in dynamic systems, 
particularly those that might arise from cyberattacks. By utilizing data-driven and 
formula-free methods, our approach focuses exclusively on analyzing time-series 
data, thereby preserving the inherent structure and dynamics of the system. 
Unlike traditional clustering methods that usually require pre-processing, our unique 
approach, known as DinCLu, employs the t-SNE dimensionality reduction technique and 
then applies a geographical distance measure to group similar data sets together. 
We also introduce a novel performance evaluation method that simulates human judgment 
and adapts to any dimensionality reduction and clustering technique, ensuring unbiased 
results. To demonstrate the efficacy of DinCLu, we successfully identified and 
visualized attack patterns on the well-known Davis power system and a realistic 
model of a nuclear power plant under attack, which shows the potential of DinCLu 
to detect cyberattacks in complex dynamic systems.

Recent research examining the utility of contemporary mathematical structures in reconstructing historical mathematical approaches has focused on infinitesimal methods from the Leibnizian calculus.  This study expands upon previous work within the differential structure of Riemannian analysis and the category theoretical framework of formalism, all while proposing an extension of the continuous dependence theory.  A detailed analysis of Leibnizian calculus within these three frameworks reveals that they offer a comprehensive understanding of the calculus, yet each faces its own limitations.  The differential structure, for instance, struggles to capture the concept of functions itself, whereas the continuous dependence theory lacks the ability to incorporate functions with singular points.  Our research aims to provide a comprehensive description of Leibnizian calculus, exemplified through the examination of basic theorems, such as the infinitesimal geometric calculus.

Upcoming HI intensity mapping experiments will employ interferometric techniques, 
which will allow for more detailed data and new analysis methods to explore the 
galactic foregrounds. This paper utilizes a theoretical model to quantify the impact 
of assuming galactic models on the recovered power spectra. It finds that current 
galactic models introduce uncertainties significant enough to influence the 
recovery of cosmological parameters. Using simulated data from a proposed telescope 
design, it demonstrates how the choice of foreground removal method and model can 
affect the recovery of cosmological parameters. This suggests that with large 
datasets, it may be necessary to include more sophisticated models to accurately 
describe galactic emissions.

We examine the connections between three key properties of Hilbert space operators, specifically isometry, shift, and cyclicity, and how they relate to independence in prediction models. Utilizing operator theory, we derive new insights into the concept of independence, and leverage this framework to investigate the relationships between these properties and independence in both finite and infinite-dimensional prediction contexts.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document context for user and item profiling have gained attention due to their data-efficient and supplementary characteristics. Nonetheless, these systems are prone to system biases and can undershoot users' true preferences. In this paper, we integrate a behavior-based recommender system with an emphasis on behavior to mitigate these drawbacks. Nonetheless, the increased model complexity and parameters lead to increased system bias and susceptibility to overfitting. Therefore, we propose an empirical framework to guide in the selection of hyperparameters and model features for optimal balance. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that the combined system significantly outperforms individual systems and off-the-shelf models.

We examine the asymptotic behavior of conjugate algebraic numbers among eigenvalues of $U_N$. Specifically, we investigate the distribution of those eigenvalues and, given a nonidentity polynomial $P(t)$, determine the asymptotic probability that $P(\lambda_i)=0$ for some $i$. Our analysis distinguishes between two scenarios, depending on whether $P(t)$ can be factored into a product of two polynomials, each of which has a root that lies on the conjugacy class of some finite group. When this condition is met, we find that the associated values of $\lambda_i$ form a asymptotically negligible subset of $U_N$'s eigenvalues. Conversely, if all factors of $P(t)$ contain irrationals as roots, the associated $\lambda_i$ converge to a single point and constitute a denser subset of $U_N$'s eigenvalues. Additionally, our study reveals that, even in cases where $P(t)$ can be factored into irreducible polynomials with conjugate roots, the associated $\lambda_i$ may fail to form a type $B$ ensemble. Nevertheless, we identify a crucial sufficient condition for a set of $\lambda_i$ to be considered openness of type $B$, thereby extending existing criteria and allowing us to prove the asymptotic freeness of $U_N$ and $M_{N,M}$, given suitable conditions on their eigenvalues and truncations of cyclotomic polynomials, respectively

This paper presents an extension of existing research on enhancing model-checking tools to efficiently analyze timed properties of digital circuit designs that incorporate time parameters. By incorporating a timed abstraction of netlists derived from timing analysis or simulation data, designers can identify potential timing vulnerabilities in circuit architecture, facilitating early and efficient detection. The proposed method utilizes a timed model obtained via automatic timing verification tools and converts the results into a timed finite-state model that can be compared to desired safety specifications. The paper specifically outlines an adapted model-checking procedure using Spin and Netlists, and demonstrates the effectiveness of this method in identifying timely hazards, even those induced at post-silicon levels.

The decay width for $\bar B_s^0$ decaying into $J/\psi$, and subsequent intermediate states $a_0(980)\pi^0$ or $f_0(980)\pi^0$ is being measured. The production rates for these two processes are compared, yielding an answer to the question of whether $a_0(980)$ and $f_0(980)$ are indeed the same particle. The study also considers other possible intermediate states and their corresponding phase factors. The LHCb experiment is in a position to provide a precise answer to this inquiry, given its operational parameters and statistical power.

The GRAVITY gathering camera was designed to facilitate the formation of a pupil slicing system for mitigating atmospheric distortion on the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI). This approach involves splitting the pupil into equal parts and reassembling them to recover the undistorted image of a shared focal plane. A linear CCD detector is used to capture and reconstruct the images, and it does so by employing an anamorphic lens to transform each pupil segment into a aligned probe. This technical note outlines the findings from various camera tests, which included assessing its overall performance, as well as probing its capabilities with different operational parameters. These experiments were conducted with the camera in a setup that mimics the functionality of 8x8 pupil slicers. Furthermore, we explored the potential of utilizing the gathering camera in conjunction with a laser beacon. This involved simulating the activity of such a beacon with a NUKII laser and an imaging probe. Our results indicate that the camera meets the requirements for VLTI integration.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs with limited doubling or freeway dimension. Our study yields two distinct outcomes: one addressing the doubling metric and another concerning the freeway metric. The key difference lies in their respective dimension characteristics. The doubling metric is divided into certain classes of graphs with doubling dimension $O(\log n)$ and a minimum constant value of $O(d)$ for a given set of $n$ and degree $d$. We aim to minimize the number of facilities needed, each serving a set of nodes, with the goal of covering these nodes at a limited geographic cost. We demonstrate that in doubling graphs with a minimum constant doubling dimension and a suitable number of facilities, achieving an additive cost violation of $O(\log n)$ is feasible under a geographic distance constraint. This shows the scalability of facilities in such graphs. In contrast, under the same conditions but with a limited number of facilities, achieving a small additive cost violation of $O(d)$ is feasible with a geographic distance bound. We prove this by constructing a primal-doubling Steiner $k$-Center algorithm that combines primal-doubling Steiner Forest and Clustering algorithms. The freeway metric involves distinct sets of points with an edge between nearby points.
