The properties of dense stellar matter, which governs the behavior of compact stars, are essentially unknown and may significantly deviate from standard nuclear matter. To better understand this matter, researchers have developed various theoretical frameworks, which often result in the introduction of a strange baryon's scalar density. However, this variable's impact on the sound speed in dense stellar matter remains unclear, largely due to conflicting constraints from neutron star radii and the Goldach-Klaus equation of state. Nevertheless, a recent study has focused on this issue by analyzing the sound speed in dense stellar matter with different types of baryons and strange hadrons. Furthermore, the study's findings on the sound speed profile in various compact stars have provided new insights into their possible existence and their general properties.

We focus on the differential compressive strain's impact on the parabolic band structure of a two-dimensional massless Dirac-Einstein photon mode coupled to a set of N single-mode optical cavities. This coupling forms a complex Hilbert space, $\mathcal{H}_{\gamma}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{c}$, where $\mathcal{H}_{\gamma}$ represents the photon mode and $\mathcal{H}_{c}$ is associated with the cavities. As lattice parameters influence the Einstein photon dispersion, the combined system maps onto a complex Fock space, prompting an exploration of its structure. Through both classical simulation and quantum bath models, our research identifies regions of the system-bath coupling space where a thermal equilibrium description is applicable. We demonstrate that a thermal equilibrium description is only possible when the photon mode's dispersion remains linear or convex. Notably, a thermal equilibrium description may be feasible even with strong system-bath coupling if the associated photon mode dispersion is linear or convex. Additionally, our findings reveal that the photon distribution in the steady state exhibits super-Poisson statistics characterized by a sub-Purcell factor dependent on N, the photon occupation number.

The underlying interface geometry plays a crucial role in driving and shaping three-dimensional multiphase flow patterns. Although the principles governing interface behavior have been extensively studied, translating these insights into practical predictions remains complex due to the inherent intricacies in predicting interface shapes and trajectories. In contrast, interface representations through one-dimensional skeletons offer a more manageable framework for analysis and understanding. This study proposes an advanced skeletal model, capable of accurately reflecting interface complexities, and validates it using direct numerical simulations of buoyant jets and swirling flows. By dissecting skeletal patterns, we identify distinctive features that are highly indicative of the underlying interface geometry, and demonstrate the ability to classify interfaces in fully developed jets between quasi-periodic and chaotic regimes. Furthermore, we illustrate the ability of skeleton features to guide the development of simplified models that reduce computational complexity, and enable the prediction of interface shapes and trajectories in scenarios not covered in the training dataset.

We investigate the rotational dynamics of non-symmetrical viruses that exhibit rapid movement on their own, fueled by internal enzymatic activity. This analysis is prompted by recent observations of bacteriophages that move rapidly by rotating at high speeds. We propose that these viruses are considered as solid bodies with asymmetrical structures, powered by a driving force and opposing resistance forces. The rotational dynamics of these viruses can be described using a simple mathematical model, which is in line with existing experimental findings. This model also predicts that the viruses' speed will ultimately be limited by their rotational velocity approaching a maximum.

We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more pronounced warping, exhibited higher percentages of jellyfish galaxies. To investigate warping in groups and clusters, we selected a subset of S and U galaxies and compared their distribution in groups of different densities and galaxy clusters. U galaxies were found in dense groups and clusters, and in some cases, were aligned in a spiral pattern. This is in contrast to S galaxies, which avoid these environments. To explain the U galaxy warp phenomenon, we propose a theory involving galaxy interactions, including ram-pressure stripping by hot gas and wind-induced stripping by cosmic rays. Our findings also indicate that U galaxies may be an early stage of the jellyfish phenomenon, caused by ram-pressure stripping, which exposes gas and leads to star formation.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that the gradient of any harmonic function on this manifold must be constant, given a specific set of conditions are met. Furthermore, we have subsituted a particular inequality into this result, thereby providing an alternative formulation. We have also considered a scenario involving a harmonic function that is bounded within a specific geometric configuration and found that its gradient must also be constant.

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique cubic arrangements called the Laves phase with a specific Fd$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The presence of gyrotropic (chiral) phonons within this structure is intriguing due to the ordered displacement of cation and boron atoms. Utilizing group theory and symmetry analysis, a set of candidate phonon modes displaying chiral properties is proposed and justified. Notably, the literature lacks systematic studies on the chiral phonons in boron compounds and proposed calculations on the properties of $A$Bi$_{2}$ may yield novel and unique characteristics.

In metals with no electronic density fluctuations, a type of Born effective load is examined 
for $d=3,4$ spatial dimensions within the framework of Fermi liquids. It has been demonstrated 
that its nonadiabatic nature arises when interactions between electrons' velocity and density 
exceed those of the Drude model. Furthermore, research suggests that even in high symmetry 
cases like the Fermi surface of the cubic lattice, the Born effective load is not adiabatic 
and its divergence is proportional to the Drude weight. This finding holds true for 
any mean squared electron displacement and temperature below the Fermi temperature.

We are reassessing the underlying principles of high-frequency fluctuations within high-Reynolds number flows. Recent research has revealed that thermal disturbances can introduce anomalous diffusion characteristics into the flow. By ignoring the assumptions of the Kolmogorov theory-forced turbulence paradigm, we analyze the properties of high-Reynolds number flows forced directly by thermal fluctuations. Using three-dimensional direct numerical simulations, we determine the scaling of the energy spectrum and cascade rate across various Reynolds number ranges. Interestingly, we find that the energy spectrum exhibits a $k^{-1}$ scaling up to approximately one-tenth of the Reynolds number, contrary to previous studies on the inverse energy cascade of geostrophic turbulence. Furthermore, we observe a dissipation rate that increases proportionally to the sixth power of the wave number, which aligns with predictions based on the turbulent transport of passive scalars.

We demonstrate that time-reversal symmetry can affect the topological properties of electronic systems, leading to significant currents at magnetoeslectric thresholds. In an explicit example, we show that a specific interaction between electrons and a local spin field generates a time-reversal symmetric phase, characterized by a $\pi$ flux and a Witten effect, both of which are connected to the magnetoelectric properties of the system. This interaction drives a transition to a half-integer quantum Hall phase, and we propose that this type of transition represents a new mechanism for topological phase transitions, in which time-reversal symmetry plays a pivotal role.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait.
For these systems, the standard two-dimensional phase space structure is expanded due to time lag considerations.
We, however, show that the conventional approach of treating time lag can significantly enhance chaotic diffusion by up to three orders of magnitude, depending on lag values.
To explain this enhancement, we propose a time-rescaled phase space model that helps interpret the diffusive behavior and time lag's diffractive capacity.

We have developed a general interpretation of the lambda calculus with randomness by incorporating continuous domains from Melling's work into the model. The proposed model treats the domain of possible outcomes as part of its own structure, making it possible to model set-theoretic constructs within the model itself. We demonstrate that the model is sufficient for expressing set-theoretic fundamentals, and yet it is still grounded in a consistent framework. Furthermore, we show that the model is capable of modeling Brouwerian intuitionistic topology, thus providing a rigorous foundation for constructive reasoning in this context.

The aim of conception stability is to assess system performance consistency across varying input data. In the context of extracting design discussions through natural language processing, this involves proving the reliability of conclusions drawn from premises. Current evaluation methods for Conclusion Stability face obstacles due to the lack of systematic evaluation criteria and adaptable representation models that can accommodate both flexibility in interpretation and one-to-one correlations between phrases and concepts. To overcome these limitations, this study develops simple evaluation standards, flexible concept embeddings, and reliable representation learning techniques all tailored to design extraction tasks. By adopting these strategies, this research achieves the first instance of proving a Conclusion Stability for a design extraction system, thereby marking a significant breakthrough in naturally sourced data convergence with conception stability.

The concept of gravity arises from the interaction between cosmic branes and the ethereal vacuum radiation that fills the universe. This ether is comprised of residual radiation from the inflationary period and also contains the fluctuations that give rise to the fundamental fields of the Standard Model, which can be considered as localized Higgs-Goldstone oscillations. The coexistence of these elements necessitates a coherent treatment of quantum states that extends far beyond the commonly studied quantum systems. The process of the universe expanding downwards through the Casimir gap between the branes gives rise to the force we perceive as gravity. Furthermore, this model may provide the basis for a new understanding of dark matter and dark energy. The model's successes include the prediction of the fine structure constant and Planck's constant in terms of the brane spacing and the universal speed limit, respectively. Additionally, this theory can potentially be applied to the structure and dynamics of particles such as protons and electrons, which could have important implications for particle physics.

Proximal methods are a powerful tool for optimizing a variety of diverse cost functions, including those that are not differentiable and have complexities such as plateaus, valleys, and local minima. A key insight of our research is that for certain non-differentiable cost functions, proximal methods are capable of accurately identifying the characteristics of these complexities, even when they are hidden within a non-linear transformation. By leveraging this insight, we are able to identify the structure of manifolds that proximal methods can recognize, and demonstrate that a manifold recognized by proximal methods is always smooth and convex. Furthermore, we show that manifold recognition by proximal methods is an invariant trait, meaning that it does not change if the underlying manifold is re-parameterized or mapped to a different dimension. Additionally, we are able to identify the specific parameters of proximal methods that influence the accuracy of manifold recognition. These findings are corroborated by numerical simulations in three practical applications, including image denoising, Mixture Modeling, and Inferring networks' parameters.

We are introducing a new concept called feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an advanced level of $1$-absorbing prime ideals. This new idea is closely related to fantastic prime ideals, a property that enjoys unique and distinctive characteristics. Several important properties of feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals have been identified, such as their invariance under localization, the ability to express $1$-absorbing prime ideals as a combination of feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals and prime ideals, and the relationship between feebly $1$-absorbing prime powers and prime powers. Additionally, the upper bound of feebly $1$-absorbing prime powers has been determined.

New measurements of fully reconstructed $B^0$ decays to a charged pion and the neutral vector pion were made using 200~fb$^{-1}$ of Belle II data. A $B^0$ decay to a charged pion and the neutral vector pion and a lepton and a neutrino was partially mapped out with the following results: The branching ratio for $B^0$ decays to a charged pion, the neutral vector pion, an electron and an electron neutrino is found to be $4.16 \pm 0.64 \pm 0.24 \pm 0.70$ times 10$^{-4}$. A lepton flavor universality ratio between $B^0$ decays to a charged pion, the neutral vector pion, an electron and an electron neutrino and $B^0$ decays to a charged pion, the neutral vector pion, a muon and a muon neutrino is found to be 0.18 $\pm$ 0.10 statistical, with much larger systematic errors.

Spectra obtained from astrophotonic devices with multiple channels can be compared by correlating them, either directly or after transforming them into phased alignments. The process of cross-correlation is often hampered by a limited understanding of its effects and uncertainties, particularly when dealing with photonic devices. This study aims to investigate the cross-correlation of photonic spectra by applying the Fourier transform, comparing different methods such as the conventional and a phase-aligned approach. The study also evaluates the performance of these methods using simulation tools and points out potential issues, suggesting the need for further research.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

Several local authorities face challenges in finding and funding repairs for road damage due to limited resources and financial constraints. The need for low-cost and efficient methods to identify road damage has led to the emergence of computer vision solutions. Recent approaches for automatic road damage detection have been developed and tested primarily within a single region. This project focuses on expanding the scope to include not only the initial region, but also adjacent areas such as the UK and Australia. The key challenge here is accommodating diverse lighting and camera settings. Our proposed model combines a feature extractor trained on UK dataset and a custom-made classifier for combined features from all datasets. The classifier is either a custom-made neural network or a pre-trained neural network with a classified layer added. The results show that our model achieves a high overall accuracy of 85.6% and surpasses the baseline accuracy by 11%.

Imitating another's behavior in a unfamiliar setting is a common challenge.
For instance, a driver trained using a simulator may struggle to drive on public roads.
We've developed an innovative approach to tackle this problem by leveraging mimicry as the primary objective.
Through extensive testing in various domains, our method has consistently outperformed current state-of-the-art imitation learning techniques that depend on rewards.

Intensifying a star's magnetic field by several orders of magnitude may significantly impact disk fragmentation surrounding a Population III protostar. A 3D simulation of radiative magnetohydrodynamics was performed to examine this effect, with the magnetic field increased by 100 times. In this scenario, despite the increased magnetic field, the protostar continued to accumulate mass at a high rate. As a result, a 0.01 solar mass disk formed, in which no self-gravitating clumps emerged due to the magnetic field's impact on particle motion. In contrast, a 1 percent intensification of the magnetic field had little effect on fragmentation. These findings indicate that a strong magnetic field can prevent disk fragmentation, but it may not be effective in all scenarios with a weak magnetic field.

In machine learning, association rule analysis is a fundamental concept. The process typically starts by performing frequent pattern mining, which helps identify association rules using a predefined flexibility threshold. The initial step involves finding the minimum-size sets that contain all items of interest. These optimal bases are then used to create the most compact association rules. The problem becomes more complex when we are dealing with large datasets and a large number of items to be analyzed. In this research, we explored different approaches to efficiently compute the smallest-size bases, focusing on a specific type of sets that represent valuable patterns. The approaches were evaluated based on how quickly they could prune associated patterns and were further extended to utilize these results. The efficiency of our solutions was heavily dependent on the underlying deduction techniques used to the optimization process, so we also analyzed the performance of several association rule analysis algorithms using a grid-based grid file organization method. The proposed solutions were proven to be either identical to or comparable to the existing optimal solution, requiring the same number of access operations to the grid. The number of operations required to compute a single base was investigated, leading to the identification of a key challenge. The associated problem was broken down into two distinct tasks, one for each direction of search, and we proposed two new solutions that focused on the associated problem in reverse. The approaches were either identical to or comparable to the existing optimal solution, but with some variants involving the use of deduction techniques. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders. A policy requiring convicted individuals to participate in cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) as part of their sentence has shown promise in addressing this issue, though the dynamics at play are complex and the extent to which such programs affect mental health and criminal behavior is still debated. 

We utilize data from the Arizona Criminal Justice System to evaluate how the CBT policy impacted both the mental health and criminal activity of convicted individuals, as well as to identify specific demographic groups that may benefit most from this policy. Our research reveals that the CBT policy led to reduced rates of suicidal behavior and arrest, particularly among those who received CBT while incarcerated and were offered parole. Conversely, individuals whose sentences did not include CBT exhibited increased rates of suicidal behavior and arrest. Furthermore, the policy's benefits on both mental health and criminal activity were most pronounced among younger, convicted individuals who were offered parole, suggesting that targeted implementation is crucial to maximizing the policy's effectiveness.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Wireless communication systems rely heavily on radio frequency signals which are affected by their environment, resulting in varying coverage areas. To address this, researchers have developed radio maps to track signal strength patterns but are limited by the need for extensive pre-deployment surveys. To overcome this, a novel approach using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) is proposed, allowing for on-the-go signal strength collection and radio map creation. Equipped with wide-channel sensing capabilities and advanced navigation systems, UAVs can collect signal strength data across multiple locations and altitude settings. For fast and efficient mapping, a deep learning-based approach is designed, training a model to predict radio maps using collected data. To account for changes in signal strength over time and varying coverage areas, a mixed model with a stochastic process and anomaly detection is included. Test results using 4G and millimeter wave maps show promising results with the predicted maps exhibiting similar patterns and magnitudes to professionally created maps.

This study presents an innovative approach to identifying behavioral anomalies in customer transactions by integrating Hidden Markov Models with Gaussian Mixture Models. The proposed method uses the output of an HMMS-based probability calculator as input to a machine learning algorithm, which can be a support vector machine or a similar technique. The paper demonstrates the efficacy of this method by showcasing its performance on a real-world data set from a contactless payment system. The method's Anthem system, which is based on this method, has successfully identified 99.97% of genuine transactions and 99.98% of anomalous transactions. Furthermore, the method has been found to be faster than a competing method using support vector machines. The method's performance in terms of false detection rate and detection accuracy has been found to be superior to another approach. The two methods were compared by switching the training and test data sets. The method's integration of HMMS and GMMs has been found to provide a 2% improvement in performance in comparison to a approach using support vector machines. The method's use of HMMS to track the movement of data and its integration with GMMs to model the distribution of data has been found to provide a 1% improvement in performance in comparison to a approach using support vector machines. The method's reduction in computational complexity by use of HMMS and GMMs has been found to provide a 30% improvement in processing time in comparison to a approach using support vector machines. This research delves into a relatively unexplored aspect of speaker recognition, focusing on the verification process. By combining audio, visual, and thermal signals, we aim to investigate their separate and joint contributions towards individual verification. The dataset used for this study is the NIST-28 dataset, which comprises speech, facial images, and thermal images. The findings reveal that using all three modalities performs better than employing a single modality, and notable improvements are seen when incorporating thermal images, yielding superior results when compared to the current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, by applying various feature extraction techniques and models of different complexities, such as GANs and DNNs, the relative performance of the used features can be evaluated. The outcomes demonstrate that thermal images contain valuable information that can enhance speaker recognition.

Current speech translation systems are hindered by substantial gaps in data availability for lesser-resourced languages. Data augmentation has shown promise in closing this gap, yet previous approaches have proven costly and impractical for widespread adoption due to the time and expertise required. Our primary objective is to make data augmentation more accessible and efficient. We've developed a new method, incorporating style-controlled non-parallel training, which leverages vast amounts of monolingual data and doesn't demand any additional annotations. This approach can be applied across multiple tasks including as input by non-linguistic features such as speech or images. We've also created two new techniques to adapt this method for tasks involving multiple speakers, which we've successfully tested on speech recognition and translation tasks and observed significant improvements. Notably, our system yields a 6.8% relative decrease in word error rate on a speech recognition task and a 2.0% relative drop in BLEU score on a translation task, with the added benefit of closing the performance gap with foreign languages such as Chinese with minimal effort and expertise.

Estimating the mean population parameter from a mixture of independent samples is a complex problem that has seen various methods and controversies over finite sample confidence intervals. This study proposes a new method of estimating the mean parameter $\theta$ using information from mixtures, based on the maximum likelihood principle for mixed distributions, and outlines a general approach for constructing asymptotic confidence intervals. Our method is particularly useful in analyzing data from populations with skewed distributions, and offers improved results in comparison to the standard estimate, primarily due to its superior performance in scenarios with small sample sizes. Importantly, the new method allows us to analyze the behavior of sample means and establish asymptotic properties, such as consistency and efficiency, for quantities like the sample mean. Our results can be applied to various population parameters, and we demonstrate this by investigating the behavior of two key statistics: the first, which relates to the sample variance, and the second, which indicates skewness in distributions. Our study further reveals that the new method enables us to establish limit theorems for quantities like the maximum value in a sample, effective degree of freedom, and the skewness of distributions, and facilitates the construction of asymptotic confidence intervals. Notably, our framework can be used to establish limit theorems for quantities like the minimum value in a sample, the Deviance, and the Pearson statistic. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of the new method to testing hypotheses in a mixture population, specifically, testing whether two independent samples come from the same or different

In one-sided differential privacy, achieving optimal utility and accurately measuring privacy risk is particularly challenging when dealing with private datasets that have mutually dependent records. The standard approach used to gauge privacy risk under the one-sided model involves calculating the probability of record identification relative to a hypothetical release of sensitive information. However, this method tends to overstate the risk of record identification when dealing with datasets that have correlated data, which in turn affects utility. Our research introduces a more nuanced framework for assessing record identification in the context of dependent datasets. This framework comprises two components: a statistical model used to quantify containment risks and a metric called risk difference, which offers a more comprehensive measurement of record identification. By leveraging risk difference, we can quantify the trade-off between utility and privacy more effectively. Furthermore, when coupled with risk difference, the proposed model enables more accurate evaluation and evaluation of privacy risk. Specifically, we found that the proposed model yields lower risk measurements compared to the traditional approach, which in turn results in better utility under the one-sided model. To illustrate the efficacy of our model, we conducted experiments using real-world datasets.

In protoplanetary disks, it is common to find gas and solid particles separated. Our investigation into the As 209 disk has revealed a $^{12}$CO gas depletion of three orders of magnitude within a 200 AU wide zone. We have analyzed the CO emission averaged across 11 epochs spanning six years and found it to remain consistently low. Our findings about the CO gas abundance are not affected by prior gas removal through planetary mass objects or other dynamic processes, as they would likely restore or increase the CO emission. Furthermore, a model based on chemical processing of CO by dust particles does not fit the observed data. It is possible that the low CO gas abundance is a result of the development of planetesimals that eventually became planets or other massive objects that created this CO gap.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the TimeTagAnalyzer (TTagAn), a robust, user-friendly, and adaptable software tool. It's designed to handle large datasets from high-resolution digitizers up to 16 bits, and can manage up to 2 gigasamples per channel per second on multiple parallel channels, with an unlimited number of tracks. Featuring an intuitive graphical interface, TTagAn offers various analysis techniques, including waveforms, spectra, timelines, histograms, projections, and fit functions, as well as custom visualization and export options. Furthermore, the software is versatile and can be applied beyond digitizer data, such as in medical, industrial, and astrophysics research, making it an invaluable resource for time-stamped data analysis.

We prove the existence of mild solutions for a mean field game involving a single controller with two distinct objectives, subject to movement restrictions within multiple, non-overlapping domains. One objective involves optimizing a Lagrangian function, while the other involves minimizing a cost function that takes into account an interaction term and a spatial constraint. The existence of these mild solutions follows from our assumption that the mapping from state to density is continuous, along with initial conditions that are relatively regular.

The latest release of the Gaia Data Release 3 includes data for 243,614 stars within the Milky Way's plane, allowing researchers to study filamentary structures in the stars' distribution. These structures, initially detected in the stars' Galactocentric residual motion, initially supported the idea of stellar filaments originating from the stars' formation in expanding bars. However, this idea might not be entirely correct. Analyzing the stars' locations and their motion, researchers discovered that the apparent filamentary structures are primarily caused by the stars' close proximity in the plane of the galaxy, resulting in similar residual motions. Furthermore, these structures are not continuous, with gaps present and varying in density. The concept of stellar filaments is found to be an illusion resulting from the limitations of the Gaia data's 0.11 mas/y error in line-of-sight velocity, and the projected density of these structures is found to be independent of their distance from the galactic plane. The Gaia data contains far fewer stellar filaments than initially thought, and these structures likely consist of early-type stars and young stellar objects. The Gaia data cannot be used to detect stellar filaments without further data refinement, and the proposed method for detecting these structures is found to be inadequate.

For visually incompatible items, such as a pair of shorts and a long coat, it's essential to determine if they are compatible based on visual characteristics. Current fashion compatibility prediction tasks are often complicated by incomplete outfit images and diverse fashion items with many variants. In this study, we introduce a novel task called visual incompatibility identification (VIID) and propose the Vision Incompatibility Transformer Observing Resources (VICTOR) model to tackle it. VICTOR relies on a unique pre-trained fashion-focused visual transformer, designed to learn visual distinctions, to determine incompatibility between two fashion items. It does this by using a contrastive learning approach to train the model, with the output improved upon incorporating outfit information. We conduct experiments on a unique dataset of visually incompatible fashion item pairs, known as the Vienna Fashion Incompatibility Dataset (VFID), and find that our proposed model consistently outperforms existing fashion-related benchmarks. Additionally, we demonstrate the VICTOR model's ability to make useful fashion insights by asking it to decide the incompatibility between random fashion item pairs.

Building on conventional light source characterizations, a advanced framework, known as the resource theory of nonclassical light, evaluates illuminating capabilities based on fundamental principles. This approach divides light sources into fundamental elements, namely operators, and analyzes obtainable transformations between them. In our review, we incorporate recent developments in the light source characterizations, encompassing nonclassical light resources and applications of quantum combs. Furthermore, we discuss models for coupling radiation fields, light-matter interactions, and the influence of nonclassical light on matter. This enables a comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics governing nonclassical light sources.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning increases, synchronization challenges arise due to differences in update speeds and sizes. To overcome this, researchers have proposed various aggregation methods that compensate for delayed or missing updates, but existing solutions primarily focus on idealized scenarios and can be impractical for real-world deployments. This leads to a gap between theoretical optimization and practical implementation. To address this, we introduce a flexible and practical decentralized asynchronous federated learning framework that allows each device to optimize at its own pace and share updates at predetermined aggregation points. Our approach utilizes a unified buffer to store and apply device updates, enabling a range of optimization techniques and dynamic aggregation methods. Specifically, we show that the gradient-based aggregation method can be inefficient due to slow convergence caused by slow-learning devices, and propose a simple bias-correction technique to address this issue. Our framework can be applied to various optimization methods, and we test its effectiveness with several realistic simulation scenarios, demonstrating superior performance compared to traditional synchronous learning methods.

This study introduces a novel functional space, denoted by $\mathcal{S}_\beta^\ast$, which is an extension of the Schwartz space. We have developed the required functionals for both continuous and weakly continuous versions of several key properties, including convergence in mean, smooth convergence, compactness, and continuous embedding within the space. Furthermore, we have established the dual space of $\mathcal{S}_\beta^\ast$ and examined the continuity of various operators mapping from $\mathcal{S}_^{\ast}{\beta}$ to various space distributions, specifically including (but not limited to) the space of tempered distributions $\mathcal{S}^\prime(\mathbb{R}^d)$. We have further applied the results to study the properties of several specific operators, including convolution operators and infinite weighted shift operators.

Recent research suggests that dark matter might be comprised of primordial black holes. Last year, researchers proposed that dark energy's rate of expansion could serve as a indicator of the presence of dark objects, such as black holes, within the Swampland. Today, further investigation into the relationship between dark matter and black holes is conducted by considering the Dark Dimension theory, which describes the gravitational force's interaction with dark energy and dark matter. Assuming that dark matter is composed of black holes, estimates suggest that dark matter's fraction comprised of these primordial black holes is relatively small, on the order of 10^-9 to 1. This has significant implications as the relationship between dark energy, dark matter, and black holes is altered, affecting the accuracy of cosmic predictions based on the Dark Dimension model. As a result, predictions of the model, which initially suggested a dark energy density-to-curve density ratio of approximately 0.51, alter to around around 0.35. Furthermore, considering the possibility that this primordial black hole fraction could be as high as 1 also leads to similar changes in the model's predictions.

To understand the relationship between membrane structure and the functioning of cell membranes, researchers studied the mechanics of fluid lipid membranes using molecular dynamics simulations. By manipulating experimental conditions in the simulations to match those of scanning electron microscopy images, researchers observed the formation of lipid rafts in membranes with and without cholesterol at various temperatures. The results showed that these structures appear due to the uneven distribution of lipids and not as a result of gaps in the membranes as previously suggested by experimental images. The presence of cholesterol increased the stability of lipid rafts by reducing their tendency to dissolve. The characteristics of lipid rafts were dependent on the size of differences in lipid properties and not just their quantity. Researchers also found that the movement of proteins within the membrane was influenced by the presence of cholesterol and the stability of lipid rafts. The implications of these findings are that cell membrane organization may be more complex than initially thought and require consideration of the movement and characteristics of individual membrane components.

The main challenge preventing further advancement in gallium nitride technology lies in its poor hole mobility. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed, involving the strain-induced modification of the hole quasi-Fermi level in n-type GaN, achieved through lattice matching to zinc germanium nitride and magnesium silicon nitride. A numerical simulation reveals that targeting specific strain values can increase the hole mobility, with the optimal conditions yielding a hole mobility of 200 cm$^2$/V s at 300 K, comparable to that of silicon. Moreover, taking cost and material purity factors into account, an optimal set of parameters is identified that balances hole mobility and strain, forecasting a notable improvement in gallium nitride performance.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  Underwater conditions are characterized by the robots' observations being noisy and inter-dependent due to the water's scattering properties. Moreover, events in the underwater environment occur sequentially, resulting in non-stationarity in temporal differences. To address these issues, we developed a Gaussian Process based TD learning method using sparse approximation techniques. This innovative method not only incorporates multi-dimensional noisy observations but also accommodates a variable step-size for more efficient learning. Our experimental evaluations demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses traditional TD learning methods in various underwater navigation tasks.

We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that contains only meromorphic functions when projected onto the Gaussian curvature function. The transformations of Darboux and Calapso are applied to these surfaces, resulting in new examples of such surfaces. Specifically, the application of Darboux transformation yields new isothermic surfaces with specific harmonic rank, while Calapso transformation leads to new meromorphically isothermic surfaces.

This study investigates the behavior of conventional estimation methods for conditional expectation operators in the context of nearly nonparametric frameworks. Our primary focus lies in the application of these expectations in optimal treatment selection problems and their subsequent use within policy evaluation and optimization. A central aspect that informs our research is the widespread reliance on these expectations in modern policy analysis, particularly in fields like medicine and social science, where researchers often face costly treatment options and require conditional expectations to inform their choices. Despite the importance of accurate estimators in these domains, existing studies often rely on parametric models or impose stringent assumptions on data without rigorous evaluation. Conversely, this research seeks to establish reliable estimation methods that account for more realistic scenarios, ultimately enabling policymakers to make more precise decisions. Our key contributions lie in the development of consistent and efficient estimators for conditional expectation operators, which we achieve by combining conventional techniques with innovative adjustments that minimize bias. Furthermore, we demonstrate the behavior of these estimators at critical points, such as corners and edges, and analyze their performance under smooth scenarios, while also accounting for the challenges posed by treatment selection. Ultimately, our research validates the potential of direct estimation methods and demonstrates their ability to overcome issues associated with alternative approaches, such as partially identified models. A accompanying supplement features additional results and numerical simulations, which support the findings presented in this study.

This research extends previous findings on the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind. Initially, we formulate the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and their recursive relationships. Subsequently, we derive identities involving the $\lambda$-analogues of Whitney-type $r$-Stirling numbers as well as their cumulative sums. Our results are further demonstrated through complementary combinatorial interpretations.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents opportunities for enhanced accuracy in various applications, albeit with increased complexity. Research has been conducted on modeling temporal contexts, but many studies still rely on static representations, neglecting the potential encoded information. This paper reexamines the utility of static models in addressing link prediction tasks for temporal knowledge graphs. By leveraging the knowledge graph's inherent connections and temporal structure, a static model can excel. To achieve this, we developed KASK, a static knowledge graph model integrated with temporal characteristics, which effectively utilizes past and present relationships to inform predictions. KASK's results demonstrate a significant improvement over existing static models and rival optimized temporal models, earning top rankings in various challenges at the Knowledge Graph Embedding Evaluation Challenge 2021.

We re-examine the definition and strengthen the concept of robust shift equivalence (RS) originally proposed for row-finite graphs and associated C*-algebras. Our modified definition is self-consistent, univocal, and aligns with the conventional notion of shift equivalence (SE) among graphs and C*-algebras. The set of robustly shift equivalent row-finite graphs and their associated C*-algebras forms a local invariant. The relationship between SE and RS is asymmetric; however, both concepts share numerous equivalences. The class of graphs exhibiting SE is closed under various operations, whereas RS showcases some degree of flexibility in these operations. The same applies to the class of C*-algebras. Our study of row-finite graphs and their associated C*-algebras through the lens of robust shift equivalence presents a novel framework that combines local invariants and bochner integrable functions, thereby bridging the gap between infinite and finite index systems.

In this research, we have examined the complex phase structure of a quark, formed by the combination of its forward propagator and its decay rate in the presence of a non-zero magnetic field. Our findings indicate that when moving in a direction perpendicular to the magnetic field, the magnetic field's strength causes the phase structure to shift towards higher temperatures, while the opposite effect occurs when the magnetic field's direction is parallel to the quark's momentum. Furthermore, we have discovered that the boundary temperatures are temperature-dependent and follow renormalization group equations. Our study also reveals that when the magnetic field's strength varies, there is a displacement in the phase structure's temperature. Notably, we observed that the central boundary temperature remains unaffected by the magnetic field, whereas the temperatures at the anisotropic directions are influenced by it. Our results can be applied to understand the behavior of heavy quark under extreme conditions and may also be relevant in studying transport properties and anisotropic flow patterns.

To accurately respond to questions, language models can benefit from referencing external knowledge databases, yet incorporating such knowledge often limits model responsiveness or compromises fluency. Our proposed knowledge inference question answering (KIQA) framework addresses this challenge by enabling language models to leverage knowledge graphs in processing questions, while maintaining efficient inference through the utilization of prefix trees and simplified logical expressions. When applied to modern language models, this approach leads to notable improvements in question answering accuracy, with results showing our foundation model achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets, and even surpassing specialized knowledge-enhanced models in certain cases. Furthermore, by allowing models to determine whether knowledge should be employed in responding to a given question, our approach prevents models from overly relying on external knowledge, resulting in more natural responses.

We introduce novel high-dimensional extenders derived from covers of simplicial complexes. This derangement gives rise to new invariants of finite simplicial complexes and enables dimension-independent relationships between volume and surface area, alongside dimension-independent bounds on section numbers. Additionally, we demonstrate that the central cut capacity exhibits a particularly strong dimension-dependent increase. Furthermore, our work facilitates the creation of a highly efficient algorithm for calculating cut capacities in high-dimensional scenarios.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence the model's performance most substantially. To this end, we undertake a comprehensive investigation of the relationship between prompt characteristics and the model's performance across multiple fixed choice tasks using the GPT-3 model as a benchmark. Our study reveals that prompts exhibiting characteristics of multiple lists (as opposed to singular statements) and utilizing the 'is' and 'you' forms of verbs (as opposed to 'am' and 'you are') tend to yield superior performance. Interestingly, the beneficial effect of prompt modification on model performance is found to be significantly larger than the variation in model parameters. It is observed that models exposed to the same task but crafted with diverse prompts consistently outperform their non-prompted counterparts and those subjected to less effective prompts. Moreover, the differences in prompt design are found to yield predictions with prediction accuracies rivaling those resulting from complex learning rules, underscoring the practical significance of prompt engineering.

In this paper, we explore the relationship between regular finite modules of a local ring and its unramified and ramified local coefficients. This investigation stems from the introduction of $\mathscr{L}$-invariants, a newly proposed concept, to gauge module properties. Notably, we examine how $\mathscr{L}$-invariants embody previously noted irregularities in Artin symbols.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve these challenges, we've 
increased the sensitivity of Rydberg atom detectors by utilizing deep learning 
models, leveraging our simulation data of random frequency spectra. Deep 
learning's ability to process complex patterns outperforms traditional methods, 
enabling the extraction of hidden signal patterns even when the frequencies 
are not initially known. This breakthrough enables more accurate Rydberg atom 
detection in demanding environments.

UGC 8839, an isolated spiral galaxy with minimal environmental impact, exhibits exceptional stability considering its prominent spiral features. The origin of this exceptional stability is puzzling, especially when compared to galaxies like NGC 891, which has similar characteristics but more turbulent motion. To resolve this mystery, we conducted detailed gas research using data from the HI JUMP survey and found that UGC 8839 contains an extensive, highly stable disk of neutral hydrogen. The HI gas in UGC 8839 follows the expected rotation curve and exhibits minimal velocity dispersion, indicating its remarkable stability. The HI gas distribution in UGC 8839 also precisely mirrors the optical image, suggesting a unified system. The HI research suggests that the interaction between the dark matter halo and the HI gas is consistent with the parameters established in a previous study. The exceptional stability of UGC 8839 can be explained by its dark matter halo and hydrodynamic processes that have slowed down radial gas flows, preventing bar formation and maintaining its distinctive features.

For a quasiregular self-map of 3D space that's not a rotation or inversion, we've found a few theorems relating to its Hausdorff measures and how they interact with the dynamically natural invariant sets it creates. Specifically, if a given quasiregular map has a natural invariant set that conforms to a certain dimension-bound in a specific sense, then it will also have maps associated with it that adhere to particular equations, effectively filling in spaces, such as the entire 3D space, consistently across various scales. Additionally, under the same map, measures that behave according to certain scaling rules when zoomed in will also be influenced by counts of its naturally occurring mappings, effectively giving the map's action on these measures a sort of'maximum' or upper bound in a specific sense, effectively filling in spaces, such as the entire 3D space, consistently across various scales.

Using the Earth's gravity field, the atmospheric behavior is analyzed to identify and model gravity waves in the Mars thermosphere. The analysis utilizes data from four spacecraft: Mars Global Surveyor, Mars Odyssey, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and ODY/MRO/MAVEN spacecraft, collecting density measurements over the 100-500 km altitude range. The ODY/MRO/MAVEN dataset encompasses 1210 days of observations at the Ares Polaris site, spanning from 2006 to 2019. The ODY/MRO/MAVEN measurements exhibit variability in frequency and period, ranging from a few days to several weeks, and are affected by solar activity, wind patterns, and the site's latitude. Zonal winds were observed at the Ares Polaris site, contrasting with the standing wave patterns seen in the polar region, which were unaffected by solar activity. The presence of wave periods aligning with the ODY/MRO/MAVEN orbital periods is noticed, and the amplitude of these waves shows correlation with the orbit and density fluctuations. The observations support the idea that the ODY/MRO/MAVEN spacecraft are detecting gravity waves caused by their own revolution. The persistent, modulated gravity waves in the MAVEN mission's early phase remain unexplained, but may be induced by atmospheric soliton waves. The analysis confirms that the ODY/MRO/MAVEN spacecraft are effectively measuring gravity waves, but the origin of all observed waves cannot be determined without considering the role of

The LHC holds great potential for studying nuclear phenomena via relativistic heavy-ion collisions, particularly photoproduction interactions that occur when particles collide with nuclear targets. One notable phenomenon that can result from these interactions is the forward photoproduction of charmonium states, which are sensitive to the cold nuclear matter effects of cold quantum chromodynamics. Recent discoveries at the LHC have opened up new avenues for investigating exclusive charmonium production in heavy-ion collisions. This report outlines recent findings from ALICE's research on the forward J/ψ production in Pb--Pb ultra-peripheral collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV and a detector forward rapidity range of 3.4 to 5.4. The research considers differential yields, nuclear modification factors, and nuclear luminosities as critical factors. The differential yields of exclusive charmonium production are presented as functions of rapidity, energy, and transverse momentum, while the nuclear modification factors are examined in relation to the centrality of collisions and discrete rapidity intervals. Additionally, this report compares these findings with theoretical models and draws relevant conclusions.

Recent breakthroughs in audio synthesis research have made it possible to create high-quality sounds tailored to visual stimuli, but visually guided sound generation remains a difficult task, especially when it comes to producing diverse sounds. Existing models require precise frame-by-frame direction, making it challenging to generate sounds for longer periods or when there's no guidance. This challenges their use in tasks like sound track creation. Our study addresses this limitation by allowing our model to forget and adapt to new cues at any frame. This makes it suitable for tasks needing extended audio synthesis. Our model discards cues that aren't relevant to the current sound generation. Cues are considered relevant if they lead to improved sound quality, based on feedback signals. Our model, Self-Tuning TPG, can effectively utilize and update its cue priorities. By forgetting unhelpful cues, it can generate more relevant sound. Our study shows that prioritization leads to sound quality improvements. Additionally, since human-runnable feedback isn't available until the end of an audio clip, we use the model to predict and select the most helpful cues. This "exploration" process leads to better sound quality. Our work was validated through objective evaluations and by successfully generating high-quality sounds for both short and long periods in multiple scenarios.

Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential and temporal data in various applications, differing from traditional neural networks in their ability to maintain temporal relationships. Key innovations have refined recurrent neural networks, addressing limitations imposed by the unidirectional flow of information, resulting in several variants such as LSTM and GRU that are widely employed in contemporary research. Despite these advancements, fewer resources are available that provide an overarching understanding of the fundamentals, causing a knowledge gap in the field. To bridge this gap, this chapter delves into the principles of recurrent neural networks, evaluating both early and state-of-the-art developments in the field.

Achieving a balance between economic well-being and public health during a pandemic pandemic is a pressing issue. Mathematical models can be employed to model policy measures that maintain this equilibrium. In this research, a basic pandemic model with basic public health interventions is presented. It's proven that there's a universal solution that satisfies two critical conditions: 1) the pandemic must decline at some point in time, and 2) the second wave must decline before the first, and this solution can be calculated exactly. Additionally, policies that align with this universal solution minimize both health damage and economic loss. Historically, similar models have been used to study pandemics and economic crises, and it's been assumed that some public health interventions are necessary to maintain economic stability, but this assumption is invalidated by our findings.

The development of more sophisticated computer programs to carry out tasks is crucial, 
but the increasing complexity of these programs also makes them more difficult to create and debug.
Machine learning systems, which can perform tasks like image recognition, are particularly hard to debug 
because the problems that occur during execution often differ from the issues in the data used for training.
In response to these challenges, researchers are working to develop tools that can help with debugging machine learning programs. 
This paper describes a new technique called Shapley Significance that can be used to debug problems with machine learning programs. 
To test its effectiveness, the technique was applied to two real-world scenarios, including a project for identifying problems with images of plant leaves and another for estimating the value of items sold online. 
The experiments demonstrated that Shapley Significance can identify up to 90% of issues with data sets and 95% of problems with machine learning models, while also confirming the accuracy of the models and data used in the programs.

The underlying structure of numerous statistical models, which are used to analyze random phenomena, can be elucidated through the application of algebraic and combinatorial principles. By employing tools from enumerative geometry and combinatorics, researchers can derive precise counting formulas, leading to statistical conclusions. For instance, studying Poincaré polynomial enables analysts to calculate moments and distribution functions, while utilizing generating functions provides access to limiting behavior, including Lyapunov instability and central limit theorems. Building complex network models, which are ubiquitous in modern biology, physics, and engineering, offers another area of application for these geometric and combinatorial techniques. Examples of successful modeling include social networks, viral evolution, and traffic patterns. By modeling network behavior using topological methods and calculating key properties using enumerative geometry, researchers can gain valuable insights into network dynamics.

This study provides an in-depth examination of how the anomalous Hall effect operates under various conditions in the triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn. Initially, we find that the anomalous Hall effect is present at low temperatures, and its value can be maximally enhanced when the temperature is around 100 K. Furthermore, this research investigates how pressure affects this phenomenon by utilizing diamond anvil cells to apply pressure and observe the results. The experiments reveal that increasing pressure transforms Mn$_3$Sn from a state with a single phase to a state with three phases, specifically a hexagonal close-packed phase, a face-centered cubic phase, and a L$_1$$_0$ martensitic phase. The most intriguing finding is that the anomalous Hall effect either increases or decreases in response to pressure, and these two scenarios correspond exclusively to the initial and final phases, respectively. The maximum anomalous Hall effect resistance can be as high as 3.8 million ohms, making Mn$_3$Sn a unique material for studying magnetoelectric phenomena and exploring the anomalous Hall effect in response to pressure.

In the digital age, individuals and organizations are increasingly leaving behind digital trails that consist of varied online content. One essential aspect of content is connections, which can take many forms such as physical links, attachments, or citations. These connections hold crucial implied meaning that can be exploited by algorithms to infer implied relationships and perform tasks like sentiment analysis, data summarization, and text translation. Despite their significance, connections remain unaddressed by state-of-the-art methods for content analysis. Recent research has explored the potential of deep neural networks to automatically identify and interpret implicit relationships within content. A thorough literature review has enabled the creation of a comprehensive taxonomy that subclassifies connection extraction tasks into explicit, implicit, and sequential extraction tasks, and also highlights prominent methods and evaluation metrics. Experimental evaluations have been conducted to compare the effectiveness of different approaches for extraction tasks. This study provides an extensive overview of recent developments in connection extraction using deep neural networks, and addresses critical issues such as data scarcity, evaluation reliability, and robust model generalization.

We resolve the Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem by analyzing a generalised eigenvalue problem for the Dirac operator, where it's established that the Steklov-Robin eigenvalues coincide with those of the Dirac operator, while the corresponding eigenfunctions are connected to the spectral decomposition of the Dirac operator.

We introduce a novel approach to restore a primal problem's underlying hypergraph structure from the perspective of a given dual problem. Our proposed method, guided hypergraph reconstruction, facilitates the reconstruction of a primal problem's hypergraph by maximizing the dual problem's objective function. We demonstrate the equivalence of maximizing the dual function to finding the maximum number of vertex disjoint hyperedges in the dual problem's constraint structure. Our computational experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that GHM efficiently constructs a primal hypergraph that effectively represents the dual problem's complex structure. Additionally, GHM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in predicting the dual problem's optimal solution and achieving dual feasibility.

Previous research on interpreting X-ray images has focused on understanding medical reports in conjunction with annotated images.  However, there are inherent limitations to using image-data pairs, particularly when it comes to reading X-rays, as many reports contain essential information not visible on the X-ray image itself.  To better capture the content of medical reports, we've developed an enhanced dataset of annotations that includes text-only descriptions of patients' chest X-rays.  To create this dataset, we used the CRNN model to generate annotations, but found that simply using the model's output wasn't enough - we had to incorporate expertise and add constraints to ensure the accuracy and consistency of the annotations.  To achieve this, we implemented a novel technique for controlling the annotations, allowing us to tailor the output based on the report's content and ensuring that the generated annotations conform to the requirements of the dataset.  We've found that by adding flexibility to the annotation generation process, we've been able to create a dataset with higher quality annotations.  As a result, we've seen significant improvements in our model's performance - our approach has allowed us to achieve a state-of-the-art F1-score of 0.715 for machine reading of medical reports on chest X-rays, establishing a new benchmark for future research.

Previous research linked the Euler characteristic of a tight contact 3-manifold's underlying union of embedded curves to the first integer division of its genus. This investigation extends that connection to incorporate Euler characteristics of more general tight contact 3-manifolds, derived from modifying the embedded curves' union through surgery operations.

This study evaluates the role of entropy in the emission direction of lasers with microcavity configurations. The analysis begins with a general model of entropy, followed by a numerical investigation of the entropy of the photon field as a function of microcavity shape and emission direction. The results reveal that elliptical microcavities produce more directional emissions, achieving lower entropy levels compared to circular cavities for the same emission patterns.

Our research identifies three essential factors that contribute to the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. These factors are (1) stable storage, (2) secure transactions with low fees, and (3) the ability of users to efficiently use cryptocurrencies. We examined the historical period from December 2017 to December 2020 in detail. During this time, cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin maintained their value due to high liquidity and substantial market capitalization. We found that altcoins typically could not compete with Bitcoin in providing a stable store of value, leading to volatility. Furthermore, when altcoins facilitated fast and low-feese transactions, they experienced significant price declines as users reduced demand. Therefore, cryptocurrencies offering all three functions cannot be compared to traditional fiat currencies, while those providing only two functions have yet to meet the standards of stable mediums of exchange set by Bitcoin.

Solving the inverse problem for the Zakharov-Shabat system allows us to link certain statistical properties of KPZ equation's averaged height in the weak noise regime to system parameters. Combining this with mathematical models of KPZ height with noisy inwards growth, we can show that certain statistical measures, such as the distribution of height's slow component and its second moment, can be expressed as finite sums of system's spectral functions. These measures can be calculated through numerical methods, effectively answering corresponding KPZ questions: we can quantitatively confirm that the width of the resulting distribution, ~x^(1/3), and the second moment's growth, ~t^(2/3), hold over both large t and x. This confirms the predictions made by mathematicians towards the broader class of "2a/b, a/b>1" KPZ universality classes based on existing mathematical models. Notably, this calculation yields precise numerical coefficients for these quantities: the distribution's shape, previously theorized to be gamma-like; the second moment's growth rate; and the resulting "universal" finite system's behavior, all of which are now precisely quantified.

We analyzed calm solar plasma compressive waves measured by the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission at 1.1 AU on October 24, 2016. These waves exhibit low-frequency fluctuations of 0.1 Hz with significant variations in density and temperature. Our analysis focuses on electron dynamics, utilizing the spacecraft potential and electron drift time measurements. This revealed fine-scale structures within the waves, approximately 60 cm, associated with electron temperature fluctuations. These structures contain both electron currents and temperature disparities, suggesting heat conduction plays a crucial role. Two key findings support this role: the temperature fluctuations moderate larger scale pressures and the electron distribution function exhibits the expected random phase relationships. These findings are consistent with hydrodynamic behavior.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a novel strategy, the Chirp and Taper (CT) scheme, to break these limitations. By adjusting the undulator parameters and allowing for electron beam manipulation, CT allows for optimized pulse sharpening, with promising results achievable with current production-line FEL facilities. Simulation outcomes indicate that pulses with durations as low as several hundred attoseconds can be obtained for wavelengths around 10 nm, while pulses in the soft X-ray domain may be narrowed down to roughly 300 fs. The CT scheme holds potential to yield high-power, short-pulse FEL sources with outputs in the range of hundreds of watts.

A mathematical model of a viscous and stratified shear flow is developed using a two-dimensional idealized scenario. The model incorporates a flow profile that varies linearly in one dimension and remains undisturbed in another, characterized by different regions of constant and varying viscosity. The effective viscosity of the model is calculated based on an energy balance between the flow's inertial and viscous forces, resulting in an estimation of the flow's instability. The model relies on a dimensionless instability parameter, known as the EL parameter, which exists within a range of 0 to 1 and significantly affects the flow's behavior. The extension of the model to account for finite amplitude disturbances is also explored, leading to a new equation that describes the growth rate of these disturbances in terms of the EL parameter. The model performs well in comparison to high-resolution numerical simulations, with some discrepancies observed at low EL values. The model's applicability to real-world atmospheric scenarios is examined through the analysis of observational data, considering various factors that might influence the flow. The model is found to provide a reasonable approximation of the flow's behavior, but certain assumptions of the model may not accurately represent the flow's non-linear characteristics in these instances.

The United States electoral system has undergone significant changes following the landmark Supreme Court case of Citizens United v. FEC in 2010. These modifications have led to the manipulation of voting districts for partisan advantage, a practice known as electoral gerrymandering. The community has developed various metrics to quantify this type of manipulation. However, these metrics have yet to be extensively tested in terms of their reliability and ease of use. In response, we introduce a novel method utilizing simulated annealing, a probabilistic optimization technique, to evaluate the effectiveness of different metrics in detecting electoral gerrymandering. Our findings demonstrate that several established metrics can effectively detect the phenomenon, while others prove to be inefficient.

A novel defect identification approach for patterned fabrics is proposed, featuring a unique descriptor called G-rotation, which provides an optimized solution. Additionally, a technique using low-rank decomposition is developed to eliminate repetitive background information in images. The described method combines Grade-level O-rotation Gradient (GHOG) and low-rank decomposition to create a robust and efficient descriptor for defect identification. The proposed descriptor leverages the unique properties of GHOG to describe defects' characteristics more accurately and reduces computational complexity. The low-rank decomposition technique further enhances the descriptor's performance by eliminating noise and background information, thereby improving overall results. Experimental outcomes confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method in identifying defects across diverse patterns and backgrounds.

To create versatile reinforcement learning agents across various domains, it's crucial to prevent them from overemphasizing minor fluctuations in their environment. The current research applies an information-measuring constraint to the reinforcement learning framework and assesses its effectiveness on image-based navigation tasks. The proposed method incorporates an informational penalty term into the optimization process, which stops the agent from exploiting irrelevant environmental details. The experiment results demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses conventional reinforcement learning models, showcasing its capacity to resist noise-induced distractions. The research suggests that regularizing the reinforcement learning framework with an informational penalty term is vital for developing agents resistant to environmental fluctuations.

Research indicates that stars experiencing strong gravitational interactions typically undergo mass loss. The extent of mass loss and its associated mechanisms have been extensively studied, but the amount of material lost and its associated cross-sectional area remains unclear. We utilized observations from the Gaia satellite to determine the frequency of compact binary productions from diverse stellar interaction types, then applied these findings to estimate the rate and typical cross-sectional area of stars undergoing mass loss through gravitational interactions. Our research indicates that this typical cross-sectional area ranges between 1.9*10^13 cm^2 and 1.6*10^14 cm^2. We discovered that many binary systems comprising white dwarfs experience mass loss due to the rosyinstability, resulting in fewer such systems observable in Gaia data, likely because they become invisible soon after the associated transfer of material. Our research indicates that most stars undergoing gravitational interactions experience some mass loss, but the extent of that loss is highly variable.

We examine the generation of gravitational waves from the remnants of the first stars that form in the centers of early formed galaxies and nuclear star clusters. These stars, primarily with masses in the range of 100 to 1000 solar masses, emerge in areas with high density where the initial accretion of material is hindered. As a result, they develop rapidly and evolve into the most massive objects in their surroundings before eventually running out of fuel. Depending on the initial mass of these stars, they either collapse directly into white dwarfs or undergo collapse via instability and explosive binary mergers, resulting in the formation of a neutron star or black hole with a mass of 2.3 to 3.0 times that of the sun. The entire process of collapse is a significant event that produces intense bursts of gravitational waves over a wide frequency range, with powers that can reach as high as 50 percent of the energy emitted via other mechanisms such as the collapse of individual stars in the universe. The gravitational waves emitted have a characteristic shape, with the frequency determined by the mass of the stars and the distance between them, or less than a few millimeters, while the amplitude is primarily an function of the initial mass of the stars, with the actual value subject to variation. The frequency of the waves typically spans from a few millihertz to 300,000 hertz, with the average energy content per unit of logarithmic frequency range within the LIGO/Virginia Tech range having an energy

In modern city-life, reliable power distribution systems (PDS) are currently operating at maximum capacity, providing essential services to both residential and industrial areas. However, PDS instability and congestion incidents frequently occur, causing significant losses for companies and potentially jeopardizing supply contracts. Conventional methods used to identify these incidents usually rely on manual data collection from newspapers and company websites, which is inefficient and cannot guarantee accuracy or timely results. To address this limitation, this research proposes a novel approach, involving the creation of an advanced database to collect and process PDS data, enabling the development of an innovative detection system. By analyzing transaction records of real-time data, the proposed system can accurately identify incidents and estimate their durations. Furthermore, to safeguard user data and maintain system security, the research outlines a comprehensive strategy to safeguard the database and incidence data. To validate the proposed system's effectiveness, case studies were conducted in two major areas, showcasing the method's capabilities. The proposed system can seamlessly integrate with existing real-time monitoring systems, providing a versatile solution that can be applied to various domains beyond PDS incident detection.

Our study focuses on examining the radiative and radiative double decay processes of the $X(3872)$, specifically investigating the contributions of different components and their interrelations. Additionally, we aim to determine whether the X(3872) can be solely described by a $0^{+}$ $c\bar{c}s\bar{s}$ system or if it also includes other possible configurations. The X(3872) is observed to undergo both decays with considerable branching ratios, with the X(3872)$\rightarrow$ J/$\psi \pi \gamma$ and X(3872)$\rightarrow$ J/$\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ branching ratios ranging from $5.7\cdot 10^{-4}$ to $3.1\cdot 10^{-3}$ and $1.1\cdot 10^{-4}$ to $6.4\cdot 10^{-4}$, respectively. These findings also imply specific sensitivity to the X(3872)'s decay width and resonance structure, which could be crucial in resolving its nature.

We provide a comprehensive description of smooth quadrics in terms of categories equipped with additional structural components, specifically linearly generated subcategories of FM-modules that are full, closed, and possess scalar symmetry. Our description subsequently yields a characterization for quadrics based on their Goresky-MacPherson charts and Hilbert schemes of points, reducing the characterization to properties of these objects.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
