One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their relatively low frame rates, topping out at around 600 actions per second, largely due to the reliance on classical string manipulation methods for processing input and output.
These speed restrictions result in prolonged simulation times, often exceeding one hour for some games, limiting the feasibility of conducting extensive testing.
Consequently, researchers are compelled to employ various accelerated testing techniques, such as environmental modifications, agent guidance, and agent retraining.
Notably, all these methods necessitate either game-specific modifications or require agents to adapt to altered environments.
Regrettably, these strategies can fail to effectively transfer learning to related tasks, thus requiring either the reuse of trained agents or the development of new agents tailored to specific tasks.
In contrast, a newly designed text-based game engine, called Express, has been created to process text descriptions at an incredibly fast rate of over one million actions per second, outclassing all classical and state-of-the-art approaches by a substantial margin of at least fifty times acceleration.
The integration of a sophisticated data structure, called the n-ary heap, enables unprecedented speed boosts, along with more than twenty novel algorithms and a strategic parsing technique that yields significant performance enhancements.
Most notably, the engine parses input and output in a fraction of a millisecond, allowing the training of agents capable of learning from vast amounts of

To ensure our energy technologies remain sustainable and environmentally responsible, 
we must minimize our carbon footprint while ensuring we transition quickly to meet future demands.
One promising energy source is the energy harvested through the quantized currents generated by chiral edge states along the boundary of topological insulators.
Topological insulators are unique as they allow chiral edge states to travel freely without dissipating, making them a great source of quantized energy.
However, when defects form in topological insulators, their impact on chiral edge states needs to be better understood in order to ensure the continued existence of these valuable assets.
In this research, we use mathematical models to study topological insulators with defects by transforming the boundary conditions that govern chiral edge states.
Our findings reveal that some defects have a positive impact, preserving the quantized current and edge states, while others have a negative impact, destroying the quantized current and edge states.
Our mathematical models confirm that topological insulators with defects remain reliable sources of quantized energy under specific circumstances.

Consider a function u defined in an open sector in the plane, subsumed within a half-plane, that is p-harmonic and has a finite limit as approaches a bounded angle in the sector. We demonstrate that the rate at which as approaches this bounded angle is proportional to a constant, regardless of the value of p. This constant is dependent on the location in the sector and its proximity to the angle where the limit is finite. We calculate the constant for a specific location in the sector when the value of p is greater than one. Our research extends similar results from the study by Lehtelä-Marola on subharmonic functions in the plane.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between extreme wave heights and storm directions is analyzed. Wave resourcing is modeled as being dependent on both position and storm direction, with the strength of this relationship accounted for in the model. The model assumes that wave conditions and storm directions are not inherently connected, except through the user's perspective. The model utilizes a combination of real-world data and simulation-based methods to estimate the shapes and asymptotes of extreme value distributions, as well as the structures of their dependencies and spatial components. The model's accuracy is validated through simulations and the analysis of Nantucket wave data confirms the presence of conditions not typically associated with standard marine weather patterns.

We consider Corsi and Várilly-Alvarado's theorem from 2015, which established an upper limit on the number of non-constant morphism applications between two given varieties defined over a specific field. This was extended by Evnina and Várilly-Alvarado's corollary in 2020 to cover scenarios over number fields. Building on this work, we present new results by providing upper limits on the number of $K$-morphisms from a given variety to another, under specified conditions, over number fields $K$. This is applied to scenarios involving finite morphism families and results in upper limits on the number of finite morphism applications from a given variety to another, under specified conditions, over number fields $K$. This work is also extended to cover scenarios involving functors such as the Chow motive and the zeta zero functor.

A crucial step in planning cross-robot manipulation tasks is converting information from one robot to another. We develop a method to transfer manipulability distributions, which describe a robot's joint movement possibilities, from one robot to another based on shared experience. Our approach involves using these distributions to prioritize joints with the greatest impact in order to optimize new motor schemas. To accurately transfer the distributions between robots, we employ an iterative closest point algorithm that takes into account the complex geometric relationships between their bodies. This method requires transporting points across robots to match anatomical features, and we leverage this process to improve the alignment. Additionally, we use manifold-aware techniques to ensure that the transportation of manipulability distributions and related points across robot bodies does not lead to distorted or fictitious data. This method has been thoroughly tested in a virtual environment and shown to successfully perform manipulability domain transformation, retain critical information, and preserve the original manipulability distribution's characteristics.

In a search for Higgs boson pairs, the matrix element method is utilized to identify the $\textrm{H} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}$ and $\textrm{W} \to \textrm{q}\bar{\textrm{q}}'$ decays within the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ process at the LHC. The simulated results from this method are compared with the findings from $m_{\textrm{T}}$ and $DR$ methods, all of which are based on the theoretical prediction of $\sigma(\textrm{gg} \to \textrm{HH}) = 1.14$ femtobarns at an Luminosity of $300 \,\text{fb}^{-1}$. The signal efficiency and purity are specifically examined for signal events produced by the $\texm{H} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\texm{b}}$ and $\textrm{W} \to \textrm{q}\bar{\textrm{q}}'$ decays, resulting in pure signals in up to $40\%$ of the cases. Furthermore, using the matrix element method yields more rigorous exclusion

A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, 'in-the-wild' video footage where objects are rotated by chance. These incidental turntables offer several key benefits: they require minimal manual annotation; provide more comprehensive view transformations than synthetic 3D rotations; and offer a more authentic training environment for models. To harness this potential, we develop ViewRank: a data augmentation technique where models are fine-tuned on various view increments from a single model trained on a large synthetic dataset. By applying ViewRank to real-world video data, it is possible to teach models to anticipate and handle novel views that have not been seen during training. In practice, ViewRank significantly boosts the accuracy of 3D object pose estimation models, outperforming current benchmarks in several datasets. ViewRank's versatility also allows it to enhance models for related tasks such as PASCAL3D+ object detection, reaching state-of-the-art accuracy without the need for annotation.

The rapid spread of misinformation through social media about COVID-19 is a severe issue. Concerned health experts, governments, and technology companies are working to address the problem, yet efficient strategies for countering misinformation are still in development. To aid them, we've created and evaluated two machine learning models that can analyze user tweets and predict acceptance or rejection of misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines. Our models, trained on a unique dataset of human-labeled examples, demonstrate impressive performance, covering various vaccine-related topics and sources. By identifying which tweets may contain misinformation and whether it is accepted or rejected, we can provide valuable insights on which information is spreading and being believed, allowing researchers to create targeted interventions. We've also discovered that contrastive pre-training, combining multiple datasets, and training models to classify both acceptance and rejection of misinformation enhance performance.

A key feature of high-energy attosecond pulses in irradiating solids is their coherent interaction with the driving laser field, which stabilizes and enables precise control over pulse generation. Through numerical simulations, we investigate the mechanisms behind coherent attosecond pulse generation in strong laser-field interactions with solids. Furthermore, we demonstrate the strong-field coherent regulation of pulse generation, allowing for the production of isolated, high-energy attosecond pulses with 0.1-100 attosecond durations and total photon flux exceeding 10^6 per square nanometer. This enhances our understanding of strong-field coherent radiation, offering a pathway for experimental implementation.

Eclipse systems known as DDMs (double DDJs) are theoretical binary star systems predicted by astrophysical simulations, comprising two DA white dwarfs in a rigidly attached configuration. Despite numerous searches, no conclusive evidence has been found for DDMs in space observations yet. Our study started with a small sample of 19 white dwarf eclipse systems, and through spectral decomposition, we successfully separated the spectra of the companion stars in 13 systems. This resulted in the discovery of 9 new companion star types, and 4 existing systems now display multiple companion star types. Additionally, our findings revised the estimated masses of the companion stars in 7 systems and their synthetic photometry was produced. Our discoveries include the identification of 3 candidate DDMs: HLASB3, HLASB5, and HLASB7, exhibiting characteristics that are indicative of DDJs. These systems show the spectral features of hydrogen-rich DA white dwarfs in eclipse phases and observed photometric patterns consistent with predicted DDJ models. Although the data is not sufficient to confirm these systems as DDJs, they do display properties that are indicative of this configuration.

This paper investigates the nonlinear Schrödinger equation under the effect of a repulsive potential in three-dimensional space, allowing for initial data with high energy and moderate oscillations. Our research concludes that for a certain range of repulsive strength exceeding a certain threshold, which is influenced by the soliton parameter, an explosive solution will arise, characterized by infinite blow-up in both space and time, resulting in nearly radial oscillations with exponentially decreasing amplitude.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to PINNs can be made, specifically in their scalability to complex problems. Creating a dense grid of training points within the input domain is a typical approach to enhance training, though this typically results in the "dimensionality curse" which significantly increases required data and computational resources. To address these limitations, this research introduces Residual-based Adaptive Node creation using Gaussian processes, a flexible nodal creation method that autonomously determines the number and distribution of nodes based on the problem complexity. When applied to well-established problems, such as the Burgers equation and a chaotic system, RANG demonstrated dense grids of nodes that closely related to the number required by traditional methods, yet did so without needing additional parameters. Furthermore, RANG demonstrated improved accuracy and reduced training errors when compared to methods that create a fixed and uniform number of nodes within the input domain.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of a multi-domain ferroelectric FET (FeFET) based on a 20nm technology node. The FeFET's gate driver circuit communicates with multiple gate domains across the channel through a complex system involving various capacitances. A recently identified capacitance effect, adverse capacitance, has been found to have a significant impact on FeFET performance. The research delves into the physics behind adverse capacitance and develops a numerical model to analyze it. Additionally, the study investigates how domain wall statistics and domain motion influence adverse capacitance. The results show that adverse capacitance can result in up to a 30% reduction in driver rise and fall times in FeFET gate driver circuits, and may lead to driver failure in some cases.

A knowledge graph of dependencies for JavaScript projects in the Cargo ecosystem has been created by analyzing project relationships. Analyzing this graph allows for identifying isolated projects and those connected to vulnerable projects, as well as mapping project families and clustering projects with similar patterns. By examining project lifecycles, it's possible to determine the prevalence of vulnerabilities across different stages of a project's lifetime and predict vulnerability dissemination. Our study reveals that a significant portion of Cargo projects contain security vulnerabilities, some even in their initial versions, and that many of these projects continue to harbor vulnerabilities throughout their lifetime. Furthermore, we've discovered that when a new vulnerability is introduced in a project, it typically spreads to other projects in the same family within two months, and also increases the likelihood of reaching twenty or more dependent projects.

For analyzing stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to understand and differentiate irreducible and reducible components of these systems. This study focuses on a stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equation with pure leap noise and demonstrates that it consists of an irreducible subset. This outcome is then utilized to establish the asymptotic equivalence of stochastic dynamical systems, including those that are finitely factorizable and have a non-density drift. Additionally, the research proves that certain stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations are asymptotically equivalent to irreversible deterministic systems.

The power graph of a finite group is obtained by connecting elements that commute with each other. In this study, we verify that the power graph of any finite nilpotent group is Kosage. Furthermore, we determine the minimum possible vertex degree in the power graph of a finite nilpotent group, given a specific prime number divisor. Specifically, we find the minimum possible vertex degree in the prime divisor-regular power graph of a finite nilpotent group. In this research, we also establish the minimum possible vertex degree in the prime divisor-regular double coset power graph of a finite nilpotent group, and then extend our findings to the minimum possible vertex degree in the double coset power graph of a finite nilpotent group, given a specific subgroup and coset system. In this study, we also examine the homogeneity of the double coset power graph of a finite nilpotent group under particular subgroups and coset systems. In addition, we investigate the minimum possible vertex degree in the double coset power graph of a finite nilpotent group, given a specific subgroup and coset system, and obtain upper and lower limits for the minimum possible vertex degree in this case.

HADES is a relativistic heavy-ion detector specializing in the study of light systems produced in nuclear reactions. The latest upgrade to HADES introduced new particle identification capabilities, particularly for systems containing the vector meson ρ and the light vector mesons $\omega$ and $\phi$. The new capabilities enable researchers to conduct thorough investigations of the production mechanisms of these mesons within a wider energy range and individual nucleon-target interactions. This technical document presents the upgraded HADES detector and its enhanced features.

Deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) are the most widely used model for image recognition tasks. However, using traditional even-priority convolution on square grids in image recognition tasks may not be the most efficient approach, as it often results in overlapping and wasted calculations. We present the direction convolution (DConv) operation, which addresses this issue by applying filters in specified directions, such as horizontal and vertical, effectively reducing calculation redundancies. We implement the DConv operation within DCNNs and test its effectiveness on common image recognition datasets, revealing a notable improvement in accuracy with decreased parameter count.

This study seeks to clarify the optimal practice for designing graph convolutional networks (GCNs) for point cloud learning. In particular, we re-examine the common approach of assembling a fixed-size feature matrix from local neighborhoods to form the graph adjacency matrix, as well as the reliance on differentially-weighted aggregation operations. Our empirical observations indicate that the construction of this matrix can significantly influence the performance of the model, while also impacting computational efficiency and memory requirements. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the conventional method of matrix construction and the associated aggregation operations may not always be optimal, highlighting a potential source of performance degradation. Our proposed approach, featuring adaptive matrix construction and unbiased aggregation, serves as a reliable benchmark, achieving consistently superior results and substantial reductions in computational burden and memory usage. Our revolutionary techniques achieve remarkable gains in accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art models by 2.0% and 2.4% in benchmark datasets linemssion and classification respectively, while also significantly outperforming leading models in ablation studies in various domains.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses semantic similarity to bypass model-based detection systems without relying on backdoors embedded in input data. The novel approach enables the development of host-free Trojan horses, capable of navigating diverse networks to target specific models, while remaining undetectable by on-board security defenses. Our Trojan attack combines elevated activation of trigger inputs with semantic similarity between trigger inputs and class labels, employing advanced neural network decoding techniques to facilitate activation. To showcase the effectiveness of this method, we successfully design and execute semantic Trojan attacks against four prominent image classification models, defending against six model-based detection systems in the process.

We are developing an image slicer for an integral field device, ROSIE IFD, to work with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. By splitting the 50.4 x 53.5 field of view into four subfields, and further segmenting these into 21 individual 0.6 x 53.5 slices, we'll create 84 unique spectral channels, each just 0.6 arcseconds apart along the spatial axis and 53.5 angstroms apart along the spectral axis. The project's current status, including our most recent results from a prototype version of the device and plans for the production version, are discussed here.

Cyclic fusion rates among light, stable nuclei are still unclear and require further investigation. The Trojan Horse Method, a highly sensitive method for measuring extremely low-energy astrophysical $S$ factors, has been significantly enhanced in recent years by the development of more precise beam calibration methods. In this article, the current status of these improvements is reviewed. Calculations reveal that an upgrade of the THO calibration technique, incorporating novel arguments related to the nuclear structure of the target nuclei, can reduce uncertainties associated with THO calibration uncertainty. Specifically, this upgrade could reduce uncertainties related to the gamma-decay branch and the nuclear structure of the compound nucleus, which could potentially be achieved with just a single exposure of about 3 full days. In the context of $S$-factor measurements, an upgrade of this technique could lead to nearly "experimental" zero-energy $S$-factor values. Additionally, the potential for analyzing high-energy $\alpha$ particles emitted during the $^{12}{\rm C}+{}^{12}{\rm C}$ reaction, using accelerator-based experimental setups, is explored.

A key objective in studying habitable-zone planets is to determine their potential for life by determining their internal composition. To achieve this goal, researchers need accurate information about the elemental abundances of these planets, which can be obtained by analyzing their host stars. Abundances in stars follow the mixture model of their planetary interior formation theory, which suggests that metal-enriched material rose towards the star's surface sooner than iron-rich material. We applied this theory to analyze ten G-type stars, compiling new data and incorporating it into existing samples. We calculated the likelihood of seven key elements being present in a habitable-zone terrestrial-planets' core, mantle, and iron-rich components. Our results indicate that these planets tend to have cores composed of $44^{+13}_{-18}\%$ silicates, $38^{+11}_{-16}\%$ nickel, and $18^{+9}_{-7}\%$ others, with the remaining consisting of refractory elements. Our core masses range from $0.6 to $ 3.3 Earth masses. We found that iron enrichment varies greatly, with iron potentially making up as much as 90% of a planet's mass in some cases. These findings may aid in understanding planetary formation and habitability.

Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks can effectively use
Wi-Fi signal strength data to determine a device's location. However, the
quality of the data is often affected by external factors like building
structures and other interfering signals, which can vary greatly depending on
a device's specific line of sight. Different indoor spots may therefore
require different preprocessing methods to ensure accurate readings. To address
this issue, we suggest the use of Attention Mechanism, a technique that
dynamiclly adjusts the importance of previous data according to the current
input. By incorporating this mechanism into our DNN model, we have
experimentalally verified faster localization and higher accuracy, achieving
an IoU of 0.81 using only 30% of the initial data samples.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework, top category theory with topological categories, that incorporates a range of modal logics and their corresponding semantics. It defines specific structural elements - top categories, fibrations, objects with modal structure, and modal subcategories - which form the foundational framework. This structured approach allows for the systematic development of modal logic. The method is then specifically applied to the categories of topological spaces, uniform spaces, and compact Hausdorff groups to derive well-known modal logics and their respective semantics.

A graph's edge coloring can be defined as an assignment of colors to edges such that neighboring edges receive distinct colors. In a 2-edge-coloring, neighboring edges use different colors, whereas in a k-edge-coloring with odd k, at least one set of neighboring edges may share a color. Achieving edge colorings for specific graph classes has been focal points for researchers. particularly when it came to constructing overcomplete edge coverings - edge colorings where each edge is part of at least two colored pairs. Researchers initially proposed a conjecture that overcomplete edge coverings could be done with three colors on cubic bipartite graphs, but we found a counterexample disproving this, leaving us with an open question about whether two-edge colorings are sufficient for such graphs.

We investigate the minimum possible values that quadratic functions, such as the Frucht's function and the Grigorchuk's function, can take on the Hamming graphs, based on spectral parameters. Our results demonstrate that these minimum values are equal to the maximum values of the corresponding functions on the cube, and we explain these findings by proving that these functions exhibit ground-state transitions at certain energies. We also indicate how our methods can be extended to other functions.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but previous efforts to enhance user interaction were hindered by limitations in coding and user libraries. To address this, a new web-based interface, ShinyCOPASI, has been developed using the R language to provide a more interactive and responsive experience. This platform offers a suite of widgets and tools to explore and visualize model results, track simulations, and identify key dynamic characteristics. Additionally, it features a module selection system, enabling users to customize their workflow and save models, operations, and parameters for later use.

Scientific learning techniques, driven by advances in data science and machine learning, aim to address fundamental problems affecting modern science and engineering. However, distinguishing between accurate and inaccurate predictions remains a significant obstacle in scientific learning. To address this, scientific learners need reliable measures of uncertainty that can inform post-processing techniques and various applications. This study examines popular uncertainty evaluation methods in scientific learning and assesses their effectiveness across seven diverse datasets from multiple fields. A comprehensive comparison of these methods is provided, along with recommendations for future research and potential avenues for further exploration. The research code and additional resources are accessible via a public repository.

We are investigating the von Neumann algebra generated by category functions of integer categories with a single object, and we believe it is equivalent to the tensor C*-hull of the L\u{u}sz\u{a}j-Gerg\u{a}di algebra. A detailed proof of this allegation, along with information about finitely presented groups with a finite abelian second homology group and a specific nilpotency level for their first homology group, is provided. Additionally, we describe the standard faithful GNS-weight, the dual weight associated with the Luze-Renault morphism, and the relative faithfulness of the relative Casimir Cas*.

In this research, we introduce the Imprecise Generalized Minimum Error Recovery Algorithm (IGMERA) - a novel policy iteration method for solving Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). IGMERA enhances the precision of the approximated posterior value function at each iteration by adjusting its parameters. This makes IGMERA a hybrid approach, combining the Generalized Minimum Error Recovery Algorithm (GMERA) - which uses a type of non-parametric regression called Imprecise Kernel Regression (IKR) - with a parametric regression technique. We investigate the convergence properties of IGMERA and establish a relationship between its parameters and the error made at each iteration. We also conduct experiments to evaluate the performance of IGMERA, comparing it to other state-of-the-art approximation methods such as Kernel Regression (KR), GMERA with fixed parameters and no re-evaluation (GMERA) and the parametric regression counterpart of GMERA (km-GMERA). The results show that IGMERA outperishes previous approaches in solving large-scale MDPs.

Let $G$ be a weighted directed graph, and consider the edge ideal $I(G)$ and its symbolic and typical power ideals $I_k^{(s)}(G)$ and $I^{(t)}_k(G)$. We investigate the relationship between these ideals, specifically examining their similarity in powers and the extent to which their corresponding Betti numbers match. Our study covers a broad range of edge ideals, and we provide detailed proofs as well as numerous illustrated examples to support our findings.

To improve public health, scientists use computer simulations to analyze the effects of policies and predict outbreaks, but these models often require experimental input in the form of data, further needing statistical interpretation to provide actionable results. This research focuses on an underlying inverse problem that these predictions depend on, which involves presenting multiple possible scenarios to inform efficient policy decisions. Employing a statistical model designed for complex simulations, this study proposes a method to accurately estimate these simulations' parameters, which initially presented as challenging due to issues with model misspecification and computational difficulties. This study tackles these issues by initially simplifying the problems through statistical modeling and estimation, which involves leveraging the Multiple Contour Estimation method to present a range of possible parameter results, thus providing scientists with uncertainty ranges to inform their predictions. A series of tests, which included real-world scenarios of influenza and HIV outbreaks, as well as synthetic data, demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, specifically the utility of displaying results in the form of credible intervals, which provides scientists with a range of possible outcomes, thus enhancing the scientific understanding of these outbreaks and predictions.

Intriguing patterns in labeled data can be deceiving, with adversarial manipulations or flaws often underlying them. To mitigate this issue, researchers have proposed robust learning methods that resist attacks on data. However, the existing literature largely focuses on coping with data corruption and provides limited insight into how to deal with more fundamental label uncertainties stemming from the natural imperfections of human annotation. To address this gap, we establish a theoretical framework to study the effects of local inquiries, which aim to utilize knowledge from specific annotation contexts to improve model robustness. By categorizing local inquiries into two types - label uncertainty and model uncertainty, we provide a rigorous evaluation of their effectiveness. Our numerical studies confirm the validity of our theoretical findings. Moreover, we demonstrate the practical value of our framework by developing novel algorithms that effectively handle both types of local inquiries, leading to enhanced robustness in learning models.

For understanding how jets interact with hot, dense matter in heavy-ion collisions, it is vital to analyze modifications to jet fragmentation. Quantitative measurements of these alterations require careful consideration of biases induced by selection criteria, including jet momentum and the relationship to the event's central region. This study uses collisions of lead-lead with center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV and central-momentum corrections to measure modifications to fragmentation. Utilizing isolated photons as a probe, and comparing full- and lead-ion collisions, modifications to fragmentation are found across a range of jet transverse momentum. Although previous research revealed altered fragmentation jets above a certain threshold, this study reveals similar alterations, though less pronounced, below that threshold, suggesting that collective effects extend beyond high-energy interactions.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using Fourier and Dickson types of techniques, this study investigates alternating central binomial series with mixed parity indices. Employing a combination of Fourier and Dickson's approach, novel results are derived for several series, including an alternating central binomial series with sum indices 6k and 8k, linked to level 8 colored multiple zeta functions. Furthermore, using Fourier and Dickson's approach, hypotheses regarding Apéry-type inverse binomial series with sum indices n = 2 (mod 8) or n = 4 (mod 8) are formulated.

We obtained multiple $YJH$ filters images of WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, an unusual brown dwarf that appeared larger in older images from the WISE survey, suggesting it may belong to a particular evolutionary phase where the point-spread function changes significantly. However, these images failed to provide conclusive evidence for this phenomenon due to severe crowding prevented further observation. Instead, we examined the possibility that the system contains multiple objects. Sharply analyzing the available images, we determined that the system consists of three objects, and further analysis using a gravitational lensing model confirmed our finding. Additionally, we calculated the properties of these objects, including distances of 292 and 276 parsecs, that are likely to either be at the same distance or remarkably similar in mass. We also propose that the brown dwarfs are young and short-range binaries. Unfortunately, these objects are too crowded to be further studied with current technology, but may become observable in upcoming large telescopes projects.

The LHCb strangeness rocket has fired 1.7 trillion Xenon nuclei at 2.6 TeV per nucleon to investigate particle creation in relativistic Xenon-Xenon collisions. Analyzing data from these events, the production rates of various particles, such as pions, kaons, (anti-)protons and $\phi$ mesons, have been determined as a function of momentum and rapidity. Comparing these results to theoretical models, including relativistic perturbative QCD and PHENOMENON, reveals promising agreement, suggesting these models effectively describe particle creation in Xenon-Xenon collisions.

I suggest utilizing the methods of effective theory to further understand how parton distribution functions evolve. In evolution equations, certain higher-order terms are omitted using certain assumptions. However, when these assumptions are breached, higher-order terms become theoretically relevant, necessitating a reevaluation of how they're included. This is reminiscent of similar concerns in electroweak theory and supergravity theory from the early 2000s. A successful approach addressed these concerns by employing effective theory to systematically include relevant terms. This can be mimicked in DGLAP evolution equations by utilizing effective theory to incorporate relevant terms, such as how rapidity divergences interact with parton distribution functions. This involves shifting DGLAP equations to effective evolution equations using a renormalization mode that incorporates the removal of rapidity divergences. This route has already shown promise in rapidity evolution equations and in saturation theories like the BFKL and Balitsky-Fudzaki-Kovaetz evolution equations. In particular, a effective-theory-based incorporation of color-dipole renormalization group equations addresses color-evolution issues, providing insight into how parton distribution functions interpolate between small and large-$x$ values. This includes how parton distribution functions transition from saturation-dominated behaviors at large-$x$ to traditionally-calculated behaviors at small-$x$, including the nature of the transition and key features at small-$x$. This effective-theory-based approach also includes key features such as parton distribution function nonlinearities and color-fl

Specimens made of Martian and Lunar soil substitutes were created using a combination of saltwater and heat, and then fired at various temperatures to analyze their internal structure, strength and contraction. The internal structures of these materials were studied under a microscope and their properties were tested using standard engineering methods. The results showed that after being fired, the internal structures of both Martian and Lunar soil substitutes resembled traditional ceramics, with similar pore patterns. However, the size of these pores varied significantly based on the firing temperature. Furthermore, both Martian and Lunar soil substitutes displayed similar patterns of mechanical property and contraction behavior with respect to firing temperature. The optimal firing temperature was found to be around 1200°C, at which both Martian and Lunar soil substitutes achieved their strongest points and contracted the least, resulting in solid blocks that could support their own weight. The specifics of mechanical strength and contraction varied between Martian and Lunar soil substitutes, with Martian soil requiring a higher firing temperature to achieve these properties.

The dynamics of a liquid layer on a fiber influence the fiber's removal process, considering the liquid's withdrawal force. Depending on the liquid's surface tension and the rate at which it is being removed, the liquid can become stuck to the fiber, resulting in a standing wave pattern, or it can experience a wave-induced detachment that leads to unique, slip-enhanced versions of the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The slip-enhanced Rayleigh-Plateau instability produces second-order corrections, increasing the liquid layer's instability threshold. The regular Rayleigh-Plateau instability, which occurs when there is no slip, has a much lower threshold, but it can be influenced by the liquid's viscosity, leading to a new instability threshold. The liquid's removal process can also produce a steady state as well as an oscillating state, based on the liquid's viscosity.

By comparing various methods for estimating star formation rates, we reveal a clear hierarchy of agreement among different techniques. While strong correlations exist between some rates, others are less connected. Historically, factors like resolution and wavelength have been cited as potential sources of discrepancy, but our findings suggest that these factors do not solely account for the variations observed. By analyzing data from the SPLASH sample, consisting of 1061 galaxies at a distance of roughly 100 Mpc, we use Br$\gamma$ emission as a standardized measure to evaluate the accuracy of sSFR estimates derived from Pa$\alpha$, Hα, U-band, and J-band photometry. SED fitting results from two codes, MAGPHYS and PRODIGAL, are presented, with the former exhibiting greater agreement with Br$\gamma$ based on U-band data and the latter displaying greater agreement with Br$\gamma$ based on J-band data. These findings suggest that broadband photometry can capture key SED features, but the use of sharp UV data can significantly improve accuracy.

This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a substantial number of the type II quantum subgroups within the specified categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. In this particular study, we establish the symmetries existing between regional modules within the categories under discussion, which are linked to the quantum subgroups of interest. These regional modules correspond to parallel weight modules that contain significant elements of the FSL$(N,k)$ group. These elements form a substantial subset of the type II quantum subgroups. Notably, the regional modules associated with duals of the fundamental modules hold substantial importance as their central objects. In the follow-up to this paper, we will apply the findings presented here to thoroughly classify all the type II quantum subgroups within the specified categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$.

We introduce an innovative method to solve the $N$-dimensional anisotropic Langevin equation, providing a simulation tool that works well even when the diffusion matrix is poorly conditioned. In addition, we demonstrate that making the Langevin equation time-dependent is feasible and offer an efficient method for achieving this. Furthermore, we illustrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to high-dimensional statistical physics problems, specifically in the contexts of simplified protein folding and polymer maps.

This research focuses on recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions captured through an electronic stylus on a touchscreen device. The signal collected during stylus interaction is analyzed to extract essential features for an advanced machine learning model. This model, built on a convolutional neural network design, is then trained to produce highly accurate outcomes. We also investigated the feasibility of using the collected time-series data directly as input to a deep learning network, specifically one with recurrent elements, with great success. We demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art pen-based input methods for mathematical expression recognition.

This study presents an innovative method to synthesize speech durations by merging two extreme output orders - short and long durations - based on the median of predicted values generated by a neural network. The median approach simplifies the sample selection process, eliminating the need for probability calculations. The proposed method is non-parametric and doesn't rely on specific assumptions about the distribution of predicted values. The study evaluates this new method in conjunction with three popular output ordering techniques on two diverse corpora. The results show that the median-based method achieves comparable performance to the best output ordering methods and is distinguished by its simplicity and adaptability across various datasets.

Species distribution analysis can be conducted through multiple methods, including binary, multi-species, state occupancy, and integrated analyses that combine multiple data types. Despite the availability of various R packages for modeling, we observed a lack of comprehensive tools for spatial presence modeling and data integration. To address this gap, we developed spOccupancy for single, multiple species, and integrated presence models that utilize Gaussian random effects to account for spatial correlations. The spOccupancy package incorporates functionality similar to sinclairbayes, uniqueBayesR, and Stan, while providing unique features through Bayesian inference and multiple model integration. This package supports single, multiple species, and integrated presence models that can accommodate various data types, including observational records, abundance surveys, and genetic sampling data. It provides functionality for model checking and diagnostics, as well as simulation studies, making it a versatile tool for analyzing species distributions and presence/absence data in various applications.

The Skincare initiative is focused on developing innovative AI solutions to combat skin cancer. This project has collaborated with the IEEE to create a groundbreaking challenge, showcasing cutting-edge technology in dermatological practices. Despite significant advancements in AI, treating malignant skin lesions poses considerable difficulties. To address this problem, a differential diagnosis system was proposed, combining the skills of dermatologists and machine learning experts to enhance diagnostic capabilities. However, accessing expert consultation can be a major obstacle. To overcome this limitation, an artificial neural network-based system was developed, enabling quick and efficient differential diagnoses. Additionally, the proposed system includes a comprehensive educational database, facilitating the training of future generations of dermatologists. This technical report outlines the mathematical foundations of the proposed method, before presenting the results of extensive evaluations.

To capture the intrinsic variability of Type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a probabilistic autoencoder that can identify a supernova's individual characteristics while ignoring noise and random fluctuations. This model treats variability as a normal aspect of data and allows superfluous information to be considered, differing from previous studies that focused solely on essential characteristics. By incorporating noise in the encoder, the model ensures that the encoded characteristics only represent a supernova's intrinsic behavior. Furthermore, we applied total variation regularization to the decoder to prevent the encoded signals from being rewritten verbatim. Utilizing the Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes method for parameter optimization, we evaluated our model across multiple datasets, which showed that it could accurately predict a supernova's phase and detect fluctuations within noisy spectral data. This model will likely contribute to discovering hidden patterns in various time-series datasets throughout the universe.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been observed in a starburst galaxy approximately 2.09 billion light-years away, as observed by the ALMA telescope. This outflow has a diameter of approximately 1.5 kpc and is oriented perpendicular to a dust lane visible in high-resolution images. Spectral analysis indicates that the outflow is composed of gas with temperatures ranging from 68 to 257 Kelvin. Data also suggest a compact active galactic nucleus contribution, but it does not significantly affect the observed outflow. This outflow has an average mass flow rate of approximately 490 +/- 131 solar masses per year and carries an energy flux of about 1.6 x 10^43 ergs per second. With an estimated mass loss rate, the outflow may impact the galaxy's star formation more than it loses mass, as it expands at a speed of approximately 500 to 560 km per second. This outflow is one of the most detailed neutral gas outflows observed at such a high resolution, and its properties are consistent with those of other similar outflows at the same redshift. This observation suggests that massive neutral gas outflows may play a crucial role in the feedback mechanism that regulates galaxy evolution, but their observed properties are not representative of the outflows' actual physical conditions, as they suggest a much faster expansion velocity than previously estimated.

We examine how fluid moves into a plume that contains particles filling a channel below a surface. This is modeled as an unsteady flow with particles present, which has yet to be studied extensively. To simplify this complex scenario, we use two established models, one for pure fluid and another that accounts for the particles. Our main goal is to understand the percentage of fluid that gets drawn into the plume for both scenarios. This is calculated using a complex mathematical equation that considers initial conditions, while also taking into account the ratio of fluid and particle densities, as well as a critical parameter for particle movement. Our findings show that for both scenarios, the percentage of fluid that gets drawn into the plume increases significantly as the rate of fluid entering the plume increases, particularly under certain conditions. Additionally, the percentage of fluid that gets drawn into the plume for the particle-filled channel is always lower than that for the pure fluid channel, with the decrease in this percentage being relatively smaller for lower rates of fluid entering the plume. Our findings are seen to fill a gap in existing knowledge on this topic, with the percentage of fluid that gets drawn into the plum being a crucial aspect in understanding hydrodynamic processes, particularly during episodes of high-energy input in natural environments, such as those seen in the formation of columnar structures in lakes.

For complex networks that use hyperedges to connect groups of interested individuals to topics, like viruses or infectious ideologies, we create a model that predicts the outcome of an epidemic spread. Focusing on the intrinsic properties of the network and disregarding disease specifics, our framework allows the determination of critical thresholds beyond which epidemics inevitably occur, regardless of initial infection conditions. To investigate these critical thresholds, we develop two theorems: the First, which applies to networks composed of trees and specifies upper and lower bounds for the threshold; and the Second, applicable to all networks, which determines the threshold by maximizing a spectral parameter over the space of positive semidefinite matrices. Related theories for the intrinsic properties of networks are also discussed.

Recent findings on 2D magnetism have led to a surge in curiosity, particularly due to potential applications in spintronics. Research has focused on manipulating spin and its related effects in 2D magnets. This study explores the spin dynamics within the $ab$-plane of a specific ferromagnetic monolayer, engineered from the hexagonal CrI$_3$ compound. By applying an in-plane distortion, the magnetically ordered structure transforms into an arrangement resistant to spin reversal, allowing for unique control over spin. This control arises from a distorted magnetic configuration that generates a distinctive spin pattern. Interestingly, this spin pattern is influenced by an inherent spin manipulation resulting from crystal distortion, which can be attributed to an internal mechanism inherent to the material and not a result of applied external forces. Additionally, studies have been conducted on evaluating the effectiveness of spin-orbit interactions in generating the observed spin patterns. Potentially, manipulating this spin pattern could enable the use of spin as a controllable entity.

The sun's internal rotation exhibits distinct patterns of rotation rates, with faster rotation near the equator and slower rotation near the poles. In contrast, there's an unusual rotation pattern, referred to as the anti-solar rotation rate, where the rotation speed in the polar regions exceeds that in the equatorial regions. The solar-type dynamo theory seeks to explain the sun's magnetic properties, with considerations including the impact of rotation and magnetic activity. To investigate potential magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars, we used a simplified solar-type dynamo model, modifying it to accommodate the anti-solar rotation rate. The results indicate that slow rotation results in weak magnetic activity, with the possibility of detectable cycles only occurring at very low rotation speeds. Additionally, we found that the mean magnetic field throughout the convective zone remains nearly balanced, with the pole and equator differences arising primarily from the dynamic transport and differential rotation. The resulting mean magnetic field is dominated by the effects of pumping, with the geostrophic decomposition playing a relatively minor role.

Recent advancements in deep learning have successfully resolved various real-world challenges, albeit primarily focusing on single-task applications. In contrast, this study proposes a versatile, general-purpose framework for addressing multiple-related tasks, such as real-time object recognition, scene understanding, and more. By incorporating multiple input modalities, such as color and grayscale, our framework facilitates the simultaneous learning of task-specific and shared representations across multiple tasks. Furthermore, a new K-fan multimodal deep learning architecture is designed with an expanded fan-shaped connection mechanism, enabling the efficient integration of shared information. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in achieving shared, task-independent feature representations, ultimately resulting in improved performance and enhanced generalization capabilities.

McMini is a new model checker designed to validate the correctness of multithreaded programs. It uses an innovative approach that leverages McMillan's DPOR algorithm and introduces customizable policy-driven reasoning frameworks. This model checking system specializes in sequential anarchy, which assumes that race conditions result in arbitrary output production. Although this assumption tightens the gaps between predicted program outputs, it can lead to false negatives if certain races have predictable effects. To address this issue, the system includes support for explicit race assumptions, enabling users to incorporate prior knowledge and tailor the model checker's conservative estimates to match actual program behavior more closely. By allowing users to tailor McMini's operation, this system improves the model checker's precision and reduces its runtime costs.

The widespread circulation of false information is exacerbated by messaging apps, which allow users to share content with numerous contacts at once, leading to rapid digital spread. An investigation of this issue is initiated, centering on the effect of limiting message forwarding on the incidence and spread of misinformation. An analytical model is developed from an empirical study to quantify the impact of limiting message forwarding on the incidence and spread of misinformation, particularly in relation to false news spreading that prompts immediate action. The incidence of misinformation is found to be less common than other types, such as non-actionable misinformation. An optimal control strategy is identified to reduce the incidence of misinformation by limiting message forwarding, and this strategy is found to be effective in reducing the incidence of misinformation, even if it is not the most common type. However, such a control strategy may not be sufficient to eliminate the incidence of misinformation. Our findings are supported by numerical examples. The implications of our work are two-fold: first, the effectiveness of limiting message forwarding in reducing the incidence of misinformation depends on the specific characteristics of the misinformation; second, combining this control strategy with other methods, such as promoting digital literacy, may be necessary to eliminate the incidence of misinformation.

We analyze a general branching population, allowing for individual reproductive success to be randomly determined, with the condition that expected reproductive success exceeds one. The population's allelic frequency distribution is initially modeled using a continuous representation and then through discrete approximations. Ultimately, we investigate the convergence of these discrete models to the continuous formulation.

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We suggest a new system design, featuring an end-to-end architecture that incorporates a countermechanism to combat speech impersonation. To enhance the system's ability to focus on relevant input characteristics, we propose introducing attention layers that can selectively filter high-frequency signals. Furthermore, we propose the incorporation of Leaky ReLU as an activation function to improve the system's sensitivity to artifacts. Our proposed system, utilizing a combination of Leaky ReLU and attention layers, demonstrated superior performance in detecting speech impersonation, surpassing the performance of a system with a standard ReLU activation mechanism and countermechanism. Specifically, our countermechanism achieved an AUC of 0.λεί1 on the SIVT dataset, surpassing AUC values of 0.8051 for the countermechanism without attention layers and 0.8122 for the countermechanism without attention layers but with attention layers.

We analyze the supergravity modifications to inflationary models in the context of globally supersymmetric effective field theories. Considering the properties of these modifications, we identify general criteria for inflationary models to maintain their original features. Our findings indicate that when the scale of supersymmetry breaking is larger than the horizon during inflation, the supergravity corrections are negligible. We apply these principles to several field theoretical models, including a constant potential model and quadratic and quartic stabilization mechanisms, to demonstrate their preservation of key properties. Additionally, we examine the impact of heavy fields on inflationary observables in supergravity models and show that with realistic mass assumptions about additional fields, the predictions of inflationary models remain largely unchanged.

The standard model describes nonphoton processes at a particle accelerator's collision point, but reveals discrepancies with experimental data in photon pair correlations. We argue that asymmetry in photon polarization should be considered a possible explanation for these discrepancies. Our proposal includes two experimental tests: one to observe left-right asymmetry by adjusting the angle between the photons and another to observe forward-backward asymmetry by adjusting the collision point's distance from the photon production point. If a notable effect is observed at existing experiments, it's likely that asymmetry causes the standard model's discrepancies. Also, if observed, this phenomenon could be studied to determine the dialion's mass. Ultimately, a more precise measurement of the dialion's mass could be made at a future experiment specifically designed to observe the dialion's influence on photon pair correlations.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide-etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce leakage and perfect matching.
We demonstrate that the union of countably many Borel sets on the real number line is either countable or has a cardinality of $2^{\aleph_0}$.

In the 2000s, commodity trading advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in commodity futures. But their performance declined sharply in the 2010s, leading some to speculate that other investment tactics may have siphoned off existing strategies' returns. This study aims to verify that hypothesis through the use of an agent-based model. It employs a red-blue agents framework, simulating the effects of varying numbers of red (commodity trading) advisors on blue (active) agents' returns. Our results show that when the number of red advisors is low, they enhance blue agents' overall returns. However, this only occurs when red advisors' trading algorithms prioritize commodity futures and they maintain a dominant market presence. When these conditions are met, our model indicates that blue agents can enjoy higher long-term returns relative to a pure active approach. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the decline in commodity trading advisors' returns may not be attributed to the proliferation of active investment tactics or market dominance by a single strategy. Rather, their subpar performance can be attributed to their limited range of trading algorithms and market presence.

This paper delves into the limitations of widely used network traffic analysis methods, specifically examining the vulnerabilities inherent in parsing-based detection methods. By manipulating binary traffic, attackers can exploit parsing weaknesses, causing network traffic analysis tools to produce false positives, misleading alerts that can hinder incident response and resource allocation. To counter these vulnerabilities, this research proposes three tactics:

1. Crafting malicious traffic to exploit parsing errors in Open Source Security Monitoring Tools.
2. Identifying and mitigating the risks associated with parsing-dependent detection methods.
3. Developing a method to validate parsing results using Deep Learning techniques.

Deep Learning-based detection methods have shown promise in analyzing complex protocol structures. However, parsing-dependent detection methods remain prevalent due to existing implementation complexities. To enhance reliability, this research recommends verifying parsing results with Deep Learning models.

The integration of superconducting proximate materials into magnonic circuits holds great promise for generating and controlling quantum states within these systems. To achieve this, it is crucial to understand how the interaction between superconducting spins and nearby magnons functions as a means of filtering out unwanted frequency ranges. By applying a combination of numerical techniques and analytical modeling, we investigate the efficiency of a superconducting-induced barrier in regulating the flow of magnons. Our results indicate that this barrier effectively prevents low-frequency magnons from passing through while allowing higher-frequency magnons to pass. Additionally, we found that the direction of the superconducting spin's spin-polarization exerts a significant impact on the magnon's transmission probability. Therefore, the precise control of the spin-polarization in proximate superconductors offers a potential means of manipulating and filtering magnonic signals.

A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, a key challenge remains: allowing the model to learn novel classes on the client-side without requiring any of the sensitive training data to be transmitted. We propose a unified framework to tackle this problem by leveraging the principles of transfer learning and multi-task learning. The framework employs a local fine-tuning stage on each client, allowing it to adapt and evolve, while a global aggregation stage consolidates knowledge from diverse sources. We test this approach using a real-world application and demonstrate its efficacy in enabling successful class adaptation from unlabelled data encountered during federation.

A new concept for determining quantum entanglement, known as quantum complexity, has been studied through theoretical measurements of complex quantum systems. This paper examines the quantum complexity of a high-dimensional GHZ state and proposes an efficient method for its measurement. Initially, the entanglement complexity of GHZ states is assessed in multidimensional spaces using a simple probabilistic method, which reveals an interesting relationship with the central binomial coefficient. Next, a more sophisticated method is developed to measure the quantum complexity of GHZ states, which allows for partial state information and offers advantages in terms of resource efficiency over existing approaches. This method can be executed experimentally with hyperentanglement of photons or other systems and could contribute significantly to the study of quantum complexity.

This research paper delves into the problem of uplink cascaded channel estimation in multi-user multiple-input-single-output systems supported by intelligent-reflecting-surfaces. The proposed solution utilizes pilot signals transmitted by each user and reflected by the IIS, enabling simultaneous estimation of the user and channel phases. The high computational complexity of traditional estimation methods is circumvented, yielding a more efficient algorithm with lower complexity. The efficiency gain is particularly pronounced in scenarios with larger numbers of users and phase estimation methods.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and demographic characteristics of news audiences. Our findings show that local news coverage of COVID peaked in Winter 2020, followed by a gradual decrease over time, with hotspots including certain cities in Florida, Arizona, Texas, and Wyoming. We identified a correlation between COVID news and regional case rates, but not deaths, and observed variations in COVID-related stories based on news source politics and the demographics of their audiences. Our results also show that local news coverage of non-COVID topics returned to pre-pandemic levels sooner in areas with high COVID news coverage. Furthermore, local news on COVID was more prevalent in news sources with a liberal perspective and in areas with higher populations of older adults, who are more vulnerable to severe COVID symptoms. These findings provide insights into local news coverage of COVID and its connections to regional epidemiology and demographic characteristics of news audiences.

Human counting abilities advance with experience, taking into account not only current visual information but also previously learned concepts. To simulate this complex process, we created a sophisticated neural network model that integrates basic counting knowledge with information from prior experiences. We then tested this model using data from both categorization and counting experiments, investigating how it progresses with varying levels of training. Our advanced model outperformed a simpler rival and accurately predicted human counting progress reported in earlier studies.

Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory.  A crucial tradeoff exists between filter size and false positive rate.  Independent filtering simplifies design, though it demands additional memory.  Cuckoo filters eliminate the need for additional memory at a cost of increased storage and computation.  A new design, xor filters, surpasses both in performance, surpassing cuckoo filters in size and false positive rate.  Compared to Bloom filters, xor filters demand 3-4 times less storage while possessing half to two times the acceptable false positive rate.  Furthermore, xor filters remain resilient in the presence of deletion operations, requiring only one pass over the remaining elements to restore accuracy.  A variant of xor filters, known as skip xor filters, is also proposed, allowing for efficient additions and deletions while retaining a low false positive rate and minimal storage needs.  Experimental results validate the designs' effectiveness, demonstrating a wide range of applications where xor filters can efficiently replace both Bloom and cuckoo filters.  A public implementation of xor filters is available on GitHub.

This note reflects on correspondence principles linking convex geometry with complex analysis. It highlights three key relationships: 
1. The connection between K-stability and and alpha-stability in stability theory for Calabi-Yau varieties and stochastic dominance in convex geometry.
2. The correspondence between the various notions of stability and dominance in the context of differential geometry and super-rigid algebraic varieties.
3. The equivalence between the various notions of positivity in convex geometry and super-rigid algebraic models.

A proposed market prediction model leverages sequence analysis of trade data to determine future direction, with results indicating the model's effectiveness across various scenarios. The model's ability to pinpoint the optimal trading parameters is discussed, along with the model's potential Pitfalls. The model relies on non-parametric regression analysis and an advanced time series algorithm known as RSI (Relative Strength Index), using real-time NYSE trade data between 2010 and 2012 to generate significant results.

This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to collaboratively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without accessing private user data. Concurrently, clients create clusters of related data and mask individual data points with anonymous vectors when sending an average of their group to the server. Upon receiving these averages, the server calculates anonymous gradients, which clients use to update their local models. We evaluate FLVoogd using MNIST and EMNIST datasets and find it offers improved efficiency and privacy compared to current FL methods.

Our solution successfully took first place in the NeurIPS 2021 - Sim2Real Challenge with a score of 0.8168 by utilizing a novel method that incorporates image gradients to create a realistic synthetic environment for training autonomous vehicle navigation networks. This method exploits the connection between the network's response to synthetic gradient maps and real-world collisions, allowing for the network's performance to be optimized through reward maximization using gradient information. Our approach significantly outperformed the challenge baseline, achieving a 41.8% improvement, and showcased the effectiveness of using gradient maps to bridge the gap between synthetic and real-world scenarios for autonomous vehicle navigation networks.

Deepfake creation techniques continue to advance at a rapid pace, allowing for the production of highly convincing videos with minimal visual errors. Current detection methods are largely adapted for use with YouTube-like platforms and are primarily tested on videos with marked boundaries and clear foregrounds. In contrast, determining deepfake authenticity within the context of unrestricted media, such as photos and naturalistic videos with complex backgrounds, poses significant challenges. In response, there is a need for more sophisticated deepfake generation algorithms capable of producing orginal-like materials and novel detection methods that consider autenticy as a continuous rather than binary trait. In this article, we assess the current limitations of deepfake detection methods, particularly when applied to visually complex content, and propose new approaches for both creating and detecting deepfakes within this more stringent context. Our evaluation utilizes a previously unexplored dataset, 'X-X', containing nearly 300,000 media items, and demonstrates the potential for our strategies to future-proof this challenging new frontier of deepfake research.

The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's revitalized the prospect of discovering potentially habitable worlds over the coming decade, with some temperate planets potentially harboring liquid water oceans, provided they do not possess massive H2/He envelopes that would cause them to be excessively hot. Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses of 1.7 to 3.5 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate that small differences in mass between a gas-rich super-Earth and a mini-Neptune exoplanet, both of which receive irradiance levels similar to Earth's, can be inferred from their transit spectra around early morning in the Earth analog model versus mid-afternoon in the HD 219079 model. While the Earth analog is likely a terrestrial planet with a small mass of 2.3 Earth masses that has a liquid water ocean and no volatile species, the HD 219079 exoplanet has a mass of 13.6 Earth masses and is thought to be a mini-Neptune characterized by a small rock core and a massive H2/He envelope. In the Earth analog model, the carbon and oxygen atoms present in the atmosphere are in a state of chemical equilibrium and have rocks dissolved in the atmosphere, whereas in the HD 219079 exoplanette, the carbon and oxygen atoms are in a state of thermochemical equilibrium where carbon and oxygen

Inspired by biological neurons, spiking neural networks have the potential to replace traditional neural networks, despite their complex learning dynamics. A significant hurdle has been the lack of an efficient learning algorithm, but recent breakthroughs include modified backpropagation and gradient descent methods. However, these adaptations still raise conceptual difficulties. Our work addresses this challenge by developing a learning protocol grounded in bio-plausibility, informed by metabolic constraints. Unlike existing learning algorithms, our approach doesn't rely on continuous weight updates or elaborate memory mechanisms. Instead, we utilize local, short-term synaptic changes and leverage the network's structural properties, as well as the temporal dynamics of spike sequences. We illustrate the efficacy of our protocol, called Synaptic Learning Rule, through simulations of binary and graded-spike neurons, and show that it compares favorably to existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

This paper presents our approach to the McCacken Foundation's out-of-category challenge, where we evaluated four methods to determine how effectively they handle mislabeled data in machine learning. Our investigation focused on detecting anomalies in both visual and textual formats. Our analysis reveals that using consensus scoring to combine multiple model predictions is a reliable approach to handling data errors. Furthermore, we observed that models trained on clean data with robust regularization tend to generalise better from limited samples, even in scenarios where data is partially labelled incorrectly. Our findings are substantiated through both theoretical analysis and comprehensive empirical evidence.

A specific type of generalized polynomial chaos expansion is verified in this study. The verification process involves establishing an error bound that can be controlled. Existing error analysis in various contexts relies on statistical properties of the differential operator involved, but these results fall short for crucial cases. For example, verification is impossible for partial differential equations with chaotic parameters. To address this shortcoming, a novel approach utilizing an iterative process is proposed. This approach, however, introduces an unappealing aspect - it imposes extremely strict restrictions on the smoothness of the solution function. In an effort to overcome this obstacle, a iterative process is proposed, allowing a degree of instability in exchange for improved smoothness. Although this approach is explored primarily with regression in mind, it is also applicable to partial differential equations.

To effectively monitor and detect deviations in adaptable systems with varied patterns, such as those found in cyber-physical systems, we need to identify and isolate abnormalities in real-time. However, due to constraints like limited resources and complex architectures, it's often impossible to obtain complete and precise data. Therefore, we've developed a new adaptive approach that can identify and isolate abnormalities in real-time, even with imperfect observations. Our approach employs model-agnostic techniques, allowing it to be widely applied across various cyber-physical systems that exhibit piecewise linear behavior. To resolve the computational challenges, we've developed an efficient and progressive algorithm that utilizes the concept of Viterbi decoding, allowing it to run in real-time and efficiently tackle large-scale systems with complex patterns. Additionally, we've devised a graphical representation to visually understand and validate the performance of our approach, even near its performance limits. Through case studies and simulations, we've verified that our approach outperforms existing methods by a significant margin - up to 30% improvement. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that our approach's performance gains are substantial, with up to  Born to Risk: 5.75 vs 8.15 (our approach's average number of false alarms per hour vs existing methods' average number of false alarms per hour).

We analyzed the composition of light elements within six dwarf galaxy remnants, specifically early-type dwarf galaxies that reside in the vicinity of massive siblings like the Milky Way. By comparing our findings to theoretical models of star creation histories, we gained insight into the fundamental processes that shaped these galaxies and influenced their chemical development. Our analysis revealed that early-type dwarf galaxies with close proximity to massive siblings follow distinct chemical patterns, characterized by lower metal content and differing star creation history patterns compared to those that are more isolated. This discovery implies that massive siblings' gravitational influence affects the fundamental processes that shaped their satellite galaxies. Moreover, our cross-validation with cosmological simulations revealed that early-type dwarf galaxies either gain or lose mass due to their relation with massive siblings, leading to altered star creation histories and resulting galaxy profiles.

We define a homotopy action spectrum as an intrinsic, profinite group-based space that emerges from the continuous orbit graph of an action, incorporating unstable homotopy classes and establishing a connection with finite homotopy action spectra. By doing so, we obtain a straightforward method for constructing a profinite group-based homotopy classification of finite CW-complexes, and this result is combined with previous research to provide a profinite group-based classification of finite CW-complexes up to homotopy, characterized solely by their homotopy groups.

Document extraction models have seen significant advancements in recent years, 
however, the high cost associated with data labeling has greatly impacted their 
practical application. For visually rich documents, each data point can be 
extremely labor-intensive to label, hindering progress. This challenge can be 
addressed through the efficient use of semi-supervised and zero-shot learning 
techniques. By combining these methods with a simple, yet effective, dataset 
generation approach using table queries, we have substantially decreased data 
labeling costs while maintaining model performance. This strategy not only reduces 
costs but also accelerates model training by a 1.5 multipler by leveraging 
unlabeled data. As a result, we have successfully applied it to extract text and 
visual information from invoices and receipts.

The electronic properties of the EuS/InAs interface were studied using theoretical calculations and found to exhibit unusual behavior. Unlike common 2DEG systems, this interface produces a 2D Fermi glass with intrinsic ferromagnetic properties.
