The unique electronic properties of this interface arise from peculiar electronic transitions that occur at the interface and are influenced by the alignment of dopant atoms. The calculations showed that these properties could be modified by adjusting the arrangement of the dopant atoms, and this was confirmed through measurements of the system's magnetic properties. The most ferromagnetic stable configuration was identified, and the electronic properties of the system were found to exhibit significant resistance to change at high temperatures. The unique properties of the EuS/InAs interface make it an interesting system to study due to its potential for high-temperature magnetic applications. The electronic properties of this system can be adjusted by adjusting the interface properties, and this makes it possible to develop novel magnetic applications. A simplified classification system for Borel Wadge classes is presented, using a priority code representation that refines the standard Borel Wadge classes. It is shown that this improved classification maintains the key properties of the original Borel Wadge theory, including continuity and compatibility with the Borel hierarchy. Additionally, it is demonstrated that each Borel Wadge class corresponds to a unique solution to a lattice-based equation involving infinite binary trees, and that this framework has applications in solving decision problems related to Borel Wadge classes.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are increasingly preferred, but efficient training on them is a significant challenge. While pruning can help with this issue by reducing the size and weight of models, previous research on pruning has been a hindrance in further progress, as most methods compromise both the accuracy and the computational cost of the models they prune. Consequently, previous efforts to accelerate deep network training have focused on the inference stage only. We propose ClickTrain, an innovative approach that efficiently prunes both training and inference stages, allowing for models to be accurately trained and efficiently deployed. We achieve fine-grained pruning, averaging a substantial 80% reduction in model size, by analyzing the distribution of filter outputs and accurately identifying crucial elements. We also introduce a universal threshold-based quantization scheme that enables efficient ClickTrain model execution on various hardware. Overall, ClickTrain enables end-to-end training and inference on deep CNNs with reduced computational cost, achieving state-of-the-art results, and surpassing previous pruning methods by at least 2-3 times, while providing near-ideal accuracy and performance improvements. Additionally, ClickTrain allows for rapid model reconfiguration, enhancing adaptability by executing both full- and prune-model training, and efficient results retrieval by executing inference on various hardware after training.

This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored for substructural modal logics. By applying duality principles, we demonstrate that every modal logic derived from the distributive complete Lambek calculus has a Kripke model, if it adheres to a structured syntax. Furthermore, we establish a dual relationship between certain mathematical structures, specifically modal algebras and topological Kripke spaces, utilizing a topological model developed from Priestley spaces.

The collisions of neutron star-black hole mergers produce diverse signals across various gravitational wave frequencies, spanning from 2 Hz to 1024 Hz, providing scientists with a rich dataset to study compact objects. By using synthetic signals from numerical simulations, researchers have developed a GPGPU-based approach to train a neural network that can identify and differentiate neutron star-black hole mergers. The trained network, called NeuroMBH, achieves a 0.02% error rate in distinguishing collisions involving neutron stars, and accurately classifies signals with a low signal-to-noise ratio as accurately as 80 dB. Furthermore, NeuroMBH outperforms previous methods by 99.9%, demonstrating the effectiveness of neural networks in analyzing gravitational waves. The team is now working on improving NeuroMBH by incorporating multiple masses and spin systems, laying the groundwork for using this technique in analyzing real gravitational wave data from collisions between neutron stars and black holes.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, TOI-5542 b, which orbits a 4.5 billion-year-old host star. TOI-5542 b, described as a warm Jupiter, has a mass similar to that of Saturn and orbits its star at a distance of approximately 1.2 astronomical units. Researchers determined the exoplanet's mass by analyzing three transits caused by the exoplanet's passage across the host star as observed using the TESS telescope. TOI-5542 hosts an additional exoplanet, TOI-5542 c, a sub-Neptune exoplanet with a mass less than that of Neptune and a close orbital distance to the host star. Both exoplanets are believed to have formed through different planetary formation mechanisms. TOI-5542 b is notable due to its older age and unusual mass compared to other exoplanets. Additionally, the detection of TOI-5542 d, a valid candidate for confirmation, could provide further insights into planetary formation.

In solving complex decision-making problems with constraints, researchers utilize Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs). They present a new primal-dual method that produces an exact solution within a predetermined time limit for anytime performance. This method can be applied to a variety of practical scenarios, such as traffic signal control and medical decision-making. It provides a precise estimate of the time required to achieve an ε-approximate solution, which is not easily determined in these scenarios. By analyzing the complexity of solving CMDPs, they determine that solving ε-approximate CMDPs is achievable in polynomial time, but finding the exact solution may take longer.

Mathematical notation writing plays a crucial role in the mathematical inquiry process. Unfortunately, handwritten math often necessitates manual data entry, which can be time-consuming and error-prone. Recent advancements in the recognition of handwritten mathematical notation have primarily focused on the evaluation of systems using predetermined test sets and have overlooked the feasibility of using real-time corrections to improve recognition accuracy. This study employs the Math recognition dataset, a extensive collection of math expressions taken from the system's real-time recognition output with corrections annotated by experts, to train a model. Our results indicate that, in comparison to conventional training, the performance of the model on the dataset's evaluation set is substantially enhanced when trained using corrected output. Moreover, the study shows that selecting instances characteristic of poor recognition and incorporating them into the training set is highly effective in improving the model's robustness and accuracy in challenging situations.

A widely recognized analogy exists between superconformal quantum field theories and the growth of cohomology classes within sheaf theory. In superconformal field theory, this correspondence manifests through the mapping of superprimary fields to elements in cohomology spaces, which follows saturation rules analogous to those governing Dimca's theorem. Furthermore, superprimary operators corresponding to observables that commute with the superhamiltonian, such as invariant superprimary fields, map to cohomology classes that exhibit particularly intricate structures. Specifically, they form a homotopy equivalence class of mappings from a Borel sheaf to a satified sheaf, displaying an intricate, often non-compact form. In three-dimensional superconformal theories, a relationship exists between the spectrum of superprimary operators and the L^2 sheaf cohomology spectrum, which is characterized by an explicit, combinatorial rule. Additionally, in theories possessing a hamiltonian reduction, a Borel sheaf transformation emerges, whose superprimary image forms a homotopy equivalence class of mappings from the transformed Borel sheaf to a saturated sheaf.

Our analysis of complex networks reveals a normal distribution for the variability of interactions among linked nodes. This observation holds whether the network's structure is prescribed randomly or organically, and this finding persists even when the distribution of degrees within the network is non-uniform. This research provides empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis that complex networks exhibiting organic growth tend to have fewer bilateral interactions. Furthermore, our study indicates that the normal distributions of these interactions are independent of the network's specific structure, suggesting a universally applicable principle governing the variability of interactions in complex networks.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning has significant practical applications and has been extensively explored. Yet, its convergence largely relies on the assumption of Markovian systems, which is not always the case in real-world scenarios. The actor-critic model is prone to sample gradient estimates and often experiences slow convergence, especially when dealing with high-dimensional systems. The model's efficiency also heavily depends on the choice of action space, which can be challenging. Our research introduces an actor-critic framework combined with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampling to address these limitations. The HMC approach transforms the action space into a Gaussian distribution, facilitating the use of automatic gradient or matrix logarithm. The model's performance is then evaluated on a 2D pendulum system and a 3D robotic system, demonstrating notable improvement in sample efficiency and easier action space exploration.

Theorem 1.1 (Twin Prime Conjecture): There are infinitely many prime numbers $p$ such that $p$ and $p+2$ are prime numbers.

A simple proof of Theorem 1.1 is proposed and supported by an important lemma. 

Lemma 1.1: For any natural number $k$, there are infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that $n$ and $n+k$ are not prime numbers.

The simplicity of the proposed proof of Theorem 1.1 relies heavily on this lemma. Unfortunately, the infinity of natural numbers $n$ such that $n$ and $n+k$ are not prime numbers cannot be determined for any given $k$. However, for specific values of $k$ equal to 2, 3, or 5, a finite upper limit to these natural numbers $n$ has been verified through extensive prime number counting up to a very large prime number $P$. 

Therefore, if Theorem 1.1 is true, then the natural number $k$ should be 2. Consequently, a proof of Theorem 1.1 can be achieved by first proving the correctness of the above statement for any natural number $k$.

This paper addresses the navigation challenge in simulated search and rescue missions, focusing on environments where sonar technology is employed to map underground tunnels and similar spaces. Our proposed solution aims to facilitate the movement of a robot through these areas in real-time, incorporating sonar data for precise mapping and obstacle avoidance. To achieve this, we devised a navigation controller with multiple layers, incorporating sonar data within a machine learning-based framework that ultimately enables the robot to efficiently traverse the space. To implement this controller, we selected popular libraries and executed the simulation within the Gazebo framework, utilizing a Turtlebot-equipped with sonar sensors for the simulation setup.

Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the outermost discovered, exhibits an irregular orbit. Nereid was spotted in 1973 by the Voyager 2 spacecraft, but was missing from observations until its re-detection in 2013 by the New Horizons mission. Extensive analysis of the capture factor and dilution model for phyllosilicates on Nereid is presented. By employing a simplified model, spectra blending of various water- and methane-ice spectra with three distinct organic compounds was analyzed. This was followed by an inverse modeling of phyllosilicates on Nereid to determine the water- and methane-ice thicknesses, using constraints from two distinct capture factors. Our findings indicate that Nereid's surface is composed of up to 60% water ice, with additional organic compounds, where the length of the spectral window allows for the determination of ice thickness at 100-300 micrometers. This is consistent with those found on other Neptune satellites, particularly Halimede, with Nereid exhibiting a notable exception in its low-ice content for portions with high albedos. By analyzing capture factors, it is evident that non-organic compounds on Nereid cover up phyllosilicates, with their detection dependent on several factors including the thickness of water- and methane-ice. Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of order $n \geq 2$, consisting of elements from the finite field $F(q)$ of order $q \geq 2$. Additionally, let $V_{2n}(q)$ be the free left module of the form $V_{2n}(q) \simeq \mathcal{R}_n(q) \otimes_{F(q)} F(q)^{*(1)}$. Studies have proven the existence of an affine plane over $V_{2n}(q)$ and further show that a projective plane over $\mathcal{T}_n(q)$ can be derived from this affine plane by imposing a faithful module with a specific set of invertible elements. Conversely, it is also demonstrated that any overfield of $V_{2n}(q)$ containing an affine plane of this form will necessarily have its projective line isomorphic to $\mathcal{T}_{n+1}(q)$.

In 1986, Pawlikowski established crucial requirements for constructing continuous real functions within specific parameterized sets. We build upon his work by introducing models that rely on these conditions and using them to create an ordering system. Our order, an extension of Tukey-order, is used to construct upper models within a specific family of interval orders. It was discovered that the existence of upper models is tied to second-countable spaces with unique path-lifting properties. Additionally, our models provide a continuous function that cannot be obtained through any countably-finite construction.

A new method is proposed to improve a key concept in causal inference, called negativity, in the context of changing treatment policies over time. Unlike existing techniques that optimize a causal value related to negativity and require knowledge of treatment policies, this proposed method, called the Bayesian Optimality Criterion, allows for an unstructured treatment policy without this requirement. We examine the uniqueness of its optimal solutions and offer conditions under which they exist. We also investigate a simplified version of this problem, in which the treatment policy is fixed and only needs to be optimized. This simplified problem is related to a well-known optimization technique called the Bayesian information criterion. We illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed method through simulations and a real-world study involving patients with acute conditions who have undergone surgery.

Dualities between stationary-torsion-free nonprime modules over certain types of rings have been investigated and their implications on homological properties examined. Specifically, a duality between nonprime modules over a ring with a certain characteristic property is discovered, which suggests the presence of dualities for all nonprime modules. This leads to the conclusion that a particular ring has a certain homological property everywhere. Our research focuses on resolving this duality and determining the ring's homological property. Alongside, we investigate the dualities involving torsion-free modules. Additionally, a duality between nonprime ideals in a ring with a certain characteristic property is discovered. This duality is found to have several consequences, including the incidence of a particular ring with a certain homological property. Our research also examines the consequences of this duality on homological properties of rings with a certain characteristic property.

A study on the entanglement and nonorthogonality within a modified $E_8$ system is conducted, where a fixed set of states in a 16-dimensional space, labeled $E_8^{(1, R)}$, is examined. It's noted that these states avoid zero projections when interacting with a particular subset of matrices and form a 16-dimensional space, distinct from the original $E_8$ system. Furthermore, a specific analysis of entanglement within this system is performed, followed by a investigation of nonlocality using a proposed set of interactions, resulting in a finding that indicates a higher degree of nonlocality compared to a previously related system. Finally, a potential connection is drawn between nonlocality and the complexity of these systems, suggesting that nonlocality could be enhanced through complexification.

A model has been developed that incorporates the effects of disorder and electron interactions within a two-dimensional non-Abelian smooth band system with a fixed topological characteristics. It was discovered that the system transitions into a phase of multiple coexistence of fermionic condensates as the level of electron interaction increases, particularly when protected by a sufficient band curvature. Additionally, it was found that this phase exhibits non-Abelian properties and that its edges exhibit chiral, non-Abelian topological characteristics. It was further determined that multiple coexistence of fermionic condensates is realized through a Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer mechanism, and that a system transition into a superconducting state of collective mode is possible at a higher level of electron interaction. Lastly, it was assessed that the system's topological characteristics and the non-Abelian properties of its edges are resilient to the effects of interaction-induced band folding.

In 1930, Polya established that a continuous, homogeneous function of degree d on the positive real numbers is either symmetric or anti-symmetric. We extend Polya's theorem to groups of locally compact, Abelian structures that are one-dimensional and possess linked properties.

Presence-absence data characterised by a large number of species-presence indicators poses significant analytical challenges, primarily due to the theoretical and computational intricacies associated with such data sets. These data types are commonly found in scientific fields such as ecological research, genetic studies and statistical chemistry. This research paper evaluates the efficacy of widely recognized clustering methods suitable for such data sets and introduces an innovative evaluation strategy incorporating both internal metrics and external validation tools. The internal metrics assess the resulting clusters using conventional criteria, whereas the external metrics simulate human judgment through the consideration of data-generated class models. The simulated classes mirror the data collection process, where data points are grouped based on prescribed class affiliations. The results show that clustering approaches indicating hierarchical or absence-based data patterns perform better overall, with certain methods excelling in specific inner structures. The presence of species data is better captured by clustering evaluations emphasizing clustering purity, while the clustering approaches often fail to outperform each other in such scenarios. These findings could have far-reaching implications for the scientific communities generating such data sets.

In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB-D data still presents challenges due to the increased computational burden and difficulty in balancing features from both color and depth signals. This paper proposes an efficient and unified framework that effectively integrates cross-attention, cross-encoding, and cross-fusion mechanisms to tackle these issues, ultimately achieving an optimal balance between performance and efficiency. By disentangling the encoding and representation processes and harnessing the potential of recurrent neural network, our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on various datasets while being remarkably efficient in terms of computational cost and memory requirements. The source code of our approach can be freely accessed at the GitHub repository.

The second dataset from the 2019 SemEval Social Bias and Hate Speech Challenge was used to test the performance of three distinct strategies in identifying aggressive language on Twitter. The task necessitated the use of binary classification, where a post was either classified as containing aggressive language (present) or not (absent), from a three-category original classification that included mild, moderate, and severe aggression. Our approach involved a BERT-based transformer model and two support vector machines, one utilizing frequency counts and the other, the bigram matrix. The combination of these strategies in an ensemble resulted in a macro F1 score of 0.8233, securing 13th and qualifying our team for the final round in the competition. In the subsequent round, our ensemble performed better than 10 out of 18 submissions in the SBS subgroup, while in the HSL subgroup, our ensemble outperformed 7 out of 29 submissions.

A number, N, is defined as palindromic if its decimal representation reads the same way forward and backward. In this study, we examine numbers of n digits that quote other numbers of n digits, with those numbers exhibiting palindromicity or not. Firstly, we establish that both a palindromic N and its quotient are palindromic. Conversely, if not both, but either of these conditions holds true, we categorize N as 'half-palindromic'. Similarly, we define a non-palindromic N as exhibiting the property that its decimal representation does not read the same way forward and backward. In contrast to N's decimal representation, the decimal representation of its quotient may or may to read the same way forward and backward as the quotient's digits. In the case of N being palindromic, this means the decimal representation of the quotient may or may not be palindromic. In the case of N being half-palindromic or non-palindromic, this means the decimal representation of the quotient may or may not be palindromic as well. We aim to explore these phenomena and present related results.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Typically assuming a single energy spectrum, CT technology may not always accurately produce satisfactory results, particularly when scanning materials exhibiting multiple polyenergetic spectra. Our proposed framework seeks to simultaneously address four interconnected reconstruction tasks: it considers a weighted sum of data and golden-angle binomially weighted measurements to restore a CT image, incorporates a non-convex, physics-based forward model to handle varying material spectra, employs a contrastive learning approach to improve iterative gradient descent convergence, and treats material decomposition as a self-organizing map task. Our framework, evaluated using simulated data, has shown promising results in performing four distinct reconstruction tasks and has demonstrated improved performance compared to conventional iterative deep learning and contrastive learning methods.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR), though established, still faces obstacles in regions with limited resources. To overcome this challenge, this research introduces an innovative approach for HTR system development. Typically, HTR systems are trained using datasets that require extensive effort to create and label. To circumvent this challenge, this research proposes an unsupervised training method that utilizes real-world events, such as voting, to instantly obtain compositional data. These events are then simulated using an automatic handwriting system to produce relevant labels. The process is demonstrated with a simple 3-digit recognition system. The efficiency and effectiveness of this method were verified through experiments involving simulations of real-world data. The results show that the approach can generate high-quality data and achieve high accuracy, comparable to systems trained on synthetic data with ground truth labels.

To merge results from ab initio method computations for heavy nuclei with small core calculations, a new approach called the full $T$-method is proposed. This method combines accurate finite nucleon-nucleon potential calculations with small core scattering phases and large space ground state correlations, enabling the merging of calculations for large closed-shell nuclei and their single-particle or single-hole excitations. The efficiency of the full $T$-method is demonstrated by applying it to the excitation energy of the neutron $\beta$-decay in $^{16}$O.

Concepts in topological quantum phenomena often face misconinterpretations due to the lack of clear understanding. The Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, serving as the quintessential model for topological quantum phenomena, is examined to clear up common confusions. Basic assumptions of the model are analyzed, its band structure and topological invariants are explored, and prominent misconceptions are addressed through the solution of common puzzles.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space and the weighted Bergman spaces of analytic discs in C^2. A novel approach has been adopted, focusing on the operator's action on its image under the Riemann mapping theorem. This methodology enables a direct comparison of the operator's compactness with that of the original mapping. This technique has yielded new, non-trivial examples of compact composition operators. Furthermore, in addition to providing a straightforward metric representation of compactness, this framework facilitates exploration into the continuity of compactness among composition operators. Specifically, it is demonstrated that compactness is a continuous characteristic within a particular subclass of composition operators that map one-dimensional intervals to one-dimensional intervals.

We derived a two-loop amplitude for four gravitons in supergravity from the AdS$_5\times$S$^5$ background, utilizing the Strassler formula. The formula expresses the amplitude as a sum of two-loop six-point amplitude in $\mathcal{N=}4$ super Yang-Mills theory. We verified that the amplitude is consistent with the standard two-loop supergravity results provided by Berghofer et al and by Zuber. Additionally, we found that by applying the AdS/CFT correspondence, the boundary dual of the supergravity amplitude is the same as the two-loop finiteness of the six-point amplitudes in various strata of the Grassmannian, as identified by Alvarez-Gaumé et al and by Delgado et al. This suggests that certain six-point amplitudes in the six-dimensional superconformal series are finitely calculable at any loop order.

This paper introduces DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator designed for use on GPUs with thousands of processing units. It is unique in that it caters to the unique memory needs of object-based programming models, while also including features that guarantee consistent memory allocation. To optimize performance, it leverages a self-organizing approach that eliminates the need for a central authority to manage memory, allowing for more efficient use of device memory. By employing inter-thread communication and a innovative strategy for handling full bins, DynaSOAr ensures that memory allocation is fair among threads. We implement DynaSOAr on top of CUDA and conduct several experiments that validate its performance. Specifically, it outperforms a leading industrial-strength memory allocator by a margin of at least 2.3 times when allocating large numbers of small structs, and by a margin of at least 1.6 times when allocating larger arrays of type int. To give context to these results, the average real-world CUDA application allocates memory at a rate of 11.2 MB per second, while the allocator we compare against manages this with a rate of 7.4 MB per second. Consequently, DynaSOAr provides a notable improvement in memory allocation efficiency, thereby reducing the overhead and enabling more parallel computations that were previously restricted by memory allocation bottlenecks. As a result, it leads to considerable performance gains of 1.6 times, thereby enabling the computation of certain industrial-strength applications up to 3.3

A single choice of exotic $U(1)_X$ charge for each of the three generations can be made by following the rules derived from SO(10) grand unified theory. This rule states that the charges of the three generations must add up to a multiple of the smallest non-trivial value, which in this case is 3. Additionally, any standard model gauge-symmetry extension that respects SO(10)$ U(1)_X$ gauge invariance does not introduce any new choices for the exotic $U(1)_X$ charge, whereas certain popular variations such as the Pati-Salam model offer additional choices. Within the standard model and minimal $U(1)_X$ dark matter frameworks, we identify the possible charges for the three generations of SO(10) matter multiplets that satisfy the rules of charge consistency and minimality. This includes cases with one, two, and three family charges below 25, and we explore the associated phenomenology. This work also clarifies the relationship between SO(10)$ U(1)_X$ and E6, and the consequences for neutrino mass generation are examined. Finally, we discuss the potential discoveries of exotic states at the LHC, such as $SU(2) L$-octets with unusual electric charges.

A detailed analysis of a cane tube's mechanical properties has been conducted, 
investigating the relationship between internal pressure and hoop/warp resistance.
The study employed a refined analytical model to calculate tensional forces 
resulting from pressurization, followed by stability assessments using the Euler-Columb 
formula. To validate findings, a relevant experiment was designed and carried out.

In various fields, Bayesian networks have seen wide-ranging applications for modeling and decision-making, yet they often fail to account for uncertainties inherent in data, which can lead to inaccurate results. Our research focuses on enhancing the reliability of these networks for classification tasks by providing guarantees on their performance under uncertain conditions. Our approach, which utilizes probabilistic circuits as a concise representation of uncertainty, involves analyzing the effects of epistemic uncertainty on network queries. By addressing the issue of maximization, we developed an efficient algorithm that ensures optimal classification outcomes with maximum confidence, which led to the creation of a well-defined class of Bayesian networks, termed 'MaxCred'. This new class offers a framework for selecting networks that can withstand data uncertainty. Furthermore, we introduced an innovative metric, measuring the robustness of a network and its query results. Our experimental findings demonstrate the efficacy of MaxCred in achieving robustness guarantees, which proves to be valuable in identifying networks that can provide reliable classification answers.

Waves in a rigid medium do not undergo phenomena like diffraction, yet they can exhibit oscillations analogous to Bloch oscillations through Wannier-Stanley flux. Our theory demonstrates that this occurrence is feasible with ultrasonic waves if there is sufficient scattering within the medium, and we typically achieve this by utilizing a mobile ultrasonic projector and stationary receivers. Both theoretical and experimental studies validate the existence of these oscillations, and the observed results align well with the predicted outcomes.

In a generalised quadrangle, a code is a subset of the vertices with its minimum distance determined by the shortest path between distinct elements. The elements of this subset are divided into distinct sets based on their distance from the code itself. Given a linear code in a generalised quadrangle, if it remains transitive under the action of a group and has a specific ratio of non-code vertices to code vertices, it must be a neighbor-transitive code. This criterion has implications for codes within quadrangles derived from ovoids, spreads, and grids. Additionally, it is proven that if a linear code fulfilling these conditions is also an oval, it must either be a grid or a spread.

Our goal is to determine how the Central Molecular Zone's density changes in anisotropic directions using two-dimensional correlation functions. By analyzing the Corotating Frame data from the Parker spiral frame, we calculate how density varies in different directions over varying radial and vertical distances. Our results indicate a significant increase in density towards the Galactic plane and a corresponding decrease in density radial to the plane by a factor of at least three. This significant radial density gradient may influence the Moon's dynamical evolution and confirm that anisotropic density is essential for understanding the CMZ's dynamics.

The interpretation of high-fluence X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy relies on accurately modeling non-linear effects. A rate model that simulates electronic excitation dynamics has been developed to account for specific processes such as exciton condensation and spin-flip scattering for various fluences of ultrashort X-ray pulses. Electronic groups are initially in a ground state and transition to an excited state at a specified rate, with subsequent applications of X-rays increasing the excited state population in accordance with the Beer-Lambert law. The model applies quantum statistical corrections to account for changes in the electronic groups' energy levels and spin degeneracy as excited state population grows. It also incorporates a quantum field theoretical approach to model spin-flip scattering, providing a basis for comparing experimental and modeled spectra. A thorough examination of the quantum behavioral changes is presented, along with recommendations for data acquisition and modeling protocols that could facilitate reliable data analysis.

A microtemperature sensor incorporating an inherent temperature-to-voltage converter was designed to reduce power consumption and eliminate the need for an external ADC. The design leverages a resistorless CMFB structure to increase input dynamic range and improves thermal stability. Utilizing a 0.6V to 1.8V supply voltage, this temperature sensor achieves a resolution of 0.24 degrees Celsius with an error margin of $\pm$1.4 degrees Celsius. The design was fabricated using a standard 0.5$\mu$m CMOS process technology and demonstrated an energy efficiency of 1.06 nanojoules per conversion on the silicon die. Furthermore, the design exhibits a fast conversion time of 0.22 microseconds and is highly resistant to noise with a 0.15 degrees Celsius NDR depth.

Quantum entanglement, a pivotal concept in quantum science, holds immense promise for future quantum technologies. Despite extensive research, numerous quantum systems remain unsuitable for entanglement generation due to limitations in existing methods. A new approach, known as quantum scissors, enables the extraction and modification of entangled states derived from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC), a widely available entangled resource. We integrate this technique with a technique called polarization framing to create a new device for generating polarized entangled photons. The new device can create entangled states of various polarization configurations rapidly and efficiently without the need for complex manipulation of SPDC. Additionally, it can create entangled states with specific properties, such as alignment of horizontal and vertical polarization modes, without the need for sophisticated measurement techniques. This new device has the potential to enable a range of applications in quantum information processing, including quantum computing, quantum teleportation, and quantum cryptography, by providing access to entangled photons in a reliable and predictable manner.

This paper investigates weakly spanner-type networks, specifically focusing on base w-degrees, to establish a lower bound in the number of bits required to construct a w-spanner of sublinear stretch in the binary realm. To address this concern, the researchers designed a family of 3-approximate, sublinearly-scaled additively-competitive weak spanners. To achieve this, an iterative method was employed to construct these spanners, utilizing a novel application of the Johnson's algorithm. Building upon prior work in obtaining Omega(n) lower bounds in the real numbers, the researchers established a binary realm Omega(n^k) lower bound, for any constant k. To derive this result, a probabilistic algorithm counting the number of linearly independent vectors in a linear combination was utilized.

Accurate classification of IoT devices is a critical requirement to ensure the security and integrity of IoT systems. Typically, distinguishing between IoT devices involves analyzing characteristic features, but choosing the right features to use can be a complex task. Existing methods for feature selection are usually based on a predetermined cost function and either ignore expenses or have an excessive number of them, which is unrealistic. Moreover, many of these methods are computational efficient but lack accuracy, or vice versa. This work introduces a novel, efficient approach to feature selection that is both cost-aware and accurate. Specifically, we propose a new metric called cost-wiseness, which helps choose the optimal feature subset for maximum gain with minimal expense. Our approach is based on the concept of local structural holes theory and utilizes a simple, unbiased method to calculate the centrality of each feature subset. By selecting features with local structural positions of high cost-effectiveness, we achieve subsets with low expense and high accuracy. Moreover, calculating the centrality of each subset allows us to efficiently prune expensive features and prevent exhaustive searching. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to various feature selection tasks, including those with imbalanced data.

Godel modal logic's complex model theory and the associated algebraic approach are less understood compared to other modal logics. This study delves into new classes of Godel modal and Kripke semantics models, along with their corresponding algebraic counterparts, all of which guarantee that the modal logic's semantics is duality-theoretic. These classes are based on two extensions of finite Godel algebras with an emphasis on their relational counterparts. These extensions originate from the literature on substructural or noncommutative modal logic. The study also explores the simultaneous treatment of these extensions and their counterparts for negation-free modal logic.

This research presents a novel and efficient method for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms or bilingual dictionaries. It overcomes the limitations of previous alignment techniques, which rely on extensive annotated education data or pre-trained translation models. Our proposed technique focuses on individual word translations and does not depend on sentence-level translations, making it suitable for models and domains where sentence-level translations are not available or cannot be predicted. Moreover, this method enables on-the-fly word alignment in domains with limited training data. Our experiments demonstrate that it can achieve comparable results to state-of-the-art techniques but with the added benefits of efficiency and domain adaptation.

We suggest an distorted resolvent algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium issues, with a distorted version of the resolvent being introduced based on a non-monotone proximal algorithm. This approach results in an infinite sequence that converges to a Nash equilibrium, and includes a parameter that influences its iterative process. We also explore the conditions under which finite convergence is possible and provide a range of numerical examples to illustrate its effectiveness.

I generate primordial black holes (PBHs) throughout a given mass range and density of matter in the universe, taking into account various factors such as the rate of neutrino production and inflationary patterns. For each PBH mass, I determine the initial density of matter in the universe and the rate of neutrino production that would result in dark matter consisting solely of PBHs of that mass. The program then evaluates these findings at multiple points in the parameter space to facilitate Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analyses and other studies. Furthermore, I demonstrate the effectiveness of model constraints that involve gravitational wave observations and apply various adjustments to account for potential biases in dark matter density measurements, which may be of interest in MCMC analyses.

We conducted molecular-dynamics simulations to investigate the phase behavior of wedge-like molecules, where each molecule consisted of four connected spheres represented by basic geometric shapes, in three-dimensional space. Dimentionsless potential with cutoff was applied for modeling molecule interactions. Our simulation results indicated the existence of four distinct phases: body-centered tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, and tetragonal phases. Additionally, we analyzed the conditions under which these phases occurred and found that the presence of splay modulations in the monoclinic phase could significantly affect its symmetry, leading to potential mesoscopic characteristics.

Several domain-specific recursive formulas have been developed, allowing for fast evaluation of distance-based interpolation and synthesis on the surface of the sphere. These formulas are tailored to take advantage of the sphere's symmetry and efficiently utilize memory by computing only one value at a time. While interpolating or synthesizing a point, we can simultaneously prepare the next value, thus avoiding unnecessary computations and memory allocations. These recursive methods are particularly suitable for use in iterative algorithms such as Loopy Belief Propagation and have been shown to provide a 50% reduction in computation time in such cases.

A long-standing issue with quantum imaging techniques is the presence of "dark" areas containing undetected photons in the reconstructed images. We developed a method to eliminate these "dark" areas by designing a single-pixel quantum visualization scheme that utilizes undetected photons for measurement. The proposed scheme employs two options: utilizing undetected photons for classical illumination or for quantitative measurement. Experimental results indicate that both methods can achieve comparable levels of visibility and efficiency. The employed technique might have implications for quantum information processing and coding, particularly for overcoming dark-state limitations.

The interaction between a liquid foam and a solid surface involves complex processes influenced by the friction between the two materials in question. This study investigates how the frictional interaction between a liquid foam and a solid surface is affected by the presence of surfactants. When surfactants are applied to a silicone oil and water mixture forming the foam, we observe a substantial decrease in the frictional force required to move a solid through the foam. This effect is more pronounced when the surfactants reduce the surface tension of the foam further, indicating that the decreased friction is primarily caused by a reduction in the foam's viscosity. When the surfactants are insufficient, leading to an increased range of values for the surface tension, the frictional force exhibits an intricate relationship with this variation. A possible explanation for this complex behavior is that the frictional force is influenced by two competing processes: the friction induced by the blocking of flow channels at higher surface tensions and an increased ease of flow due to reduced bubble sizes at lower surface tensions.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with metadata anomalies was utilized to develop an outcome prediction model. The dataset's irregularities were initially identified through statistical analysis and the Shannon entropy method. To diagnose skin cancer, a combination of convolutional neural networks and machine learning algorithms was applied, taking into account image features and metadata. The specific techniques employed included the transfer of pre-trained models, multi-channel CNNs, decision tree classification, random forest, k-nearest neighbors, support vector machines, and gradient boosting. The chosen models were selected following assessment of various algorithm candidates. The diagnosis model's effectiveness was evaluated using metrics including accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, AUC-ROC, and MCC from 10-fold cross validation. The dataset's metadata outliers were utilized to investigate their impact on model performance and demonstrate the model's capability to detect inliers among noisy data samples.

We measured the lifetime of electrons that have been perturbed in sodium, a metal with very weak electronic interactions. Our findings agree with theoretical predictions from the relaxation-time approximation that uses the density of states near the Fermi level. Additionally, we calculated the density of states and found that it exhibits fluctuations at very short ranges due to sodium's complex structure. These fluctuations are a result of the large density of magnetic impurities in pure sodium, which can be minimized by adding small amounts of gadolinium to it.

Building on a novel theory, a novel method has been developed to bridge the gap between two Hamiltonian dynamics in phase space. This theory overcomes traditional limitations associated with a decrease in phase space volume, particularly during free expansion. In contrast to traditional trajectory analysis, our method leverages the underlying deterministic nature of dynamics. It deforms each trajectory type (quasi-periodic, periodic, and chaotic) in phase space to match the target Hamiltonian's structure. To accomplish this, the trajectory is altered by consistently scaling the time axis, resulting in non-uniform time steps. This approach employs the underlying structure of the Hamiltonian dynamics, unlike traditional methods which rely on probability distributions. A detailed analysis of free expansion dynamics illustrates the method's efficiency and accuracy. By utilizing this method, the underlying structure of the initial distribution can be precisely identified from an observed, coarsely sampled trajectory, even in scenarios where the initial distribution is unknown or poorly sampled.

This passage provides an in-depth, detailed computation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll examine graph weights based on the underlying graph type, as well as the local structure of the symplectic Poisson configuration, which corresponds to a simplification of a specific section 4.3's consideration. While our analysis primarily concentrates on the weight's real value aspect, we also explore an alternative formulation that enables the representation of weights as rational functions. This weight formulation can be efficiently computed by examining the local symplectic structure's configuration, which proves particularly convenient for weight determination.

We explore solitary waves known as "nanoptera," characterized by extremely small amplitudes, that can occur in two systems: a model of gentle oscillations in elastic beams and a model of vibrating strings with evenly spaced imperfections. In both cases, we analyze how the modes of vibration become distorted due to a slight increase in energy input, revealing that the rates at which this distortion changes vary significantly. By examining how solitary waves move past each other, we uncover new insights into how forces interact at very small scales, shedding light on observed phenomena in experiments that involve gently shaking plates made of soft material and studying the movement of waves at very small amplitudes in those settings.

Extra dimensions beyond our familiar three-dimensional space can give rise to new types of particles called quasi-Brane Klein-Gordon (qBKG) bosons. Our investigation focuses on the classical collisions occurring when these bosons originate from nearby universes or cosmological fluctuations. We derive exact expressions for their dispersion relations, which we then use to analyze their interaction with our universe's cosmic background radiation. Interestingly, our findings indicate that the natural cutoff associated with the bosons' occupation number is significantly higher than the typical energy scale of our cosmos. This makes it possible for these bosons to occupy our universe until quite recently, thereby potentially explaining large-scale structure perturbations. In particular, our analysis reveals that the bosons' wavelength is much larger than our universe's radius, which implies that their wave functions decay rapidly due to the cosmological expansion. Consequently, their occupation number remains large until recently, specifically until our universe's age was about 17 times the Planck time. Moreover, their wave-like interactions with our cosmos's cosmic background radiation may induce observable quasi-Deliberate Radial Fine Structure. Our theory also predicts the presence of quantum relic fluctuations, which can leave lasting imprints on our universe's cosmological inflationary patterns.

A graph is considered accordion-like if it consists of a pair of nearly identical cubic graphs connected by exchanging vertices. This unique structure leads to intriguing properties and questions surrounding these graphs. The main findings of this study involve proving that a graph exhibiting this accordion structure has a unique tight spanning cycle, proving it is perfect pairing, and demonstrating that two such graphs are identical if and only if they share the same set of spanning cycles. Additionally, the study creates a new class of quartic graphs by applying a circulant construction and shows that this construction preserves the perfect pairing property.

In quantum walks, the dynamic process of a wave function's spread, akin to diffusion in the classical world, follows Markovian scaling. This process is analogous to classical Brownian motion but differs from the dynamic behavior observed in quantum systems, which often display anomalous diffusion. The dynamic scaling exponent found in quantum walks is typically bound by one, resulting from the conservation of probability and Coherent SuperDiffusion's unbounded growth rate. Three-state quantum walks offer an excellent opportunity to gain profound understanding of dynamic scaling as they are capable of exhibiting a wide range from subdiffusion to Coherent SuperDiffusion. Their diffusion characteristics are heavily influenced by initial states and the nature of the coin operator. The dynamic scaling behavior of three-state quantum walks was studied using non-Brownian, non-Coherent SuperDiffusion, and non-anomous diffusion processes. The resulting data, which includes the non-Coherent SuperDiffusion phenomenon, specifically in the case of $q\phi$ dynamics, contradicts previous predictions. The correct determination of the dynamic scaling exponent was achieved through the application of non-anomous diffusion equations and the use of wave function's quadratic moment. The resulting values of the quadratic scaling exponent, which describes the dynamic scaling behavior of three-state quantum walks, shows a wide range of values, resulting in the classification of possible diffusion processes.

Vision transformers (ViTs) excels at semi-supervised and self-supervised learning tasks due to its ability to leverage various large-scale image transformations, like MoCo, where it leverages momentum-encouraged contrastive loss to produce feature representations beneficial for learning. In the realm of semi-supervised image classification, ViT surpasses convolutional networks (ConvNets) when utilizing maximum likelihood supervised loss, but when incorporating self-supervised momentum coordinate (Momentum COAttn) in the model, it surpasses ConvNets and sometimes surpasses even the supervised ViT variants. Furthermore, extracting attribute information from the model and incorporating it into the self-supervised loss through attribute momentum coordination (AMCo) yields a significant boost in semi-supervised image classification performance, highlighting the significance of attribute structure in the learning process of ViTs. Consequently, the development of large-scale self-supervised pretraining strategies should prioritize momentum-encouraged learning methods that exploit both position and attribute structures within the ViT model.

A unified model for dark energy and dark matter, called the Unified Dark Substance model, is proposed and validated with observational data. This model incorporates a single function, determined by a single parameter, to describe both dark components in terms of the Universe's equation of state. To prevent divergence, dissipation is introduced into the Unified model. By analyzing phase space, we confirm that the model has an effective equilibrium point. Furthermore, we tested and confirmed the model's correctness with multiple parity transformations. Our study shows that the model provides an accurate fit to Cosmic Chronometers data, Lambda-CDM model constraints, and Planck TT data, including corrections for bias and redshift. We also found a specific range for the Unified model's dissipation parameter, allowing it to be consistent with cosmic observations.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has an issue when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, specifically those represented by the notation $L_{p,x}^{s,1}$ or $\Lambda^{s}_{p,x}$ with $p\in [1,2]$ and $s>1+\frac{1}{p}$ being a real number. This proof is simpler and based on earlier work by Catale and Muration, in contrast to previous arguments found in the literature.

Recent breakthroughs have made it possible for generative models to produce high-quality artificial images and videos through manipulation in latent space, but the quality often varies greatly depending on the quality of the training data. Since selecting excellent data is impractical for large-scale projects, we need new techniques to maintain high quality standards automatically. Our innovative stable diffusion algorithm enables the exclusion of low-quality data during training, effectively incorporating only high-quality images into the model. By promoting high-quality data, it promotes high-quality results when manipulating images. Additionally, to enhance training efficiency, we have developed an algorithm to split data into sub-sets with consistent semantic properties, resulting in more consistent results when applying latent space manipulation. Our model outperforms state-of-the-art models by a significant margin, as shown in extensive experiments on multiple datasets, including code-quality, protein-fold prediction, and semantic image manipulation.

Recent advancements in image processing technology have enabled the development of reversible image concealment techniques, allowing both concealed images and original contents to be accurately recovered after implementation. Unfortunately, traditional concealment methods often necessitate permanent modification to the input data, resulting in irreversible changes. In contrast, reversible concealment methods, characterized by recovery rates exceeding 98%, have become increasingly common. A novel approach is presented in this study that incorporates Bayesian neural networks to dynamically determine the optimal convolution kernel for an adaptive and efficient concealment method. Experimental results confirm the superior reversible performance of this method in comparison to state-of-the-art techniques.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we apply low-energy effective field theories to descriptions of neutrino interactions and dark matter properties. Our study of J/ψ decays into a photon and invisible matter reveals the considerable impact of non-zero neutrino masses on this process. Moreover, we find that dark matter-induced decays are more pronounced when dark matter weights approach a value equal to the photon weight. Our analysis also highlights the importance of precise measurements of the branching ratio and total decay width to clarify whether J/ψ decays into invisible matter are primarily caused by neutrinos or dark matter.

The Sun's photosphere contains tiny high-brightness points known as magnetic bright points (MBPs), which are primarily caused by the effects of partial ionization and the dynamic transfer of energy between the convective and photospheric layers. To understand MBPs, researchers analyzed data from the SOT on board the Hinode telescope, focusing on solar photospheric intensity images. After applying the Synchrotron model and correcting for noise, they selected areas with high MBP densities and conducted a statistical analysis. The resulting distribution showed two distinct peaks, one narrow and one broad, confirming earlier predictions that MBPs would follow a biparametric distribution. The wider peak would contain fake MBPs produced by image processing and proper accounting for these fake points would require more advanced methods.

Human vision can filter out movement caused by his or her own movement or the movement of the surroundings, a process known as minimal attention or focus. There's an interesting connection between how humans handle movement and the methods used in computer science for tracking objects while compensating for the camera's movement, a process known as structure-from-motion. We've developed a new, simplified model that combines focus and object tracking, which we've tested by creating artificial scenes that mimic real scenes captured through video footage of insects in motion. We've demonstrated that this focus model can effectively eliminate the movement caused by the camera, allowing us to analyze its underlying rules and similarities with object recognition models that take movement into account, a process known as slam.

Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries and ordinary matter through kinetic mixing result in the creation of long-lived magnetic monopoles, weighing approximately milligauss, and evaporating at temperatures near $\mu^{-1} \sim 1-100\,\mu\mathrm{eV}$. Monopoles of this magnitude can be produced in sufficient quantities to explain the persistence of galactic magnetic fields. As these monopoles break spatial symmetry, they act as efficient generators of cosmic magnetic fields, and their presence is detectable in measurements of the galactic magnetic field's diffusion rate or radius. Our investigation encompasses the magnetic monopole's charge, mass, and interaction strength, and calculates the monopole's action under resummation, yielding substantial consequences for particle physics and cosmology.

The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory Consortium (EOC) satellites provide highly detailed images of the Earth's environment, driving demand for highly accurate weather forecasting models. To meet this need, advanced models are required that can effectively analyze spatial and temporal patterns in the vast amounts of data provided by the EOC satellites. To address this challenge, a novel framework called SWC-Attention (SWCA) has been developed, based on a transformer architecture that utilizes a distinct cross-attention module. To improve efficiency, it breaks down sequences into fixed-length segments and processes them through overlapping windows, enabling parallel processing of sequential data. Additionally, a depth-wise separation technique is applied to unlock the deep sequential structure within each segment, enabling the model to capture both local patterns and longer-term trends. Experimental results show that the SWCA framework outperforms leading models by accurately predicting weather patterns for the next 6 hours.

In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a basis exists for dark matter that is stable due to accidental laws of physics protecting it. Specifically, we investigate three-Higgs-doublet models with an $S_3$ symmetry, determining the number of scalar bosons and potential, while also deriving the scalar potential's minimum conditions, including constraints on stability and the dark matter candidate's quark-mediated interactions. We calculate the dark matter-nucleus scattering cross-section and find the results to be largely determined by the $S_3$ symmetry, with the presence of a fully active inert scalar rendering the dark matter stable and potentially detecting dark matter with next-generation direct detection experiments being feasible. Additionally, we confirm that the dark matter is solely interacted with the standard model through the heavy $S_3$-odd scalar boson, making it fully invariant and thus eligible for dark matter detection via its loop-mediated interactions with the standard model fermions.

The PPT quadrilateral conjecture is a theory about entangled quadruplets of qubits, which have distinct characteristics in terms of positive partial transpose. According to the conjecture, such entangled quadruplets are only possible in scenarios where they exhibit non-separability in all possible bipartite divisions. In cases where entanglement is maximized, the PPT quadrilateral conjecture has been proven, along with a number of other insights into entangled quadruplets. However, the situation remains uncertain in other cases and our understanding of positive partial transpose and its relationship with entanglement remains limited.

In neurons, the process of removing excess substances is crucial for maintaining optimal conditions, but disruptions can lead to abnormal blockages affecting signal transmission. To analyze and address these issues, we develop a optimization model, constrained by partial differential equations, that simulates the movement of substances and prior research has demonstrated its effectiveness in optimizing parameters for uniform distribution. This study extends that approach by incorporating boundaries that reflect the complex structure of neural cells, and incorporates traffic jams modeled by means of congestion boundaries. A novel cost function is introduced to account for "traffic jams" and reference distributions are established to measure deviations from optimal substance distribution. We establish the optimization model's feasibility and determine optimal conditions, before verifying the performance of our method in a relevant numerical experiment.

Significant advancements in network analysis have yielded various metrics capable of
capturing complex relationships between entities in diverse domains. Yet, many of these
metrics suffer from a lack of clear practical implications, rendering them largely
theoretical. This study bridges this gap by developing and applying a new metric called
NeMo, which effectively captures co-occurring patterns of significance within a
network. Our proposed metric, NeMo, serves as an accessible and easy-to-compute
alternative to traditional fisher information-based measures, and demonstrates
promising results in the realm of corporate event-driven finance, where it facilitates
the identification of market movements foreseen by experts.

In a binary system consisting of a white dwarf and a black hole, a white dwarf's surface will emit matter and energy that radiate towards Earth. There's a specific scenario in which a white dwarf loses mass at a steady rate, causing its surface to shrink and increasing its temperature, resulting in a steady spectral distribution of emission. However, this situation is rare in space and can be replicated by assigning a steady mass loss rate to a white dwarf's non-rotating model, which has an uniform surface temperature. By assuming a black body emission pattern, a white dwarf's spectral distribution can be calculated based on its temperature and surface area. Furthermore, this emission will be affected by absorption when it passes through the interstellar medium, and there's also a chance it'll be blocked by Earth's atmosphere, which means there's a minimum intensity of emission that can be detected from a white dwarf. There's a specific scenario in which a white dwarf's surface will emit matter and energy towards Earth, and that's when it's located at a specific distance and has a certain temperature, which corresponds to a mass loss rate that equals the loss caused by spherical photons travelling from the star's surface to Earth.

Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions with light hadrons and CP symmetry violations, can provide insight into these processes. The form factors needed for describing the hadronic part of these interactions are calculated using light-cone sum rules, incorporating recent advancements in hadronic light-cone wave functions and accounting for uncertainty through momentum integrations. The resulting form factors allow for the estimation of several quantities, such as the $\tau$-decay width into watermelon diagrams and the ratio of the square root of the decay width for the vector $\rho$ resonance over the charm resonance. Additionally, this work finds that form factors associated with the spin-flavor structure of the weak current are highly dependent on the specific wave function used, necessitating a more in-depth analysis to fully understand these interactions.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between $0$ and $1$ and $\beta$ is greater than $0$. The inverse of the metric $d_{\alpha,\beta}(A,B)$ obtained by applying the metric $d$ to sets $A$ and $B$ and then taking the minimum, over all pairs of elements $x,y$ in the disjoint union of $A$ and $B$, of the expression $1 - \min(\frac{Z_{\alpha}(x,A)}|A|,\frac{Z_{\beta}(x,B)}{|B|}$) has previously been studied for specific values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$. However, in this research, we present a general method to demonstrate that $d_{\alpha,\beta}(A,B)$ is a continuous function of the numbers $\alpha$, $\beta$, and the Jaccard distance is a specific instance of the metric $d_{\alpha,\beta}$ when $\alpha$ equals $0.2$ and $\beta$ equals $0.8$. Furthermore, we show that $d_{\alpha,\beta}(A,B)$ is equal to $1$ minus the normalized Kullback-Leibler divergence between the probability distributions $P_{\alpha}(A)$ and $P_{

Modern non-blurry-to-blurry deblurring methods are hindered by their inability to handle real-world blurred images effectively, partly due to the fact that they rely on the assumption that motion in an image remains constant, which isn't always true. In an attempt to overcome this limitation, we developed a method that utilizes a learning-based approach to blur sharp images for comparison with actual blurred images, allowing us to differentiate between motion-induced blur and other factors. When applied to a test image, our method generates multiple blurred versions that can be used to resolve blurry-to-blurry deblurring challenges, ultimately leading to improved deblurring performance. In addition, we found that our approach outperformed existing methods in blurry-to-blurry deblurring tasks and demonstrated faster processing speeds, making it more practical for real-world applications, or even directly applying it to actual blurred images, yielding state-of-the-art results, along with a clear understanding of motion-induced blur, for the first time.

In the field of Bio-Hardware Computing, it's becoming increasingly clear that employing biological systems for computation may offer a promising pathway to achieve significant advancements in processing capabilities while simultaneously reducing energy consumption and weight. However, the various sources of noise that affect biological signal propagation must be taken into account for stable operation. Research has demonstrated that systems with multiple sources of noise can learn through the process of learning, though the specific mechanisms of such learning processes remain poorly understood. Furthermore, there is currently a notable lack of existing literature that explores the use of biological systems for computational purposes, particularly in the context of neural networks. In order to bridge this knowledge gap, we have developed a simple model of learning, which can be implemented using DNA-based molecular systems that undergo serial activation, and have proven its efficacy through theoretical analysis and experimental validation. This model's performance has been shown to outdo a control sequence, demonstrating the capability to approximate the behavior of a famous mathematical function with accuracy rates exceeding 75 percent, even under extremely challenging conditions.

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill the openness property in the refined version, whereas the openness of elements within the refined version depends on the cardinality of sequences composing it. Additionally, the openness of the refined version itself solely depends on the openness of the original set, not its cardinality.

The growing number of scientific datasets is expected to reach 100 sextillion points by 2025, making them increasingly unfeasible to work with using today's most powerful computers. This trend is exacerbated by the fact that many datasets are typically only accessed and analyzed once, often being discarded afterwards, making Reproducibility a vital concern in this field. Since computers are becoming significantly faster, the main bottleneck in data analysis is shifting towards memory bandwidth, data movement, and computation cost. This research targets these issues by developing a new approach called Dataset Profiling, which provides tailored performance suggestions specifically tailored to each scientific dataset. Our innovative technique combines three unique strategies, including: (1) finding the optimal data transformation, (2) customizing memory allocation, and (3) adapting algorithms to accommodate a dataset's distinct features, all of which are determined through our proposed profiling process, thereby enhancing Reproducibility and providing a notable performance boost in scientific simulations. Our cutting-edge framework, called Profiler, is versatile and can be applied to various programming languages, including Fortran, Python, and C, as demonstrated by our extensive experiments, which showcase an average speedup of 2.3 times across numerous benchmark datasets, ultimately enabling Reproducibility and significant performance improvements in scientific data analysis.

Hadwiger's conjecture asserts that a graph with $n$ vertices that is at least $n$ colors must have a subgraph that is a complete graph with $n$ vertices. We strengthen this conjecture by claiming that a graph with $n$ vertices and at least $n$ colors must have a subgraph that is either complete or from another graph that is a complete graph with the same number of vertices. Our proof relies on a different argument presented in a different paper and changes a certain quantity to show the subgraph with the required properties exists.

This research introduces a novel smooth graph signal reconstruction approach using the generalized correntropy metric, derived from the Gaussianized probability density function. The kernel width in this method is adaptively determined using the bandwidth selection technique, which minimizes the upper limit of the derived correntropy gradient. This adaptive kernel width allows our approach to seamlessly switch between the original generalized correntropy-based graph signal reconstruction and the traditional optimal graph signal reconstruction. Moreover, a smoothed graph signal reconstruction framework is developed by incorporating the generalized correntropy-based graph signal reconstruction with a smoothing operator, which enhances resilience to noisy observations and node failures. The proposed scheme is shown to effectively converge to the optimal solution and outperform existing methods in both smooth graph signal reconstruction and generalized correntropy-based graph signal reconstruction, while also exhibiting improved robustness and computational efficiency.

To generate highly entangled atomic states of up to $N=16$ atoms using an entangled spinor Bose-Einstein condensate (2D array of qubits) and mitigate common detection limitations, a customized state preparation technique is developed. The method employs a unique sequence of $\pi/2$ and $\pi$ pulses applied to the atoms, leveraging a generalized binary tree structure to optimize the entanglement production process. The obtained states exhibit considerable levels of $m$-fold degeneracy and 2D symmetry, allowing for an efficient extraction of highly entangled subspaces even in the presence of detection uncertainties. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of a versatile tool for entangled state generation, which can be applied in various quantum information processing applications and might be challenging to replicate with quantum gate-based systems.

The primary goal of this research is to precisely estimate the first eigenvalue of the first Robin eigenvalue problem involving the Laplacian and a nonlinear smooth function in dimension $N \geq 2$, subject to specific boundary conditions on a domain $\Omega$ and its complement. A nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a general potential and a nonlinear diffusion term is studied using similar methods. These estimates are achieved by examining the nonlinear equation's symmetry and compactness properties, as well as constructing a family of trial functions based on the volume of the domain and its complement. This approach also enables the derivation of precise estimates for the first eigenvalue of the Laplacian and a nonlinear Schrödinger equation.

Deep Neural Network structures have gained prominence in various applications, but their success in graph-based datasets has been impeded by intricate design complexities. The Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GCNN) is particularly noteworthy due to its adaptability with irregular data structures like spatial data, social networks, and text documentation. Despite its effectiveness, the underlying process remains obscure, hindering further enhancements. We propose an intuitive explanation of the GCNN operation as an analytical matching filter method, illustrating how GCNN translates irregular data structures into manageable linear structures. This analysis reveals how GCNNs are susceptible to overfitting and utilize regularization, stroke order, and graph size. Our findings also suggest the inclusion of orientation and edge weight information in graph data. We validate these findings by evaluating various graph construction methods, including the popular k-NN method, and demonstrating their implications on model performance. The proposed matched filtering approach provides a clear understanding of GCNNs, enabling the development of optimized strategies for building graph data structures.

A novel approach called Deep Contextualized Self-learning (DCS) is proposed to mitigate the low resource learning limitation in Dependency Parsing (DP). The self-learning technique has shown success in sequence tagging tasks by reusing parsing results to guide token-level modeling, but it has not been directly applied to dependency parsing. The major obstacle of low resources in dependency parsing is the lack of sufficient supervision, particularly in the form of annotated trees, needed for the self-learning method. To overcome this issue, DCS breaks down into two interconnected components: a dependency parser and a self-learning model. The parser is trained in a traditional supervised manner, while the self-learning model leverages the parser's output as pseudo-annotations to fine-tune the parser, thereby exploiting local syntactic patterns within sentences. The DCS model was evaluated on 7 languages with limited resources and showed notable enhancements in parsing accuracy, outperforming the state-of-the-art parser, Universal Dependencies, and multiple modern parsing models.

We've investigated the $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ transition form factors using the light-front quark model with light-front quantization. Our approach calculates the entire set of form factors needed for describing $B\to D$ transitions and the resulting semileptonic decay rates will be presented. Our work confirms that the light-front quark model is in agreement with other theoretical methods such as soft collinear effective theory and potential models. We've further found that while the light-front quark model may not yield an exact zero-form factor at q^2=0, it provides a satisfactory approximation.

We're exploring a theory called $O(N)$ symmetry with a twist, where braiding affects signs, and applying these symmetries to Branes from Yang-Mills is our focus. Branes in this context are reimagined as distinct objects, each representing various symmetry transformations. Moreover, we've defined a method to translate symmetry breaches into Branes and realize that symmetry breaches can coexist. Our findings also imply that certain symmetry breaches can't be realized through Branes derived from Yang-Mills, but instead, require more intricate structures such as topological invariants. Similarly, we've identified similar shortfalls in Branes from Chern-Simons theory, revealing that certain symmetry breaches necessitate more complex elements than Branes can offer.
